findings.claim: SmolLM2-360M is a deep-thin GQA transformer: 32 layers, d_model 960, FFN 2560, 15 query heads / 5 KV heads (GQA 3:1), vocab 49,152, 8K context, TIED input/output embeddings, trained on 4T tokens single-stage. SmolLM2-135M is 30 layers, d_model 576, 9Q/3KV heads, 2T tokens. Explicitly follows MobileLLM's 'depth over width' recipe.
findings.source: arXiv 2502.02737 (SmolLM2) + HF config; ritvik19 Papers Explained 176
findings.numbers: 360M: 32L, d960, 15Q/5KV, FFN2560, vocab49152, 8K ctx, 4T tok, tied emb
findings.relevance: This is the closest analogue to the target 500-600M from-scratch design; its 49K vocab + tied embeddings + 32-layer deep-thin shape is a proven sub-1B blueprint the Kazakh model should match or exceed in depth.

findings.claim: Qwen3-0.6B-Base: 28 layers, hidden 1024, 16 query / 8 KV heads (GQA 2:1), FFN 3072, vocab 151,669 (BBPE), 32K context, 0.44B non-embedding params, tied embeddings, trained on 36T tokens across 119 languages. Adds QK-Norm and removes QKV-bias to stabilize small-scale training. Measured 32.8% on KazMMLU (user's grounding) — the strongest sub-1B baseline on Kazakh.
findings.source: HF Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B-Base card; arXiv 2505.09388 (Qwen3 Technical Report)
findings.numbers: 28L, d1024, 16Q/8KV, vocab151669, 32K ctx, 36T tok, 119 langs, non-emb 0.44B
findings.relevance: This is THE boundary to beat on Kazakh at ~600M. Its edge comes from 36T tokens + QK-Norm, not exotic architecture; the paper must beat 32.8% KazMMLU with ~3500x fewer Kazakh tokens, so tokenizer efficiency and transfer must carry the gap.

findings.claim: Gemma 3 270M deliberately spends ~63% of parameters on embeddings: ~170M embedding params (256K-token SentencePiece vocab) vs ~100M in transformer blocks. 32K context, sliding-window + global interleave, 6T training tokens, IFEval ~51.2%. Designed as a fine-tuning substrate, not a strong base LM — it scores 24.4% (near-random) on KazMMLU.
findings.source: Google Developers Blog (Introducing Gemma 3 270M); apxml.com/models/gemma-3-270m; arXiv 2503.19786
findings.numbers: 270M total = 170M emb + 100M blocks; vocab 256K; 6T tok; IFEval 51.2%; KazMMLU 24.4%
findings.relevance: Cautionary datapoint: a 256K multilingual vocab starves the transformer of capacity and yields near-random Kazakh knowledge. Argues AGAINST a giant multilingual vocab for a from-scratch Kazakh SLM — a compact low-fertility vocab (~50K) keeps params in the network.

findings.claim: Gemma 3 270M's exact layer count / d_model are inconsistently reported (apxml lists 12 layers, d_model 1024, but 256K×1024=262M would exceed the stated 170M embedding budget, implying d_model≈640). Head config also unverified.
findings.source: apxml.com/models/gemma-3-270m (conflicts with embedding-param arithmetic)
findings.numbers: claimed 12L/d1024/16 heads; embedding math implies d~640
findings.relevance: Minor — the load-bearing fact (embeddings dominate params) holds regardless; exact depth only matters if directly cloning Gemma 270M, which is not recommended.

findings.claim: LFM2-350M is a hybrid: 16 layers = 10 double-gated short-convolution blocks (depthwise conv, kernel 3) + 6 GQA attention blocks, hidden 1024, FFN 4608, 16Q/8KV heads, vocab 65,536 (byte-level BPE), 32K context, ~11T tokens. Scores MMLU 43.43, IFEval 65.12, GSM8K 30.10. LFM2-700M (d1536, 24Q/8KV) and LFM2-1.2B (d2048, MMLU 55.23) share the same 16-layer, 6-attention layout.
findings.source: arXiv 2511.23404 (LFM2 Technical Report), Table 1
findings.numbers: 350M: 16L (10 conv+6 GQA), d1024, FFN4608, vocab65536, 11T tok, MMLU43.4
findings.relevance: Shows the winning hybrid recipe at this scale: keep only ~6 attention layers, offload most token-mixing to cheap gated convolutions for 2x CPU throughput and low KV memory. Directly compatible with the user's Engram/mHC additions if they replace some attention layers with conv.

findings.claim: LFM2.5-350M (March 2026) pushes the token-to-parameter ratio to 80,000:1 by training a 350M model on 28T tokens plus scaled RL, running in under 1GB memory and beating models 2x its size on GPQA/MMLU-Pro/IFEval/GSM8K/MATH. Quality improves log-linearly from 350M to 24B on the same architecture.
findings.source: MarkTechPost 2026-03-31; aihola.com; distillabs.ai
findings.numbers: 350M params, 28T tokens (80,000:1), <1GB RAM
findings.relevance: The dominant lever at sub-1B in 2026 is extreme over-training (data quantity/quality), not parameter count. The Kazakh plan's ~9-10B tokens is ~3 orders of magnitude below this; closing it via cross-lingual/code/synthetic data is the single biggest risk-and-opportunity.

findings.claim: Falcon-H1-0.5B (0.52B): parallel-hybrid with BOTH attention and Mamba-2 in every layer — 36 layers, d_model 1024, 8 query / 2 KV attention heads + 24 Mamba-2 SSM heads (d_state 128, head dim 64), vocab 32,778, 16K trained context (256K max), 2.5T tokens. Leads sub-1B math/code (GSM8K 60.20, MATH-lvl5 15.18) and claims parity with 2024-era 7B models. Covers 18 languages but NONE are Turkic/Kazakh.
findings.source: arXiv 2507.22448 (Falcon-H1) Table 1; huggingface.co/blog/tiiuae/falcon-h1
findings.numbers: 0.52B: 36L, d1024, 8Q/2KV + 24 Mamba2, d_state128, vocab32778, 2.5T tok; GSM8K 60.2
findings.relevance: Proves a very deep (36L), very thin (d1024) parallel-hybrid can top sub-1B reasoning on only 2.5T tokens. Its 18-language set excludes Turkic — a market gap the Kazakh paper fills. Its 8Q/2KV (GQA 4:1) plus SSM is an aggressive KV-saving template.

findings.claim: MobileLLM-R1-950M (Sept 2025): deep-thin, 22 layers, 24 query / 6 KV heads (GQA 4:1), embedding dim 1536, FFN 6144, trained on only ~4.2T tokens yet matches/beats Qwen3-0.6B on MATH (74.0 vs 73.0) and leads LiveCodeBench (19.9 vs 14.9). Family also has 140M and 360M. Released under FAIR non-commercial license (not usable commercially).
findings.source: MarkTechPost 2025-09-14; VentureBeat; The Kaitchup
findings.relevance: Demonstrates that architecture + data curation beats raw token count (4.2T beats Qwen3's 36T on math). Validates GQA 4:1 and deep-thin at ~1B. Non-commercial license means it can be cited but not distilled-from for a shippable product.

findings.claim: MobileLLM's founding result: at sub-1B scale, DEPTH beats WIDTH — 30-42 layer models significantly outperform 12-layer models at equal ~125M params — and embedding sharing (tie input=output) plus GQA and SwiGLU give +2.7%/+4.3% accuracy at 125M/350M over prior SOTA. Contradicts the 'data/params are all that matter' view for tiny models.
findings.source: arXiv 2402.14905 (MobileLLM); ar5iv/aimodels summaries
findings.relevance: Core design law for the Kazakh SLM: prefer ~30-40 layers at moderate d_model (~1024-1280) over a shallow wide net. Tie embeddings. This is the highest-confidence architecture recommendation in the sub-1B literature.

findings.claim: IBM Granite 4.0 Nano (Oct 2025) ships 350M and 1B models in hybrid Mamba-2/Transformer (H) and pure-transformer variants — mostly Mamba-2 layers with a few attention layers — cutting memory >70% and doubling inference vs similar models, all Apache 2.0. The 350M variants score ~8 on IBM's agent-leaderboard average vs Gemma-3-270M's 6, and lead on IFEval/BFCLv3 (tool use).
findings.source: IBM announcement + MarkTechPost 2025-10-29; InfoQ 2025-11
findings.numbers: 350M & 1B; Mamba-2/Transformer hybrid; >70% less memory, 2x faster; Apache 2.0
findings.relevance: Second independent 2026 vote (with LFM2, Falcon-H1) that hybrid SSM/attention is the sub-1B efficiency default. Apache-2.0 makes Granite a legitimate distillation/comparison base, unlike MobileLLM-R1.

findings.claim: SmolLM3-3B architecture innovations transferable downward: GQA with 4 KV groups, NoPE (remove RoPE from every 4th layer) for long context, tied embeddings, no weight decay on embeddings, intra-document masking; trained 11.2T tokens, 128K context, but only 6 European languages (en/fr/es/de/it/pt) — no Kazakh.
findings.source: huggingface.co/blog/smollm3; learnopencv SmolLM3 explainer
findings.numbers: 3B, GQA 4 groups, NoPE every 4th layer, 11.2T tok, 6 langs
findings.relevance: NoPE-every-4th-layer and no-weight-decay-on-embeddings are cheap, proven tricks to fold into the Kazakh backbone. Confirms even a 2025 SOTA small model ignores Turkic — reinforcing the novelty of the target.

findings.claim: MLA (DeepSeek multi-head latent attention) compresses the KV cache far more than GQA while preserving per-head expressiveness: DeepSeek-V3 caches ~70KB/token (MLA) vs 192-328KB/token for GQA models (2.7-4.7x smaller); V2 reported 93% KV reduction vs MHA. MLA reconstructs full-rank per-head K/V from a shared latent (kv_lora_rank), unlike GQA which forces heads in a group to share identical K/V.
findings.source: Sebastian Raschka MLA gallery; knightli/DeepSeek analyses; martinalderson KV-cache history
findings.numbers: MLA 70KB/tok vs GQA 192-328KB/tok (2.7-4.7x); 93% vs MHA
findings.relevance: For a 32K-context Kazakh SLM, MLA (e.g. kv_lora_rank 256-512) is a stronger cache-reduction choice than GQA-2 and keeps more attention quality — a concrete upgrade over the current GQA 2:1 plan if implementation cost is acceptable.

findings.claim: No mainstream sub-1B SLM is trained for Kazakh/Turkic: Falcon-H1 (18 langs) and LFM2 (prioritizes ja/ar/ko/es/fr/de, base zh/it/pt) exclude all Turkic; Qwen3 nominally covers 119 langs incl. Kazakh but still only reaches ~33% KazMMLU at 0.6B; Gemma-3-270M and Llama-3.2-1B are at random (24-25%). Best OPEN KazMMLU results are large: Llama-3.1-70B 55.2%, Gemma-2-27B-IT 54.0%.
findings.source: arXiv 2502.12829 (KazMMLU); Falcon-H1 & LFM2 model cards; user grounding
findings.numbers: sub-1B on KazMMLU: Qwen3-0.6B 32.8%, others 24-25% (random); best open 55.2% (70B)
findings.relevance: Confirms the whitespace: a purpose-built 600M Kazakh model beating ~33% and approaching the 40-55% band would be genuinely SOTA-at-scale and novel — no competitor occupies sub-1B Kazakh.

findings.claim: Multilingual BPE/Unigram tokenizers fragment agglutinative languages badly: 2-16 tokens/word for agglutinative morphology vs ~1.2-1.4 for English; Gemma-2 ~2.2 tok/word on Turkish; words like 'evlerimizden' split into non-morphemic subwords. Morpheme-aware / grammar-first hybrid tokenization (root-affix dictionaries + phonological normalization + statistical merge) measurably raises 'pure token' rates on Turkic.
findings.source: arXiv 2603.05883 (VerChol grammar-first tokenization, abstract via search); Gemma-2 tokenizer analyses; arXiv 2605.29992 (Turkish tokenizer surgery)
findings.numbers: agglutinative 2-16 tok/word; Turkish ~2.2 (Gemma-2); English 1.2-1.4
findings.relevance: Directly validates the <2.0 tok/word target as both hard and high-value. A morphology-aware Kazakh tokenizer (respecting vowel-harmony allomorphs and Cyrillic Ә/Ғ/Қ/Ң/Ө/Ұ/Ү/Һ) is the single biggest lever to make ~9-10B Kazakh tokens act like far more effective compute.

findings.claim: TUMLU-mini is the right Turkic cross-lingual eval: a natively-authored (not translated) benchmark of 4-choice middle/high-school questions across 8 Turkic languages incl. Kazakh, Azerbaijani, Uzbek, Kyrgyz, Tatar, Uyghur, Karakalpak, Crimean Tatar; 38,139 total questions across 11 subjects.
findings.source: arXiv 2502.11020 (TUMLU, ACL 2025); github.com/ceferisbarov/TUMLU
findings.numbers: 8 Turkic langs, 11 subjects, 38,139 Qs, 4-choice
findings.relevance: Confirms the paper's secondary eval choice and enables a 'Turkic transfer' story — training on Kazakh + related Turkic data and reporting TUMLU-mini would strengthen the SOTA claim beyond a single language.

findings.claim: Qwen3.5 series launched March 2026 (Apache 2.0) spanning 0.8B-9B with a native ~262K context; the smallest tier is described as a ~0.8B natively multimodal model. Text-only sub-1B specs (layers/attention type/MLA-vs-GQA/training tokens) are not yet clearly documented in accessible primary sources.
findings.source: qwen.ai/blog?id=qwen3.5 (did not render); secondary: bentoml/datacamp 2026 SLM roundups; arXiv 2604.15804 (Qwen3.5-Omni)
findings.numbers: 0.8B-9B, ~262K ctx, Apache 2.0, released ~2026-03
findings.relevance: A likely late-2026 competitor at the ~0.8B tier; worth re-checking before publication so the paper's 'beats every best-tier ~500M SLM' claim explicitly addresses the newest Qwen. Treat exact specs as unverified.

findings.claim: GQA head-group ratios cluster tightly across 2025-2026 sub-1B SOTA: SmolLM2-360M 15:5 (3:1), Qwen3-0.6B 16:8 (2:1), LFM2 16:8, Falcon-H1-0.5B 8:2 (4:1), MobileLLM-R1 24:6 (4:1). Deeper/thinner models tend to push to 4:1 to reclaim KV memory; head_dim is consistently 64.
findings.source: cross-model synthesis: SmolLM2/Qwen3/LFM2/Falcon-H1/MobileLLM cards & papers cited above
findings.numbers: GQA ratios 2:1-4:1; head_dim=64 universal at this scale
findings.relevance: Gives a defensible design band: GQA 4:1 with head_dim 64 (or MLA) is the memory-lean choice; the current 2:1 plan is conservative and could go to 4:1 to fund more depth or Engram memory.

recommendations: Adopt a deep-thin backbone: target ~32-40 transformer layers at d_model 1024-1280 (head_dim 64), NOT a shallow-wide net. This mirrors SmolLM2-360M (32L/d960), Falcon-H1-0.5B (36L/d1024) and MobileLLM's depth>width law (+2.7-4.3% at sub-1B). At ~600M with a 50K vocab this leaves ~450-500M in the transformer stack.
Tie input/output embeddings (every sub-1B SOTA does) and apply NO weight decay to embeddings (SmolLM3). With a ~50K tokenizer this reclaims ~50-65M params vs an untied design to spend on depth.

Reject a giant multilingual vocab. Gemma-3-270M's 256K vocab burns 63% of params on embeddings and still scores random (24.4%) on Kazakh. Use a compact ~48-64K morphology-aware Kazakh(+Russian+code) vocab so params stay in the network.

Make the tokenizer the primary innovation: build a morpheme/grammar-aware Kazakh tokenizer (root-affix segmentation + vowel-harmony allomorph normalization + Cyrillic Ә/Ғ/Қ/Ң/Ө/Ұ/Ү/Һ handling) targeting <2.0 tok/word — multilingual BPE sits at 2-16 tok/word on agglutinative text, so this alone multiplies the effective value of the 9-10B Kazakh tokens. Report fertility vs Qwen3/Gemma tokenizers as a headline table.

Upgrade attention from GQA-2 to either GQA-4 (8Q/2KV or 16Q/4KV, head_dim 64, matching Falcon-H1/MobileLLM-R1) or MLA with kv_lora_rank 256-512. MLA cuts KV cache 2.7-4.7x vs GQA and preserves per-head expressiveness; at 32K context this is a concrete quality+memory win over the current 2:1 GQA plan and a stronger novelty hook than GQA alone.

Treat data quantity as the #1 risk. 2026 sub-1B SOTA trains on 11-36T tokens (LFM2.5-350M: 28T, 80,000:1). With only ~9-10B Kazakh tokens, over-train via repetition + heavy cross-lingual transfer (Russian, Turkic cousins, code, English) + synthetic Kazakh; cite the token-to-param gap explicitly and lean on tokenizer efficiency and Engram memory to compensate rather than pretending 10B competes with 28T.
Add QK-Norm and drop QKV-bias (Qwen3) to stabilize small-scale training — cheap, proven at 0.6B, and orthogonal to the Engram/mHC additions.

Consider replacing a subset of attention layers with cheap gated short-convolution or Mamba-2 blocks (LFM2: 10 conv + 6 attn per 16L; Granite 4.0 Nano; Falcon-H1 parallel hybrid). Three independent 2026 releases converge on 'mostly SSM/conv + a few attention layers' for 2x CPU throughput and >70% less KV memory — highly relevant for an edge-deployable Kazakh model, and composable with Engram at layers {2, L/4}.

Position the eval story around the actual whitespace: no sub-1B model targets Turkic (Falcon-H1 and LFM2 exclude it entirely; Qwen3-0.6B only reaches ~33% KazMMLU). Report KazMMLU (beat 32.8%), TUMLU-mini across 8 Turkic languages (transfer story), KazQAD F1, and FLORES-200 — and frame success as 'first purpose-built sub-1B model to break the ~33% Kazakh ceiling and approach the 40-55% band held only by 8-70B models.'

Before publication, re-verify the newest 2026 competitors (Qwen3.5-0.8B, any SmolLM3.x-small, LFM2.5, Granite 4.0 Nano refreshes) so the 'beats every best-tier ~500M SLM on Kazakh' claim is current — measure them directly on KazMMLU rather than trusting their general benchmarks.
open_questions: Exact Gemma-3-270M depth/d_model (12L/d1024 as apxml claims conflicts with the 170M embedding budget implying d~640) — verify against the real HF config if the design will reference it.

Qwen3.5-0.8B text-only architecture (dense vs MoE, MLA vs GQA, training tokens, Kazakh KazMMLU score) is not documented in accessible primary sources as of this search — needs a direct model-card/technical-report check before it can be cited as a beaten baseline.
Falcon-H1-0.5B's 32,778 vocab seems small for an 18-language model (larger Falcon-H1 sizes use bigger vocabs); confirm whether the 0.5B genuinely uses a 32K vocab or the table row was mis-scaled.

findings.claim: Engram (arXiv 2601.07372) config: max n-gram order 3, instantiated with n-grams {2,3}; memory embedding dim d_mem=1280; K=8 independent hash heads per n-gram order; prime-sized buckets addressed by multiplicative-XOR hashing; retrieved embeddings are gated by the hidden state then passed through a depthwise Conv1D. In the two flagship models Engram sits at exactly two layers: layers 2 and 15.
findings.numbers: n-grams {2,3}; d_mem=1280; K=8 hash heads; layers {2,15}; vocab/slots 2,262,400 (27B) and 7,239,680 (40B)
findings.relevance: This is the exact spec the user's KazLLM-v2 borrows. Confirms {2,3}-gram choice and gives a concrete d_mem (1280) and K=8 hashing scheme to drop into the Kazakh design instead of guessing.
findings.source: arXiv:2601.07372 (Conditional Memory via Scalable Lookup), HTML v1

findings.claim: The MOST scale-relevant Engram experiment: a 3B-total MoE backbone with only 568M ACTIVE params, 12 layers, with a 1.6B-param Engram memory ({2,3}-grams). Pure MoE baseline validation loss 1.808; single Engram at layer 2 = 1.770; splitting the same 1.6B memory into TWO modules at layers 2 and 6 = 1.768 (best). So the paper's own small ablation used layers {2,6}, not {2,L/4}.
findings.numbers: 568M active, 12 layers, 1.6B Engram; val loss 1.808 (MoE) -> 1.770 (L2) -> 1.768 (L2+L6); delta -0.040 nats
findings.relevance: Directly validates the user's plan at ~568M active. Recommends layer placement {2,6} for a 12-layer net and confirms two smaller split modules beat one big module. But note: backbone was MoE, not dense Llama.
findings.source: arXiv:2601.07372, Section 6.2 / Figure 5

findings.claim: Engram benchmark deltas vs an ISO-parameter, ISO-FLOP MoE-27B baseline (both 26.7B total / 3.8B active; Engram trades 17 routed experts, 72->55, for 5.7B memory params): MMLU +3.0, CMMLU +4.0, BBH +5.0, ARC-Challenge +3.7, DROP +3.3, HumanEval +3.0, MATH +2.4, GSM8K +2.2; multi-query NIAH 84.2 -> 97.0. Gains are LARGER on reasoning/code (BBH +5.0) than on pure knowledge (MMLU +3.0). (Abstract quotes MMLU +3.4; the detailed table says +3.0.)
findings.numbers: MMLU +3.0, CMMLU +4.0, BBH +5.0, ARC +3.7, HumanEval +3.0, MATH +2.4, GSM8K +2.2, NIAH 84.2->97.0
findings.relevance: Quantifies expected upside. The reasoning-heavy gains matter because KazMMLU is knowledge-heavy; a +3 to +4 MMLU-class lift is the plausible ceiling of the Engram contribution, and it comes at 0 added FLOPs.
findings.source: arXiv:2601.07372, main results table

findings.claim: Engram mechanism equations: per-slot gating scalar alpha_t = sigmoid( RMSNorm(h_t)^T RMSNorm(k_t) / sqrt(d) ) modulates retrieved value; then Y = SiLU(Conv1D(RMSNorm(V_tilde))) + V_tilde, with depthwise Conv1D kernel width w=4 and dilation = max n-gram order, SiLU activation and a residual. Lookups are O(1): a constant number of slots retrieved per token, so growing the table raises total params with ZERO extra per-token FLOPs.
findings.numbers: conv kernel w=4, dilation=3 (max n-gram), gating via RMSNorm dot-product/sqrt(d); 0 extra FLOPs
findings.relevance: Exact math needed to reimplement Engram correctly for Kazakh (the conv+gating is what makes it beat a raw hash-embedding table like OverEncoding). The 0-FLOP property is the whole reason it fits a $264 single-GPU budget.
findings.source: arXiv:2601.07372, method section

findings.claim: Engram memory-scaling is a clean power law: on the fixed 568M-active backbone, validation loss improves log-linearly as embedding slots grow from 2.58e5 to 1.0e7. Optimal compute allocation is a U-shape peaking at rho ~= 75-80% of the sparse budget on MoE (i.e. reallocate ~20-25% of sparse params to Engram); at a 6e20-FLOP budget (9.9B total, 993M active) val loss improves 1.7248 (pure MoE, rho=100%) -> 1.7109 near rho~=80%.
findings.numbers: slots 2.58e5->1.0e7 log-linear; optimal rho 75-80%; 1.7248->1.7109 (delta 0.0139) at 9.9B total
findings.relevance: Tells the user how big to make the Kazakh hash tables (bigger monotonically helps, budget-permitting) and that ~20-25% of any sparse budget is the sweet spot for memory vs compute. Their ~512M memory is on the small side of the validated 2.58e5-1e7 slot range.
findings.source: arXiv:2601.07372, Sections 3.1-3.2

findings.claim: Param-accounting caveat: every published Engram result is on an MoE backbone (3.8B or 993M or 568M ACTIVE), never a dense model, and Engram's memory (5.7B in the 27B) is counted OUTSIDE the active/FLOP budget. If the Kazakh peer group (Qwen3-0.6B, SozKZ-600M, Gemma3-270M) is measured by TOTAL params, a 500M dense backbone + ~512M Engram table = ~1B total params, which is outside the <=600M size class even though FLOPs stay at 500M.
findings.numbers: 500M dense + 512M Engram = ~1.0B total params vs <=600M claimed class
findings.relevance: A fairness/framing risk for the arXiv paper: reviewers will flag that beating 500M dense models with a 1B-total (memory-augmented) model is not iso-size. Either report active-params honestly and argue the 0-FLOP axis, or shrink the table to stay <=600M total.
findings.source: arXiv:2601.07372 (param tables) vs project grounding

findings.claim: MLA (DeepSeek-V2, arXiv 2405.04434) reduces KV cache 93.3% vs the MHA baseline (DeepSeek-67B) and in ablations OUTPERFORMS MHA, MQA and GQA on downstream benchmarks while using far less cache; it enabled 5.76x higher generation throughput. KV cache per token per layer = (d_c + d_h_rope) elements; with d_c=512, d_h_rope=64 that is 576 elements = 4.5*d_h, i.e. roughly the cache of GQA with ~2.25 groups but with MHA-or-better quality.
findings.numbers: 93.3% cache cut; 5.76x throughput; cache = d_c+d_h_rope = 576 elem/token/layer (~GQA-2.25)
findings.relevance: Core case for swapping the user's GQA-2 for MLA: MLA matches/beats full MHA quality at ~GQA-2.25 cache. The quality-not-just-memory angle matters more than raw cache at 500M/short-context.
findings.source: arXiv:2405.04434 (DeepSeek-V2); the '2.25 groups' is derived from the 4.5*d_h formula

findings.claim: DeepSeek-V2 MLA exact config: d_model=5120, n_heads=128, per-head d_h=128, kv_lora_rank d_c=512, q_lora_rank=1536, decoupled qk_rope_head_dim=64, qk_nope_head_dim=128, v_head_dim=128. RoPE is DECOUPLED: only a 64-dim slice of q/k carries RoPE, the rest is compressed and RoPE-free, which is what lets the latent be cached. DeepSeek-V3 keeps the same d_c=512, q_lora_rank=1536, rope_dim=64 at d_model=7168.
findings.numbers: d_c=512, q_lora_rank=1536, rope_dim=64, nope_dim=128, v_dim=128, n_h=128, d_h=128
findings.relevance: Gives exact ratios to scale down. d_c/d_model ~= 0.1 -> for the Kazakh d_model~1536, a proportional kv_lora_rank ~= 192-256 with decoupled rope_dim 32-64. Concrete numbers to put in the spec, not 'consider MLA'.

findings.claim: MLA at sub-1B DOES transfer but with caveats. EG-MLA (arXiv 2509.16686) runs MLA at 1B and cuts KV cache to 1.54K elements/token (91.6% vs MHA) while retaining accuracy. TransMLA (arXiv 2502.07864) proves any GQA model is convertible to MLA and MLA's expressivity strictly exceeds GQA at equal cache. BUT practitioner consensus (Raschka, and others) is that below ~100B, GQA is easier to tune/get right; MLA stays competitive and can slightly beat MHA. So MLA is a quality-neutral-to-positive, cache-negative swap that costs engineering effort (decoupled RoPE + weight-absorption at inference).
findings.numbers: EG-MLA @1B: 1.54K elem/token, 91.6% cut; TransMLA: MLA expressivity >= GQA at equal cache
findings.relevance: Green-lights MLA for the 500M Kazakh model but sets expectations: expect quality parity-to-small-gain, not a KazMMLU jump. Keep GQA-2 as the low-risk fallback. Budget time for the decoupled-RoPE + matrix-absorption implementation.
findings.source: arXiv:2509.16686 (EG-MLA), arXiv:2502.07864 (TransMLA), Raschka LLM gallery

findings.claim: Multi-Token Prediction has a capability threshold ~1B-3B: below it MTP does NOT improve generative-task performance and a naive MTP objective can DEGRADE next-token performance for small models (curriculum learning mitigates). DeepSeek-V3 uses 1 sequential MTP module predicting the next 2 tokens; the 2nd-token head reaches >80-85% acceptance, giving ~1.8x speculative-decoding speedup. MTP's training-signal gain (~+2.4% avg) was measured on an 8B-active MoE, not a sub-1B dense model.
findings.numbers: threshold 1-3B; V3: 1 MTP module, depth-1, 2 tokens, >80% accept, 1.8x decode; +2.4% avg @8B-active
findings.relevance: Warns against relying on MTP for a training-quality boost at 500M (likely null or negative). If used, use it ONLY as an inference speculative-decoding head, or apply a curriculum (NTP-first, add MTP late). Not a KazMMLU lever at this size.

findings.claim: NSA (arXiv 2502.11089) hyperparams: compression block l=32, stride 16, selected block l'=64, top-n=16 selected blocks (incl. 1 forced initial + 2 local), sliding window w=512; three branches (compressed / selected / sliding) fused by a learned gate. Validated on a 27B MoE (3B active), pretrained 270B tokens @8k then extended to 32k with YaRN; surpasses full attention on average and is natively trainable. Requires GQA-style head grouping and custom Triton/CUDA kernels for the speedup.
findings.numbers: l=32, stride 16, l'=64, top-n=16, window 512; 27B MoE/3B active; 8k->32k ctx
findings.relevance: NSA only pays off at long context (>=8k-32k) and needs bespoke kernels; for a 500M Kazakh model with typical 4k context on one A100 it is high-effort, low-return. Deprioritize unless long-context Kazakh (KazQAD long passages) becomes a goal.
findings.source: arXiv:2502.11089 (Native Sparse Attention)

findings.claim: DeepSeekMoE (arXiv 2401.06066) = fine-grained expert segmentation (split each FFN into many small experts, e.g. 8.7M each vs Mixtral's 176.2M) + isolated always-on shared experts capturing common knowledge. It trades TOTAL params for ACTIVE params. At a <=600M TOTAL budget there is almost no room to separate active from total (you'd get e.g. ~600M total / ~200M active), so the MoE efficiency premise collapses; sparse budget is better spent on the Engram lookup axis.
findings.numbers: fine-grained expert ~8.7M vs Mixtral 176.2M; MoE only pays off when total>>active
findings.relevance: Concludes the user's dense choice is correct within the 600M cap. Don't add DeepSeekMoE; it needs a large total-param headroom the size class forbids. Engram is the sparsity axis that fits.
findings.source: arXiv:2401.06066 (DeepSeekMoE)

findings.claim: FP8 training (DeepSeek-V3) uses fine-grained quant: tile-wise 1x128 for activations, block-wise 128x128 for weights (Nc=128), keeping embedding, output head, MoE gating, norms and attention in BF16/FP32; validated at 671B with <0.25% relative error. CRITICAL hardware fact: FP8 tensor cores exist only on Hopper (H100) / Ada / Blackwell. An A100 (Ampere) has NO FP8 support, so the user's '1x A100 40GB spot' budget CANNOT use FP8 training and must train in BF16.
findings.numbers: tile 1x128 act / block 128x128 wt, Nc=128, <0.25% err @671B; A100=no FP8
findings.relevance: Decisive: remove FP8 from the Kazakh training plan on A100. It is not an available lever on that GPU; BF16 is the target precision. Only relevant if they switch to an H100/H200 spot instance.
findings.source: arXiv:2412.19437 (DeepSeek-V3); NVIDIA Ampere vs Hopper FP8 support

findings.claim: R1-style reasoning distillation: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B was SFT-distilled from R1 on 800K samples (600K reasoning CoT + 200K general), initialized from Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, reaching AIME 28.9% and MATH 83.9% - beating GPT-4o/Claude-3.5 on math. The smallest official distill is 1.5B; no 500M distill was released, and gains depend on a strong same-family base and abundant CoT data.
findings.numbers: 800K samples (600K reason+200K gen); 1.5B: AIME 28.9%, MATH 83.9%; smallest distill=1.5B
findings.relevance: Reasoning distillation is a real lever but (a) validated at 1.5B not 500M and (b) needs Kazakh CoT data that barely exists. Treat as a stretch post-training step (translate/synthesize Kazakh CoT), not a core architecture bet for KazMMLU.
findings.source: arXiv:2501.12948 (DeepSeek-R1)

recommendations: Keep Engram, but adopt the paper's own small-scale config verbatim: {2,3}-grams, d_mem=1280, K=8 hash heads, and split the memory into TWO modules placed at layers {2,6} of a ~12-layer net (the 568M-active ablation showed 2+6 = 1.768 beats single layer-2 = 1.770 beats pure baseline 1.808). Do NOT use {2,L/4}; use {2,6} as validated. Include the gating alpha_t=sigmoid(RMSNorm(h)-dot-RMSNorm(k)/sqrt(d)) and the depthwise Conv1D (w=4, dilation=3, SiLU, residual) - a raw hash-embedding table without them underperforms.

Size the Engram table as large as the param/VRAM budget allows (loss improves log-linearly from 2.58e5 to 1e7 slots). Their current ~512M-param table sits at the low end of the validated range; if staying <=600M TOTAL is required, this is the main tension - decide the accounting story first (see next).

Resolve the size-class framing BEFORE training: a 500M dense backbone + ~512M Engram table is ~1B TOTAL params. Either (a) shrink the Engram table so total <=600M and compete honestly by total params, or (b) report ACTIVE/FLOP params and pre-empt the reviewer objection by benchmarking against memory-augmented peers and stressing the 0-FLOP axis. The current framing ('500M model') will be challenged on arXiv.

Swap GQA-2 for MLA with concrete numbers scaled from DeepSeek-V2's ratios (d_c/d_model~=0.1, rope_dim=64): at d_model~=1536 use kv_lora_rank=256, q_lora_rank=768-1024, decoupled qk_rope_head_dim=32-64, qk_nope_head_dim=128, v_head_dim=128. This yields ~288-320 cache elements/token/layer (~85-90% below MHA) with MHA-or-better quality. Keep GQA-2 as the tested fallback since below ~100B GQA is easier to tune - decide by a head-to-head loss ablation, not by cache alone (cache is not the bottleneck at 500M/4k context; MLA's value here is quality/expressivity).

Do NOT use MTP as a training-quality lever at 500M - it is below the 1-3B threshold and can hurt next-token loss. If wanted at all, add a single depth-1 MTP head LATE in training (curriculum) purely for inference speculative decoding (~1.8x decode speedup at >80% acceptance), and measure that it doesn't regress KazMMLU.

Drop FP8 from the plan - the A100 (Ampere) has no FP8 tensor cores; train in BF16. Only revisit FP8 (tile 1x128 act / block 128x128 wt, keep embed/head/gating/norm/attn high-precision) if you move to an H100/H200 spot instance.

Deprioritize NSA and DeepSeekMoE for this build: NSA only pays off at >=8k-32k context and needs custom kernels (overkill for 500M/4k Kazakh); DeepSeekMoE's active-vs-total tradeoff collapses inside a 600M total cap. Spend the sparsity budget on Engram instead. Reserve NSA for a future long-context KazQAD variant.

Treat R1-style reasoning distillation as an optional post-training stretch, not core architecture: the smallest validated distill is 1.5B and it needs abundant same-family CoT data that barely exists for Kazakh. If pursued, synthesize/translate Kazakh CoT and distill from a strong Kazakh-capable teacher (e.g. Sherkala-8B), then measure KazMMLU lift separately.
open_questions: Does Engram transfer to a DENSE backbone? Every published result (568M-active to 3.8B-active) is on an MoE. The 0-FLOP lookup axis is orthogonal to whether the FFN is dense or MoE, so it should transfer, but there is no published dense ablation - the Kazakh model would be the first data point and should include a dense-with/without-Engram ablation.

Optimal hash-table size for a ~500M-active Kazakh model specifically: the power law was measured on English/Pile. Agglutinative Kazakh has far more surface {2,3}-gram types per lemma (vowel-harmony allomorphs), which could change collision rates and the ideal slot count vs the English curve.
Whether MLA's decoupled-RoPE actually beats GQA-2 at 500M on Kazakh, or just matches it at higher implementation cost - needs a direct same-tokens loss+KazMMLU ablation before committing.

Exact DeepSeek-V2 MLA scalar config (q_lora_rank=1536 etc.) could not be re-confirmed from a primary text source this session (PDF/HTML extraction failed); values are from strong secondary recall and should be checked against the arXiv 2405.04434 PDF Table 1 / released config.json before being written into the spec.

Interaction between Engram (which shifts effective vocabulary/knowledge to a lookup table) and a small 50K SentencePiece Kazakh tokenizer: Engram's hashed n-grams operate on token IDs, so tokenizer fertility and vocab choice may materially change Engram's hit rate - untested for Kazakh.

research.area: hybrid-efficiency (efficient attention, sequence mixing, KV-cache & quantization for a <=600M Kazakh SLM)

findings.claim: Gemma 3 interleaves 5 local sliding-window attention layers per 1 global layer (5:1); local window = 1024 tokens; RoPE base is 10K on local layers and 1M on global layers. This cuts KV-cache overhead from ~60% (global-only) to <15% at 32K context with 'minimal impact on perplexity' vs a 1:1 ratio, and shrinking the window further barely moves perplexity.
findings.numbers: 5:1 ratio; sliding window=1024 tok; RoPE local=10K, global=1M; KV overhead 60%->~15% at 32K; Gemma3-1B: 698M non-embedding params, 32K context, 256K vocab
findings.relevance: Highest-leverage, lowest-risk change for a dense 500M Kazakh backbone: near-free KV savings that make an 8GB-GPU/CPU deployment viable at long context (KazQAD reading comprehension) without hurting quality. Directly upgrades the current GQA-2 dense design.
findings.source: arXiv:2503.19786 (Gemma 3 Technical Report), Figures 3-5

findings.claim: Gemma 3 QAT: finetuning ~5000 steps with targets from the non-quantized BF16 checkpoint (per-channel or per-block int4) reduces the perplexity increase from int4 quantization by 54% and keeps Elo within a few points of BF16. VRAM for weights collapses roughly 4x.
findings.numbers: Gemma3-1B: 2GB (BF16) -> 0.5GB (int4); 4B: 8GB -> 2.6GB; 27B: 54GB -> 14.1GB; -54% perplexity degradation via QAT; ~5000 QAT steps
findings.relevance: A 500M model becomes ~0.25-0.3GB int4 weights - trivial for an 8GB GPU and CPU-friendly. QAT (not post-training PTQ) is the pragmatic edge-deployment path and is a cheap add-on after pretraining.
findings.source: arXiv:2503.19786 + Google Developers Blog 'Gemma 3 QAT Models' (developers.googleblog.com)

findings.claim: LFM2 (on-device) uses a minimal conv-attention hybrid: 16 blocks = 10 gated short convolutions (kernel k=3, double-gated 'LIV' conv) + 6 GQA attention blocks, identical layout for 350M/700M/1.2B (2.6B = 30 blocks: 22 conv + 8 GQA). Their hardware-in-the-loop search concluded 'most of the benefits of recent hybrid SSM/linear-attention blocks can be captured by their short convolutional submodules plus a small number of global attention layers.'
findings.numbers: 10 conv + 6 GQA of 16 (=37.5% attention); vocab 65,536; 32K context; 10T training tokens
findings.relevance: Direct template for a <=600M multilingual hybrid: short convs are far cheaper/simpler than Mamba-2 on CPU yet capture most SSM benefit, while keeping ~37% attention preserves knowledge/recall for KazMMLU. Stronger match to the edge target than a full SSM stack.
findings.source: arXiv:2511.23404 (LFM2 Technical Report), Table 1; HF LiquidAI/LFM2-350M

findings.claim: LFM2-350M beats Qwen3-0.6B on multilingual MMLU despite fewer params, and is within ~1.5 pts on English MMLU; on-device it is ~2x faster than Qwen3 on CPU. This is direct evidence a conv-attention hybrid competes with the best ~500M transformer on multilingual knowledge.
findings.numbers: MMMLU: LFM2-350M 37.99 vs Qwen3-0.6B 30.84; MMLU 43.43 vs 44.93; Snapdragon 8 Elite LFM2-700M vs Qwen3-0.6B: prefill 522 vs 318 tok/s (+64%), 4K decode 80.2 vs 41.8 tok/s (+92%)
findings.relevance: Qwen3-0.6B is the strongest measured Kazakh baseline (KazMMLU 32.8%). A hybrid that already outscores it on multilingual MMLU while decoding ~2x faster on CPU is the target-shaped competitor to beat.
findings.source: arXiv:2511.23404; HF LiquidAI/LFM2-350M model card

findings.claim: Falcon-H1-0.5B uses a PARALLEL hybrid block: attention and Mamba-2 run concurrently on the same input and their outputs are concatenated before projection, with channels split roughly SSM:Attention:MLP = 2:1:5. Exact 0.5B config: 36 layers, d_model=1024, Q/KV heads 8/2, 24 SSM heads, d_state=128, head_dim=64, 16K context, vocab 32,778, 2.5T tokens. Supports 18 languages but NOT Kazakh.
findings.numbers: 36 layers, d=1024, attn 8/2 heads, 24 SSM heads, d_state=128, head_dim=64, ctx 16K, vocab 32,778, 2.5T tokens; channel ratio ~2:1:5
findings.relevance: Alternative to sequential hybrids: parallel attention+SSM lets you tune attention/SSM channel budget independently. The compact vocab (32.7K) and 0.5B config is a concrete, sub-600M reference. Kazakh absence means a from-scratch Kazakh model has open room.
findings.source: arXiv:2507.22448 (Falcon-H1 Technical Report), Table 1

findings.claim: Pure Mamba/Mamba-2 models trail Transformers by ~15 points on 5-shot MMLU (recall/in-context tasks) even after 1.1T tokens, because SSMs must compress history into a fixed-size state. Adding only ~7-8% self-attention layers, evenly dispersed, closes AND exceeds the Transformer baseline across 12 tasks - attention layers absorb the 'gather-and-aggregate' recall operations.
findings.numbers: ~15-pt 5-shot MMLU gap for pure Mamba vs Transformer @1.1T tokens; fixed with ~7-8% attention layers
findings.relevance: Decisive for a KazMMLU-primary model: do NOT go pure-SSM or ultra-Mamba-heavy (Granite 9:1). Since the primary benchmark is knowledge/recall, keep attention share generous (LFM2's ~37%, or Nemotron's floor of ~8% only if maximizing throughput).
findings.source: arXiv:2406.07887 (Empirical Study of Mamba LMs); arXiv:2510.26912; arXiv:2504.18574 (Gather-and-Aggregate)

findings.claim: Sequential Mamba-heavy hybrids trade knowledge headroom for throughput. IBM Granite 4.0 uses ~9:1 Mamba-2:transformer (>70% long-context memory reduction). NVIDIA Nemotron-H/Nano-2 set attention to ~8% of layers (e.g. 4 self-attn of 52 for the 8B; rest Mamba-2+FFN), yielding up to 6-6.3x throughput vs Qwen3-8B at 8K-in/16K-out and 1.8-3x at 65K context.
findings.numbers: Granite 4.0: 9:1 Mamba:transformer, >70% mem cut; Nemotron-H-8B: 4 attn / 24 Mamba-2 / 24 MLP = 52 layers (~8% attn); Nano-2: up to 6.3x throughput vs Qwen3-8B
findings.relevance: These ratios are optimized for long-context throughput at 8B+, not for knowledge at 500M. For Kazakh, the ~8% attention floor is risky on KazMMLU; use them as the throughput ceiling, not the default ratio.
findings.source: IBM Granite 4.0 announcement (Oct 2025); arXiv:2504.03624 (Nemotron-H); arXiv:2508.14444 (Nemotron Nano 2)

findings.claim: Zamba2 shows an extreme KV-cache-saving hybrid: a Mamba-2 backbone with a SINGLE shared attention block (weights reused via LoRA) applied every ~6 Mamba-2 layers, giving ~6x KV-cache reduction vs a pure transformer while staying competitive with same-size transformers.
findings.numbers: 1:6 attention:Mamba-2; shared-attention weights reused with LoRA; ~6x KV reduction; sizes 1.2B/2.7B/7.4B
findings.relevance: Parameter-sharing trick (one attention block reused) is attractive at 500M where param budget is tight - but 1:6 attention is likely too sparse for KazMMLU; more useful as a KV-saving idea than a ratio to copy.
findings.source: arXiv:2411.15242 (Zamba2 Suite Technical Report)

findings.claim: MLA vs GQA at the KV-cache level: DeepSeek's ablations show MLA matches/beats MHA perplexity while GQA loses ~0.5 and MQA ~1.5 perplexity; MLA stores ~70KB/token vs 192-328KB/token for GQA models (2.7-4.7x smaller cache) by compressing all K/V into one low-rank latent instead of sharing heads.
findings.numbers: MLA cache ~70KB/tok vs GQA 192-328KB/tok (2.7-4.7x); GQA +0.5 / MQA +1.5 perplexity vs MHA
findings.relevance: MLA is the highest-quality-per-KV-byte option, but its advantage grows with context length and model size; at 500M with short Kazakh sequences the simpler GQA-2 already captures most of the benefit. MLA becomes worth the complexity only if long-context (32K KazQAD) is a hard requirement.
findings.source: arXiv:2405.04434 (DeepSeek-V2)

findings.claim: MLA specifically studied at SMALL scale (30M-202M params): a decoupled MLA+RoPE with latent rank r=d/2 gives a 45% KV-cache reduction at only +0.3% validation loss and 1.4x decode speedup; r=d/4 gives ~87.5% reduction but +4.4% loss. MLA needs the decoupled-RoPE variant - without RoPE it underperforms by 3-5%. (Paper did not benchmark GQA directly.)
findings.numbers: r=d/2: 45% KV cut, +0.3% loss, 1.4x speed; r=d/4: 87.5% cut, +4.4% loss; scale tested 30M-202.7M
findings.relevance: If MLA is adopted for the Kazakh model at d_model~1536, set kv_lora_rank ~= d/2 (~768) with a decoupled RoPE dim (~64). This is the only MLA-at-sub-600M data point; r=d/4 is too lossy for a knowledge model.
findings.source: arXiv:2506.09342 (Latent Multi-Head Attention for Small Language Models)

findings.claim: Cross-Layer Attention (CLA) shares K/V across adjacent layers (only a subset of layers compute KV; others reuse the previous layer's), giving 2x KV reduction on top of MQA/GQA. At 1B scale H128-MQA-CLA2 costs only +0.04 validation perplexity; at 3B CLA2 actually beat the MQA baselines (9.34 vs 9.48-9.52 ppl).
findings.numbers: CLA2 = share KV across 2 layers -> 2x KV cut; 1B: +0.04 ppl; 3B: 9.34 vs 9.52 ppl (better)
findings.relevance: Orthogonal to sliding-window and GQA - stacks multiplicatively for KV savings. A near-free way to halve KV again on the global-attention layers of the Kazakh model, validated at the closest scale (1B).
findings.source: arXiv:2405.12981 (Reducing Transformer KV-Cache Size with Cross-Layer Attention, NeurIPS 2024)

findings.claim: BitNet b1.58 2B4T (native 1.58-bit QAT from scratch, ternary {-1,0,+1} weights + 8-bit activations, W1.58A8, 4T tokens) reaches 0.4GB non-embedding memory (6.5x smaller than Qwen2.5-1.5B's 2.6GB), CPU TPOT 29ms vs 65ms (2.2x faster), 12.4x lower decode energy, and beats INT4 post-training quantization (avg 55.01 vs 51.17) - BUT still trails full-precision on knowledge (MMLU 53.17 vs Qwen2.5-1.5B 60.25).
findings.numbers: 0.4GB non-emb (vs 2.6GB); CPU 29ms vs 65ms TPOT; energy 0.028J vs 0.347J; MMLU 53.17 vs 60.25; beats INT4 PTQ 55.01 vs 51.17
findings.relevance: Native 1.58-bit is the most aggressive edge option (fits huge headroom on any device, CPU-fast) but the ~7-pt MMLU deficit is exactly the KazMMLU axis you're optimizing - high risk for a knowledge-first Kazakh model. Prefer int4 QAT unless CPU-only deployment is the hard constraint.
findings.source: arXiv:2504.12285 (BitNet b1.58 2B4T Technical Report), Tables 1-2

findings.claim: KV-cache quantization: 4-bit KV is essentially lossless (KIVI: per-channel key + per-token value, tuning-free) giving ~2.6x peak memory cut and 2.35-3.47x throughput; but 2-bit KV degrades sharply (average drops of -10 to -15 points) unless a small fraction of sensitive key channels are kept at higher precision.
findings.numbers: 4-bit KV ~lossless, 2.6x mem, 2.35-3.47x throughput; 2-bit KV: -10.15 to -15.23 avg accuracy; KIVI = 2-bit per-channel K / per-token V
findings.relevance: For the edge Kazakh model, ship 4-bit KV cache quantization (safe, near-free) but do NOT go 2-bit. Combined with sliding-window 5:1 this makes long-context inference on 8GB feasible.
findings.source: KIVI (ICML 2024, github jy-yuan/KIVI); arXiv:2511.18643 (Kitty 2-bit KV)

findings.claim: YOCO (decoder-decoder) caches only ONE layer of global KV shared by all cross-decoder layers via cross-attention, giving ~L-times less KV memory than a standard L-layer transformer while retaining global attention and near-perfect 1M-context needle retrieval; also enables early-exit prefill.
findings.numbers: ~L x less KV memory (one global KV layer); near-perfect needle retrieval at 1M context
findings.relevance: An architectural KV-cache alternative to per-layer caching. For a 500M model where weights are tiny and KV dominates at long context, YOCO-style single-cache is a candidate if very long Kazakh documents matter; heavier to implement than sliding-window.
findings.source: arXiv:2405.05254 (You Only Cache Once, NeurIPS 2024)

findings.claim: MiniCPM4-0.5B pairs an edge-tuned transformer with InfLLM-v2 trainable sparse attention (each token attends to <5% of tokens at 128K), reaching up to 7x decode speedup on edge GPUs vs Qwen3-8B with perfect needle retrieval at 128K - a proven sub-600M edge-efficiency reference point.
findings.numbers: <5% tokens attended @128K; up to 7x edge-GPU decode speedup vs Qwen3-8B; 0.5B params
findings.relevance: Concrete existence proof of a competitive 0.5B edge model, and shows trainable sparse attention as an alternative to sliding-window for extreme long context - though for Kazakh's shorter typical inputs, Gemma-style sliding window is simpler and sufficient.
findings.source: arXiv:2506.07900 (MiniCPM4); arXiv:2509.24663 (InfLLM-v2)

findings.claim: Baseline architecture to beat - Qwen3-0.6B: 28 layers, hidden 1024, 16 query heads / 8 KV heads (GQA-2), head_dim 128, FFN 3072, vocab 151,936, 32K context, SwiGLU+RMSNorm+RoPE. It scores KazMMLU 32.8% (best-tier measured ~500M on Kazakh).
findings.numbers: 28L, d=1024, 16Q/8KV heads, head_dim 128, FFN 3072, vocab 151,936, ctx 32K; KazMMLU 32.8%
findings.relevance: Defines the exact competitor config and the giant-vocab cost (151.9K) the Kazakh model can beat with a compact Kazakh-optimized 50K tokenizer - freeing params for depth/width at equal budget.
findings.source: HF Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B config; user-provided KazMMLU baseline

recommendations: Adopt Gemma-3-style sliding-window local:global interleaving on the dense backbone: 5:1 ratio, local window=1024, dual RoPE (local theta=10K, global theta=500K to match current design). This cuts KV-cache overhead ~60%->~15% at long context with negligible perplexity cost - the single best efficiency win, and it composes cleanly with the existing Engram + mHC design.

Keep attention share generous, NOT Mamba-heavy: because KazMMLU (knowledge/recall) is the primary metric and pure SSM loses ~15 pts of 5-shot MMLU, target roughly the LFM2 ratio (~35-40% attention). Concretely, replace a subset of MLP/attention layers with gated short convolutions (kernel k=3, LFM2-style) rather than Mamba-2 - short convs capture most of the SSM benefit, are much simpler and faster on CPU, and LFM2-350M already beats Qwen3-0.6B on multilingual MMLU (37.99 vs 30.84).

Do NOT copy the Granite 9:1 or Nemotron ~8%-attention ratios - those are throughput-optimized at 8B+ and will bleed KazMMLU accuracy at 500M. If a pure-Mamba variant is trained for ablation, disperse attention layers evenly and keep >=15-20% attention as the floor.

KV cache: keep GQA-2 (current) as the safe default for short Kazakh sequences; it already captures most of MLA's benefit at this scale/context. Only switch to MLA if 32K-context KazQAD is a hard target - then use decoupled MLA+RoPE with kv_lora_rank ~= d_model/2 (~768 at d=1536) and a small decoupled-RoPE dim (~64), which buys ~45% KV reduction at +0.3% loss. Avoid r=d/4 (too lossy for a knowledge model).
Stack Cross-Layer Attention (CLA2) on the global attention layers to halve their KV again (+~0.04 ppl at 1B) - it is orthogonal to sliding-window and GQA and nearly free.

Plan int4 QAT for edge deployment using the Gemma-3 recipe (~5000 finetune steps against the BF16 checkpoint, per-channel or per-block int4): a 500M model drops to ~0.25-0.3GB weights, running comfortably on an 8GB GPU or CPU with -54% less quantization damage than PTQ. Treat native BitNet 1.58-bit as an ambitious secondary track only if CPU-only is a hard constraint - flag its ~7-pt MMLU deficit as a KazMMLU risk.

Ship 4-bit KV-cache quantization (KIVI-style: per-channel keys, per-token values) for inference - near-lossless, ~2.6x KV memory cut, 2.3-3.5x throughput. Explicitly forbid 2-bit KV (avg -10 to -15 pts) unless a sensitivity-aware mixed-precision scheme is added.

Exploit the compact Kazakh tokenizer (target 50K vs Qwen3's 151.9K): the ~100K vocab saving frees roughly 100M embedding params that can be redeployed into 2-4 extra layers or wider FFN at the same <=600M budget - a direct quality lever competitors at this size cannot match.

For the paper's efficiency claims, report the concrete edge metrics the field now expects: CPU decode/prefill tok/s vs Qwen3-0.6B (LFM2 set the bar at ~+64% prefill / +92% decode on Snapdragon 8 Elite), int4 weight VRAM, and KV memory at 4K/32K context - these make the architecture reproducibly comparable.
open_questions: Does a parallel hybrid (Falcon-H1: attention+conv/SSM concurrent, outputs concatenated) beat a sequential interleave (LFM2/Gemma: alternating blocks) at <=600M on Kazakh knowledge tasks? No head-to-head at this scale exists - needs an ablation.

At exactly 500-600M with typical Kazakh input lengths (mostly <4K tokens for KazMMLU/FLORES), does MLA's KV compression justify its implementation/serving complexity over sliding-window+GQA-2+CLA? The only small-scale MLA data stops at 202M and never benchmarks GQA.

Do gated short convolutions preserve morphological/agglutinative and vowel-harmony patterns in Kazakh as well as attention? Conv locality (k=3) may interact with long suffix chains - untested for Turkic morphology.

Can native 1.58-bit (BitNet) training recover its ~7-pt MMLU deficit when trained on a focused, high-quality 9-10B Kazakh corpus rather than a broad 4T-token mix, or is the deficit intrinsic to ternary weights? Unknown at sub-600M.

Is there any published hybrid/efficient model that includes Kazakh in pretraining (Falcon-H1, LFM2, Qwen3 all exclude or under-cover it)? If none, the from-scratch Kazakh hybrid is genuinely first-of-kind for the efficiency axis.

findings.claim: Sherkala-8B (Kazakh) extended Llama-3.1's 128,256 vocab to 159,766 (+25%, +31.5K tokens) by training monolingual BPE for Kazakh/Russian/Turkish and merging the most frequent non-overlapping tokens. This cut Kazakh fertility from 4.73 to 2.04 tok/word (-56.8%), Russian 2.56->2.21, Turkish 2.23->1.82. It is the strongest published Kazakh model (KazMMLU 41.4).
findings.numbers: vocab 128,256->159,766 (+31,510); Kazakh fertility 4.73->2.04; Russian 2.56->2.21; Turkish 2.23->1.82; +31.5K tokens sufficed to halve Kazakh fertility
findings.relevance: Proves ~2.0 tok/word for Kazakh is achievable with only ~10-30K Kazakh-specific tokens grafted onto a base vocab; the user's <2.0 target is realistic. Also validates vocab-expansion path if warm-starting from a strong base model.
findings.source: arXiv:2503.01493 (Llama-3.1-Sherkala-8B-Chat)

findings.claim: Sherkala initialized new Kazakh/Russian/Turkish token embeddings with a WECHSEL-style semantic-similarity method: for each new token, average the embeddings of its top-5 most similar base-vocab tokens, where similarity is computed with OpenAI text-embedding-3-large. Training mix was 45.3B tokens at Kk:Ru+Tr:En = 3:1:3 (Kazakh 19.45B, English 19.45B, Russian+Turkish 6.4B).
findings.numbers: top-5 averaged; 45.3B tokens; Kazakh 19.45B / English 19.45B / Ru+Tr 6.4B; ratio 3:1:3
findings.relevance: Concrete, copyable embedding-init recipe for any new-token grafting. The 1:1 Kazakh:English balance (not Kazakh-dominant) is a notable design choice to avoid catastrophic forgetting of the base model's reasoning.

findings.claim: SozKZ-600M trains a ByteLevel-BPE tokenizer of 50,257 tokens exclusively on ~9B Kazakh tokens and reports a '2-3x fertility advantage over multilingual tokenizers' but publishes no absolute fertility number. Downstream it scores MC-QA 30.3%, Belebele 27.0%, SIB-200 25.5% — below multilingual Qwen-1.5B (MC-QA 37.1%) despite the far better tokenizer.
findings.numbers: vocab 50,257; ~9B Kazakh tokens; 2-3x fertility advantage; MC-QA 30.3 / Belebele 27.0 / SIB-200 25.5; Qwen-1.5B MC-QA 37.1
findings.relevance: Direct precedent at the exact target size/data. Key lesson: a great monolingual tokenizer alone does NOT beat larger multilingual models — the tokenizer is necessary but not sufficient; the from-scratch 600M/9B recipe underperforms. The paper the user must exceed.
findings.source: arXiv:2603.20854 (SozKZ)

findings.claim: A 70-language + Goldfish study found that the performance gap on morphologically complex languages is NOT caused by tokenization or fertility. Agglutinative languages actually had HIGHER morpheme alignment (MorphScore 66.3%) than fusional (53.3%, p=.008); fertility explained only R^2=0.021 of alignment variance. The real culprit is the 'byte premium' (up to 5x more UTF-8 bytes per content-matched text). When data is scaled by byte premium the gap becomes insignificant.
findings.numbers: agglutinative MorphScore 66.3% vs fusional 53.3% (p=.008); fertility R^2=0.021; byte premium up to 5x; gap insignificant after byte-scaling (t=1.18, p=0.077)
findings.relevance: Reframes the whole project: Kazakh Cyrillic (~2 bytes/char) means the 9-10B token budget is byte-inflated — effective content is smaller than an equivalent English budget. Lower fertility helps compute/context, but DATA QUANTITY (byte-premium-adjusted) is the dominant lever. Argues for maximizing clean Kazakh data over exotic tokenizer tricks.
findings.source: arXiv:2411.14198 (Why do LMs perform worse for morphologically complex languages?)

findings.claim: MorphScore-style evaluation across 70 languages finds Unigram-LM tokenization aligns with morpheme boundaries substantially better than BPE, especially for agglutinative languages (Turkish, Kazakh, Finnish, Hungarian); larger vocabularies improve alignment. The tool is released as MorphScore (code + HF datasets).
findings.numbers: Unigram > BPE morpheme alignment; effect strongest for agglutinative family; alignment rises with vocab size
findings.relevance: Direct tokenizer-type recommendation: prefer SentencePiece Unigram over BPE for Kazakh (matches the user's current Unigram choice). Provides an off-the-shelf intrinsic metric (MorphScore) to report in the paper alongside fertility.
findings.source: arXiv:2507.06378 (Evaluating Morphological Alignment of Tokenizers in 70 Languages)

findings.claim: MorphBPE constrains BPE merges to never cross morpheme boundaries (using SIGMORPHON/Farasa gold segmentations), raising morphological-consistency F1 dramatically: Hungarian 0.87 vs 0.13 BPE, Arabic 0.66 vs 0.00, Russian 0.45 vs 0.07, English 0.24 vs 0.00, at only a slight fertility increase; it lowers cross-entropy and speeds convergence at 300M and 1B, most for morph-rich languages. Hard requirement: it needs pre-existing morpheme segmentation data.
findings.numbers: morph-consistency F1: HU 0.87/0.13, AR 0.66/0.00, RU 0.45/0.07, EN 0.24/0.00; vocab HU 24K, RU 64K, EN/AR 96K; slight fertility up; 300M & 1B models
findings.relevance: Blueprint for a morphology-supervised Kazakh tokenizer that improves loss/convergence — exactly the edge needed to beat SozKZ. The blocker (need morpheme boundaries) is SOLVED for Kazakh: apertium-kaz FST + KazMorphCorpus-2025 (150K sentences, 2M tokens) can supply supervision.
findings.source: arXiv:2502.00894 (MorphBPE)

findings.claim: Kazakh has production-grade morpheme-segmentation resources: apertium-kaz (finite-state morphological transducer + CG disambiguator, compatible across Turkic), plus a 2025 hybrid FST+CRF+KazRoBERTa analyzer and KazMorphCorpus-2025 (150,000 sentences, >2M tokens across fiction/news/social/Wikipedia/spoken).
findings.numbers: KazMorphCorpus-2025: 150K sentences, >2M tokens; apertium-kaz FST transducer
findings.relevance: Removes MorphBPE's main obstacle for Kazakh — you can generate gold morpheme boundaries at scale to train a morphology-constrained Unigram/BPE tokenizer, a genuinely novel contribution vs SozKZ's vanilla ByteLevel-BPE and vs Sherkala's frequency merges.
findings.source: apertium.github.io/apertium-kaz ; Frontiers 2025 (frai.2025.1708566) hybrid Kazakh analyzer

findings.claim: SuperBPE adds 'superword' tokens that bridge whitespace via a two-phase (subword-then-superword) BPE curriculum: at 200K vocab it encodes text with up to 33% fewer tokens, gives +4.0% avg over 30 tasks (+8.2% MMLU), and 27% less inference compute — but only demonstrated at 8B params/200K vocab with no morphologically-rich-language evaluation.
findings.numbers: 200K vocab; -33% tokens; +4.0% avg, +8.2% MMLU; -27% inference FLOPs; only 8B tested
findings.relevance: Tempting but MISFIT for a 500M Kazakh model: superwords require a large vocab (200K) to pay off, and their gain comes from whitespace redundancy in analytic languages like English. Agglutinative Kazakh already packs a clause into one whitespace-word, so the whitespace-bridging premise mostly doesn't apply. Not recommended as the core tokenizer at this scale.
findings.source: arXiv:2503.13423 (SuperBPE)

findings.claim: IndicSuperTokenizer applies SuperBPE to 22 morphologically-rich Indic languages: two-stage 180K subword + 20K superword = 200K vocab, cutting fertility 39.5% vs Llama-4 (e.g. Oriya 10.51->1.65). But superwords raise training loss slightly, and they explicitly TESTED and REJECTED morphology-aware pretokenization (IndicNLP analyzer) due to latency/brittleness across languages, falling back to regex pretokenization (which alone gave 38-40% of the gain). Downstream Indic gain was only +1.5% at 1B/50B tokens.
findings.numbers: 180K+20K=200K; -39.5% fertility; superwords => slightly higher loss; morphology-aware rejected; regex pretok = 38-40% of gain; +1.5% Indic downstream; +44% inference throughput
findings.relevance: Best evidence that (a) superwords help morph-rich languages mainly via compression/inference, not accuracy (+1.5% only), and (b) at 200K vocab — too big for 500M. For a single language (Kazakh, not 22), a clean morphology analyzer IS available, so the rejection rationale (multilingual brittleness) does not apply. Confirms superwords are a compute-efficiency play, not an accuracy play.
findings.source: arXiv:2511.03237 (IndicSuperTokenizer)

findings.claim: Compute-optimal vocabulary scales with non-embedding params via a power law with exponent gamma~=0.83 (vocab params grow slower than model params). For ~300M non-vocab params the predicted optimal vocab is ~83K-91K; for ~70B it is ~212K-231K. Loss vs vocab is U-shaped for any fixed budget: too small hurts compression, too large under-trains rare tokens under limited data.
findings.numbers: gamma~=0.83; 300M non-vocab -> 83K-91K optimal vocab; U-shaped loss; Llama2-70B 'should' have used 216K not 32K
findings.relevance: For a 500M model this argues optimal vocab is ~90-120K IF data were abundant. But with only ~9-10B tokens (data-constrained), rare tokens in a 100K+ vocab are under-trained, and embeddings eat budget (see next finding). Net: pick vocab from the LOW end of the compute-optimal band and spend the savings on Kazakh coverage.
findings.source: arXiv:2407.13623 (Scaling Laws with Vocabulary, NeurIPS 2024)

findings.claim: Embedding-parameter share is a hard constraint at 500M: with tied embeddings, embedding params = V x d. At d=1536, a 50K vocab = 76.8M params (~15% of 500M); 100K = 153.6M (~31%); 200K (SuperBPE) = 307M (>60%, infeasible). Under a fixed 500M cap, every vocab doubling steals capacity from the transformer body.
findings.relevance: Quantifies why the vocab-scaling-law 'bigger is better' does NOT transfer to a 500M cap: 200K vocab is impossible and 100K costs a third of the model. Recommends a 48-64K vocab sweet spot (15-20% embedding share) — consistent with SozKZ 50K and Sherkala's ~31K Kazakh delta. This is derived arithmetic (d assumed ~1536), flag as design-dependent.
findings.source: derived from arXiv:2407.13623 + standard tied-embedding arithmetic

findings.claim: Cyrillic fertility across major tokenizers (Ukrainian Brown corpus, similar Cyrillic profile to Kazakh): Llama-3.1 1.88, Gemma/Gemma2 1.92 (best chars/token 5.20), GPT-4o 1.98, Mistral-Nemo 2.04, Mistral-7B 2.48, Qwen1.5/2 2.83 (worst). Larger-vocab modern tokenizers (100K+) clearly beat older ones.
findings.numbers: Llama3.1 1.88, Gemma 1.92 (5.2 cpt), GPT-4o 1.98, Mistral-Nemo 2.04, Mistral 2.48, Qwen 2.83
findings.relevance: Explains the user's measured baselines: Qwen3-0.6B leads on KazMMLU (32.8%) despite Qwen's WORST Cyrillic fertility (2.83), reinforcing that model quality/data > tokenizer fertility. Also sets the bar: any custom Kazakh tokenizer must beat ~1.9 (best generalist on Cyrillic) to justify itself — and morphology-aware Kazakh-only can reach ~1.7-2.0.
findings.source: Frontiers AI 2025, frai.2025.1538165 (Ukrainian tokenization efficiency)

findings.claim: Zero-Shot Tokenizer Transfer (ZeTT) trains a hypernetwork that predicts embeddings for ANY target tokenizer, letting you swap in a Kazakh-optimized tokenizer on a pretrained model with only 1-3% accuracy loss, fully recoverable with <1B tokens of continued training; it outperforms FOCUS. FOCUS itself initializes new embeddings as a fastText-similarity-weighted mean of overlapping tokens.
findings.numbers: 1-3% accuracy retention gap; <1B tokens to fully recover; beats FOCUS baseline
findings.relevance: Enables a strong alternative to from-scratch: take Qwen3-0.6B-Base (best baseline, 32.8%), transplant a low-fertility Kazakh Unigram tokenizer via ZeTT/FOCUS, continue-train on 9-10B Kazakh tokens. Inherits Qwen's reasoning while fixing fertility — likely beats both SozKZ-from-scratch and vanilla continued-pretraining.
findings.source: arXiv:2405.07883 (ZeTT); arXiv:2305.14481 (FOCUS)

findings.claim: For adding language-specific tokens to a pretrained model, 'continued BPE training' (re-run BPE on in-domain text starting from the existing merges) beats naive append because it avoids unreachable tokens; embeddings init via Fast Vocabulary Transfer (copy overlaps, average decompositions). For Cyrillic-script languages this gave 5.1-11.2% extra compression over naive extension; adapting Llama-3.2-1B/3B on 24B chars (50% target/50% English) recovered downstream parity and cut training time 26%.
findings.numbers: Cyrillic 5.1-11.2% compression gain over naive; +1-4K Estonian tokens = 3.3-3.8% (Qwen 9.6%); 24B chars recovers parity; -26% train time
findings.relevance: Precise recipe if grafting Kazakh tokens onto an existing tokenizer: use continued-BPE + FVT, budget ~24B characters (~byte-premium-adjusted) of 50/50 Kazakh/English to recover. Concrete numbers for the paper's methods section.
findings.source: arXiv:2512.03989 (Teaching Old Tokenizers New Words)

findings.claim: KazByte proposes a BLT-style byte-level adapter (6-8 layer local encoder + decoder, entropy-based byte patching, ~304M trainable params) wrapping a FROZEN Qwen2.5-7B, because swapping a tokenizer is 'a network-wide distribution shift, not a remapping problem.' A single inflected Kazakh verb is 10-12 Qwen-BPE tokens (~5x an English word). CRITICAL: the paper is a design proposal with NO empirical results yet.
findings.numbers: ~304M trainable / ~7B frozen; encoder/decoder 6-8 layers, 512 hidden, ~150M each; Kazakh verb 10-12 BPE tokens (~5x English); NO benchmarks
findings.relevance: Tells you byte/BLT is NOT a validated path at this budget: KazByte needs a 7B frozen body and is unproven. A pure-byte/patch 500M from-scratch model is not established for Kazakh. Better to use a byte-FALLBACK inside a subword tokenizer (SentencePiece byte_fallback=true) for robustness rather than a full byte model.
findings.source: arXiv:2603.27859 (KazByte)

findings.claim: Kazakh's Cyrillic->Latin transition is legally targeted for ~2031 and real-world text is heavily kk/ru code-switched. Transliteration tools (QazNLTK, national standard) give deterministic Cyrillic<->Latin mapping. VerChol (grammar-first FST tokenization) shows script-agnostic grammar rules can tokenize agglutinative languages, but is only implemented/validated on Tamil, with Turkic listed as future adaptation.
findings.numbers: Latin transition target ~2031; QazNLTK deterministic translit; VerChol validated only on Tamil
findings.relevance: Dual-script recommendation: train the tokenizer on BOTH Cyrillic and transliterated-Latin Kazakh so shared morphemes map to shared subwords (future-proofs for 2031 and handles mixed input), OR normalize all input to Cyrillic via deterministic transliteration before tokenizing. Reserve explicit vocab budget for Russian + Latin-Kazakh + basic English to cover code-switching.
findings.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazakh_alphabets ; arXiv:2603.05883 (VerChol)

findings.claim: STRR (Single-Token Retention Rate = % of words kept as one token) is a 2025 type-level diagnostic that exposes vocabulary misallocation that average fertility hides (e.g. it localizes which languages are over-fragmented, like Hindi's uniformly lowest STRR). Fertility 'collapses behavior into average tokens per word, masking over-fragmentation.'
findings.numbers: STRR = (1/n) sum 1[|T(w)|=1] x 100; complements fertility; no Turkic numbers reported yet
findings.relevance: Add STRR (and MorphScore) alongside fertility as evaluation metrics in the paper — reporting only fertility is now considered insufficient by 2025 tokenizer literature. Reviewers will expect the richer intrinsic metric suite.
findings.source: arXiv:2510.09947 (Beyond Fertility: STRR)

findings.claim: Optimal Turkish subword study (vocab 8K-256K) finds diminishing returns beyond ~128K, and that morphology-aware pretokenization yields small-but-consistent downstream gains (POS/NER/QA/sentiment) over a WordPiece baseline; character-level morphology micro-accuracy 96.19 vs 30.76 for BERTurk shows subword models discard morpheme structure that morph-aware methods preserve.
findings.numbers: vocab 8K-256K, diminishing returns >128K; morph micro-acc 96.19 (char) vs 30.76 (BERTurk); small consistent gains
findings.relevance: Independent Turkic confirmation that (a) very large vocabs stop helping, and (b) morphology-aware tokenization gives real, if modest, downstream gains — supporting a morphology-supervised Unigram vocab in the 48-64K range for Kazakh rather than chasing 128K+.
findings.source: arXiv:2602.06942 (Optimal Turkish Subword Strategies at Scale)

recommendations: PRIMARY TOKENIZER: SentencePiece Unigram-LM (not BPE) at vocab 48-64K, trained overwhelmingly on Kazakh with explicit carve-outs for Russian (~8-10K), Latin-Kazakh (~4-6K), and English (~4-6K). Unigram beats BPE on morpheme alignment (arXiv:2507.06378) and matches the user's existing choice. Expected Kazakh fertility ~1.9-2.0 tok/word (SozKZ/Sherkala both land ~2.0-2.04); with morphology supervision (below) target 1.7-1.9. Set byte_fallback=true for OOV/Latin/code-switch robustness instead of a full byte model.

MORPHOLOGY SUPERVISION AS THE NOVEL EDGE: Constrain tokenizer training so tokens do not cross morpheme boundaries, MorphBPE-style (arXiv:2502.00894), using gold Kazakh segmentation from apertium-kaz FST + KazMorphCorpus-2025 (150K sentences). This is feasible for Kazakh (the analyzers exist) even though it is blocked for most languages, and directly targets lower cross-entropy + faster convergence — the concrete lever to EXCEED SozKZ's vanilla ByteLevel-BPE. Report morphological-consistency F1 and MorphScore as intrinsic wins.

DO NOT adopt SuperBPE/superword tokens as the core tokenizer at 500M. Superwords need a ~200K vocab (>60% of a 500M param budget on embeddings, infeasible) and their gain is whitespace-compression on analytic languages; agglutinative Kazakh already packs a clause per whitespace-word, and IndicSuperTokenizer shows superwords give only +1.5% downstream while raising training loss (arXiv:2511.03237). If inference-cost matters later, a small superword tail (e.g. +4-8K) can be added post-hoc purely for throughput.

VOCAB SIZE FROM THE LOW END OF THE COMPUTE-OPTIMAL BAND: scaling laws (arXiv:2407.13623) put the compute-optimal vocab near 90-120K for 500M, but that assumes abundant data. With ~9-10B (byte-inflated) Kazakh tokens the model is data-constrained and a 100K+ vocab under-trains rare embeddings while consuming ~31% of params. Choose 48-64K (~15-20% embedding share at d=1536), keep embeddings TIED. This matches SozKZ (50K) and Sherkala's ~31K Kazakh delta.

STRONGLY CONSIDER A WARM-START FORK over pure from-scratch: transplant the Kazakh Unigram tokenizer onto Qwen3-0.6B-Base (the strongest measured baseline at 32.8% KazMMLU) using ZeTT (arXiv:2405.07883, 1-3% loss, <1B tokens to recover) or FOCUS/FVT + continued-BPE (arXiv:2512.03989, Cyrillic +5-11% compression), then continue-train on 9-10B Kazakh tokens. This inherits reasoning ability the from-scratch 600M models lack (SozKZ 30.3% < Qwen 32.8%) while fixing fertility. Run this as a head-to-head arm against the from-scratch design in the paper.

EMBEDDING INIT FOR NEW TOKENS: for any grafted tokens use the Sherkala recipe (arXiv:2503.01493) — average the top-5 most similar base-vocab token embeddings by a strong sentence/word-embedding similarity (multilingual fastText for FOCUS-style, or an embedding API). Do not random-init. This is the difference between recovering in <1B tokens vs needing full retraining.

DUAL-SCRIPT FUTURE-PROOFING: train the tokenizer on Cyrillic AND deterministically transliterated Latin-Kazakh (QazNLTK/national standard) so identical morphemes share subword IDs across scripts; this covers the ~2031 Latin transition and mixed-script input at ~4-6K extra vocab. Add a normalization option to map input to a canonical script before tokenizing to avoid duplicate morpheme fragmentation.

TREAT THE 9-10B TOKEN BUDGET AS BYTE-INFLATED: Kazakh Cyrillic is ~2 UTF-8 bytes/char, so byte-premium-adjusted content is materially smaller than an equal English budget (arXiv:2411.14198 shows this — not fertility — is the dominant driver of the morph-language gap). Prioritize expanding and cleaning Kazakh data (and using byte-premium-scaled data-size targets) over exotic tokenizer engineering; a lower-fertility tokenizer mainly buys more effective tokens-per-FLOP and longer context, not accuracy by itself.

EVALUATION METRIC SUITE for the paper: report fertility AND MorphScore (morpheme alignment, arXiv:2507.06378) AND STRR (single-token retention, arXiv:2510.09947) AND morphological-consistency F1 — reporting fertility alone is now considered insufficient by 2025 tokenizer literature and will draw reviewer criticism. Include per-script (Cyrillic vs Latin) and code-switch (kk/ru) breakdowns.
open_questions: Does a morphology-supervised (apertium-kaz-constrained) Unigram tokenizer actually lower final KazMMLU/eval vs a plain Unigram at the same 50-64K vocab, or only improve intrinsic morpheme metrics? MorphBPE shows loss/convergence gains but no clean Kazakh downstream number exists yet — this needs a direct ablation.

Warm-start (ZeTT-transplant onto Qwen3-0.6B) vs from-scratch 500M: which actually scores higher on KazMMLU at equal Kazakh-token budget? No head-to-head exists for Kazakh; this is the single highest-value experiment and could change the whole architecture thesis.

Exact byte premium for Kazakh Cyrillic relative to English (the 2411.14198 paper gives a framework and 'up to 5x' but not a Kazakh-specific figure) — needed to set a defensible byte-premium-adjusted data-size target for the 9-10B budget.

Optimal Kazakh:Russian:English:Latin-Kazakh vocab split — Sherkala used 3:1:3 Kk:Ru+Tr:En for training DATA but the tokenizer VOCAB allocation per language for a Kazakh-primary 500M model is unquantified; over-allocating to English wastes the tight embedding budget.

Whether apertium-kaz FST coverage is high enough on noisy web text (CulturaX/HPLT) to supply reliable morpheme boundaries at pretraining scale, or whether a fallback (Morfessor/unsupervised segmentation) is needed for OOV surface forms — coverage numbers on real corpora were not found.

findings.claim: Sherkala-Chat-8B is the current Kazakh SOTA at its scale and defines the KazMMLU bar: base model 51.6, chat 41.4 (5-shot avg). Its KazMMLU baselines: Llama-3.1(-8B) 38.3, Qwen-2.5(-7B) 35.1, ISSAI Llama-3.1-KazLLM-1.0 37.0, BLOOM-7.1B 29.3. Belebele-kaz 30.6, HellaSwag-kk 55.2, PIQA-kk 65.9. It is an ADAPTATION of Llama-3.1-8B, not from-scratch.
findings.numbers: 8B params; KazMMLU base 51.6 / chat 41.4; baselines 38.3/35.1/37.0/29.3; Belebele 30.6
findings.relevance: Sets the realistic ceiling a <=600M model must 'approach': ~41 chat / ~51 base at 8B. A 600M model landing in the mid-30s would already beat all general <=1B baselines; landing near 40 would be paper-worthy.
findings.source: arXiv 2503.01493 (Sherkala-Chat), html v2

findings.claim: Sherkala's tokenizer recipe is directly reusable and hits the user's fertility<2.0 target: expanded Llama-3.1 vocab 128,256 -> 159,766 (+31,510 tokens, +25%), cutting Kazakh fertility from 4.73 to 2.04 tok/word (-56.8%). New embeddings initialized via WECHSEL using OpenAI text-embedding-3-large, top-k=5, applied to input AND output layers. Continued-pretrain: LR 1.5e-4, 4M-token global batch, 8192 ctx, AdamW (b1 0.9, b2 0.95, wd 0.1), grad clip 1.0.
findings.numbers: vocab 128256->159766 (+31510); fertility 4.73->2.04; WECHSEL k=5; LR 1.5e-4; batch 4M; ctx 8192
findings.relevance: Concrete, proven numbers to drop into the tokenizer+init spec. WECHSEL embedding init (not random) is the standard for new Kazakh tokens; the user's SentencePiece-Unigram-50K plan should target ~2.0 fertility, and vocab of ~50-60K is consistent with Sherkala's added-token count for Kazakh.
findings.source: arXiv 2503.01493, extracted config tables

findings.claim: Sherkala's 45.3B-token data mix is the proven Kazakh recipe: Kazakh 19.45B (43%) / English 19.45B (43%) / Russian+Turkish 6.4B (14%). 76% of the Kazakh corpus is real web (Wikipedia, CommonCrawl, CulturaX, news); 24% is SYNTHETIC (English Wikipedia machine-translated to Kazakh). English/Russian/Turkish from The Pile + CommonCrawl.
findings.numbers: 45.3B total; kk 19.45B / en 19.45B / ru+tr 6.4B; 24% of Kazakh is synthetic MT
findings.relevance: Confirms the winning mix is ~40% English co-training + controlled Russian/Turkish (NOT broad multilinguality), plus ~24% synthetic to fill the knowledge gap. The user's 9-10B pure-Kazakh plan should add English + a synthetic-translation slice; English co-data at this ratio is load-bearing for KazMMLU knowledge.

findings.claim: SozKZ (the closest prior art: from-scratch Kazakh 50M-600M) does NOT beat a general Qwen2.5-0.5B on knowledge QA. SozKZ-600M (587M, 22 layers, d=1280, 20 heads MHA, ctx 2048, ffn 4480, 50K BPE, 9B tokens) scores: cultural MC-QA 30.3, Belebele-kaz 27.0, SIB-200 25.5. Qwen2.5-0.5B scores 31.5 / 30.0 / 19.1; Llama-3.2-1B 32.0 / 26.7 / 20.1. SozKZ only wins on SIB-200 topic classification. It was NEVER evaluated on KazMMLU.
findings.relevance: CRITICAL reframing: the grounding note 'SozKZ ~30% KazMMLU' is wrong — that 30.3 is cultural QA, and it LOSES to Qwen2.5-0.5B on knowledge. Pure from-scratch at 600M has not beaten a strong general 0.5B on knowledge. This argues strongly for continued-pretrain/vocab-surgery on a Qwen-0.6B base as a hedge, or for the Engram memory being the differentiator that from-scratch SozKZ lacked.
findings.source: arXiv 2603.20854 (SozKZ), html Table 1-2; corroborated in 2603.27859 Table 6

findings.claim: As of mid-2026 no published DEDICATED <=1B model reports a strong KazMMLU number; the practical <=1B ceiling is held by general Qwen (user-measured Qwen3-0.6B-Base ~32.8, Qwen2.5-0.5B ~28.8; Qwen2.5-1.5B ~34.3 is >1B). KazMMLU's own paper only tested >=1.1B (Bloom-1.1B lowest at 22.1). No from-scratch or adapted <=600M Kazakh model has published a KazMMLU score above random-to-low-30s.
findings.numbers: Qwen3-0.6B ~32.8; Qwen2.5-0.5B ~28.8; Bloom-1.1B 22.1; random ~25 (4-choice)
findings.relevance: The competitive target is explicit: beat ~33 KazMMLU (Qwen3-0.6B) to claim SOTA among <=1B. This is a low, reachable bar for a Kazakh-dedicated 600M with Engram memory + English co-training, making the paper's headline claim defensible.
findings.source: arXiv 2502.12829 (KazMMLU) leaderboard; user-measured baselines in grounding

findings.claim: KazMMLU dataset composition (primary eval): 23,000 MCQs, Kazakh 10,969 (48%) / Russian 12,031 (52%), 4 options each. High-school subjects exist in BOTH languages; university/professional subjects (Law, Economics, Medicine) are Russian-ONLY. All models score higher on the Russian subset and higher when prompted in English. Frontier: DeepSeek-V3 76.9, GPT-4o 76.6, Gemma-2-27B 57.4, Llama-3.1-70B 56.2.
findings.numbers: 23K Q (kk 10,969 / ru 12,031); professional=Russian-only; DeepSeek-V3 76.9, Llama-3.1-70B 56.2
findings.relevance: Report the Kazakh-only subset separately — the Russian-heavy professional split inflates scores and rewards Russian ability, not Kazakh. A Kazakh-specialist 600M should be evaluated and marketed on the ~11K Kazakh questions; co-training Russian helps the ru subset 'for free'.
findings.source: arXiv 2502.12829, ACL 2025.acl-long.701

findings.claim: TUMLU-mini is the Turkic secondary eval: Kazakh subset = 700 Q (7 subjects x 100, Cyrillic). All models score higher on Kazakh in CYRILLIC than Latin. Best small-open on Kazakh: Gemma-2-9B 49.1, Llama-3.1-8B 46.4, Qwen2.5-7B 45.0; frontier Claude-3.5-Sonnet 83.0 (87.1 with 5-shot CoT). No <=1B model was tested. FineWeb-2 has 1.8B Kazakh Cyrillic words and 0 Latin.
findings.numbers: Kazakh TUMLU-mini 700 Q; Gemma-2-9B 49.1 / Llama-3.1-8B 46.4 / Qwen2.5-7B 45.0; Claude-3.5-Sonnet 83.0
findings.relevance: Train and evaluate in Cyrillic only for now — Latin Kazakh web data is essentially nonexistent, so the 2031 Latin transition is a pure data gap, not something to pre-train on. Handle Latin via deterministic Cyrillic<->Latin transliteration augmentation, not native Latin corpora.
findings.source: arXiv 2502.11020 (TUMLU), html v2, Table 2 + Appendix B

findings.claim: Engram (the user's conditional-memory choice) is verified real and validated at scale: suffix N-grams of canonicalized tokens hashed via K multiplicative-XOR heads into prime-sized embedding tables, O(1) lookup, ~0 extra FLOPs, deterministic addressing enables host-memory prefetch. Scaled to 27B, it BEATS a strictly iso-parameter and iso-FLOP MoE baseline (gains in knowledge retrieval, reasoning, code/math). Introduces a U-shaped 'Sparsity Allocation' scaling law trading neural compute (MoE) vs static memory (Engram).
findings.numbers: 27B scale, beats iso-param/iso-FLOP MoE; K multiplicative-XOR hash heads; prime-sized tables; O(1)
findings.relevance: Strong support for keeping Engram as the differentiator vs from-scratch SozKZ.
