The U-shaped scaling law is the concrete tuning knob: at 600M, size the n-gram hash tables against neural params along that curve rather than fixing ~512M sparse params arbitrarily. Knowledge-retrieval gains map directly to KazMMLU.
findings.source: arXiv 2601.07372 (Conditional Memory via Scalable Lookup / Engram)

findings.claim: mHC (the user's residual-stream choice) is verified real (DeepSeek, published 2025-12-31): projects Hyper-Connections mixing matrices onto the Birkhoff polytope (doubly-stochastic matrices) via a differentiable Sinkhorn-Knopp iteration in the forward pass, restoring the identity-mapping property that raw HC breaks. Fixes HC training instability and memory-access overhead; demonstrated effective and more scalable than HC at scale.
findings.numbers: Birkhoff polytope / doubly-stochastic; Sinkhorn-Knopp; published 2025-12-31; DeepSeek authors
findings.relevance: Supports keeping mHC (n=4 streams). The identity-mapping restoration is what makes width-expanded residuals trainable stably at small scale on a tight A100-40GB budget. Note both Engram and mHC were validated at >=27B — their retention at <=600M is an open empirical question and a natural ablation for the paper.

findings.claim: MLA gives a concrete cache win over the user's planned GQA-2. DeepSeek-V2 MLA config: kv_lora_rank d_c=512, decoupled-RoPE per-head dim d_h^R=64, q_lora_rank 1536, v/qk head dim 128, 128 heads, d=5120. KV cache per token = (d_c + d_h^R)*L = 576*L elements — equivalent to GQA with only 2.25 groups, a 93.3% reduction vs MHA, while scoring STRONGER than MHA (GQA/MQA lose quality to save cache; MLA does not).
findings.numbers: d_c=512, d_h^R=64 -> 576*L elem/token = GQA-2.25 groups; 93.3% less than MHA; stronger than MHA
findings.relevance: Actionable swap: replace GQA-2 with MLA. At d~1280-1536 for a 600M model, set kv_lora_rank~256-320 and qk_rope_head_dim~32-64; cache per token ~ (288-384)*L vs GQA-2's ~2*n_kv*d_head*L. This roughly halves-to-quarters the KV cache vs GQA-2 with equal-or-better quality, freeing A100-40GB memory for longer ctx or larger batch.
findings.source: arXiv 2405.04434 (DeepSeek-V2), html v5 architecture tables

findings.claim: Real deduplicated Kazakh web-corpus sizes (ceiling is ~9-10B unique tokens, matching SozKZ's 9B): HPLT 2.0 kaz_Cyrl deduped 27.43 GB / 5.16M docs / 2.00B words (cleaned 20.24 GB); HPLT 3.0 kaz_Cyrl 7.34B tokens / 5.12M docs / 17.21B chars; FineWeb-2 Kazakh ~1.8B Cyrillic words. Overlap across CulturaX/HPLT/mC4/MADLAD is heavy (CulturaX<->FineWeb2 share 25.8B tokens globally), so naive concatenation double-counts.
findings.numbers: HPLT2.0 kaz 2.00B words/27.43GB; HPLT3.0 kaz 7.34B tokens; FineWeb-2 kaz ~1.8B words
findings.relevance: Budget realistically: HPLT 3.0 (7.34B) is the single largest clean Kazakh source; add FineWeb-2 (~2.5B tok) + curated (kz-transformers multidomain, news, Wiki) and cross-dedup to reach ~9-10B UNIQUE tokens. To train longer than ~1 epoch you MUST add English/Russian/Turkish co-data or synthetic — the pure-Kazakh well is ~10B and repeating it >2-3x risks overfitting.
findings.source: hplt-project.org/datasets v2.0 & v3.0; arXiv 2511.01066 (HPLT 3.0); FineWeb-2 count via arXiv 2502.11020

findings.claim: Broad multilingual coverage HURTS Kazakh via sibling-language interference: Aya Expanse (100+ languages, incl. Turkic) collapses to 15.7% on Kazakh (vs 82.3% English) because it frequently emits KYRGYZ instead of Kazakh. Cross-lingual-transfer pipelines give only marginal Kazakh gains (+0.4pp CLT aggregate; +2.2pp for bilingual models). Kazakh-Kyrgyz-Turkish proximity causes generation leakage, not free transfer.
findings.numbers: Aya Expanse Kazakh 15.7% vs English 82.3%; CLT +0.4pp; bilingual +2.2pp
findings.relevance: Design implication: do NOT chase broad Turkic multilinguality. Use CONTROLLED co-training (Kazakh-dominant + English for knowledge + limited Russian/Turkish), exactly Sherkala's mix — not an Aya-style 100-language soup. Add a language-ID / script guard in eval to catch Kyrgyz leakage. Turkish co-data helps tokenizer/morphology sharing but must be capped to avoid output drift.
findings.source: arXiv 2603.21036 (cross-lingual transfer); Aya numbers corroborated across 2 sources

findings.claim: Morphology-aware tokenization is a validated lever for Kazakh. A CSE-guided (Complete Set of Endings) SentencePiece tokenizer that pre-segments on morpheme boundaries yields shorter sequences and up to ~33% neural training-time reduction; SentencePiece Unigram beats BPE on morpheme-boundary preservation and lower fertility for agglutinative Kazakh. Kazakh morphotactics: 64 theoretical affix slots, only 15 linguistically valid (vowel-harmony/morphophonemic constrained). Open tooling exists: Apertium-kaz transducer + UD Kazakh treebank.
findings.numbers: up to ~33% training-time cut; 64 affix slots, 15 valid; Unigram < BPE fertility
findings.relevance: Concrete tokenizer upgrade over plain Unigram-50K: pre-segment the training corpus with a CSE/Apertium-kaz morphological analyzer before training SentencePiece-Unigram, so subwords align to real morpheme boundaries. This is the mechanism to actually reach fertility<2.0 AND improve morphological generalization — validate fertility on UD-kaz/Apertium gold segmentation.
findings.source: MDPI Information 17(2):128 (CSE-guided, Jan 2026); github walsher46/Kazakh-tokenizer; Apertium-kaz

findings.claim: A byte-level alternative to BPE is being staked for Kazakh but is UNPROVEN: KazByte/ByteKaz (arXiv 2603.27859, 29 Mar 2026) proposes a BLT-style entropy-patch byte encoder+decoder (~304M trainable, 6-8 layers d=512 each) wrapping a frozen Qwen2.5-7B, motivated by a single inflected Kazakh verb costing 10-12 BPE tokens (~5x an English word). It is a PROPOSAL PAPER with NO empirical results ('ByteKaz results marked —, not yet measured').
findings.numbers: ~304M trainable / ~7B frozen; 10-12 BPE tokens per inflected verb (~5x English); zero results
findings.relevance: Signals byte/morpheme-level tokenization as the live frontier for Turkic, but there is no evidence it works yet — do NOT bet the architecture on byte-latent. The safer, evidence-backed path is morphology-aware SentencePiece (finding above). KazByte can be cited as related work the proposed model empirically outperforms.
findings.source: arXiv 2603.27859 (KazByte), html + Table 6

findings.claim: Qolda (ISSAI, Qwen3-4B base, 4.3B params) is the strongest recent Kazakh SLM data point above 1B: zero-shot ~60.37 avg across KazMMLU+KazCulture, rising to 76.00 with naive-RAG web search in reasoning mode. It is a Qwen3 ADAPTATION, not from-scratch, reinforcing that adapting a strong base + Kazakh data beats building from zero.
findings.numbers: 4.3B params; zero-shot 60.37 -> 76.00 with web-search RAG
findings.relevance: Two takeaways: (1) at 4B, adapting Qwen3 reaches ~60 zero-shot — adaptation scales cleanly, supporting a Qwen3-0.6B warm-start hedge for the 600M model; (2) retrieval/RAG adds ~+16pp, a cheap orthogonal booster the paper could add as an inference-time option without extra params.
findings.source: MDPI MAKE 8(5):128; HF issai/Qolda

recommendations: TOKENIZER: Train SentencePiece Unigram ~48-64K on Kazakh-dominant + English + Russian + Turkish text, but PRE-SEGMENT the Kazakh side with a CSE/Apertium-kaz morphological analyzer so subwords align to morpheme boundaries. Target fertility <=2.0 tok/word (Sherkala proved 2.04 is reachable at 159K multilingual vocab; a Kazakh-specialist vocab hits it at ~50K). Validate fertility against UD-Kazakh / Apertium gold segmentation, and initialize any transplanted embeddings with WECHSEL (k=5) rather than random.

ATTENTION/CACHE: Replace the planned GQA-2 with MLA. At d~1280-1536 use kv_lora_rank~256-320, qk_rope_head_dim~32-64, q_lora_rank~768. This makes KV cache ~(288-384)*L elements/token (DeepSeek-V2's formula (d_c+d_h^R)*L), roughly 2-4x smaller than GQA-2 at equal-or-better quality, freeing A100-40GB memory for 8K context and larger batch. Keep RoPE theta=500K on the decoupled RoPE dim.

MEMORY (Engram): Keep Engram {2,3}-gram conditional memory as the core differentiator (SozKZ from-scratch 600M FAILED to beat Qwen2.5-0.5B on knowledge precisely because it had no memory axis). Size the hash tables against neural params using Engram's U-shaped Sparsity-Allocation scaling law rather than a fixed ~512M; run an ablation at 600M since Engram was only validated at 27B. Place at layers {2, L/4} as planned.

RESIDUALS (mHC): Keep mHC n=4 with the Birkhoff-polytope/Sinkhorn-Knopp projection for training stability at small scale, but include a with/without-mHC ablation — mHC's gains are documented at large scale, so the paper needs to show it helps (or is neutral) at 600M.

DATA MIX: Do NOT train on ~10B pure Kazakh alone (that well is ~9-10B unique after cross-dedup: HPLT 3.0 kaz 7.34B + FineWeb-2 ~2.5B + curated). Adopt a Sherkala-style controlled mix: Kazakh-dominant + ~30-40% English (for KazMMLU knowledge) + a capped Russian/Turkish slice + ~15-25% synthetic (MT of English Wikipedia/textbooks into Kazakh). AVOID broad 100-language multilinguality — it causes Kyrgyz output leakage (Aya collapsed to 15.7% Kazakh).

STRATEGIC HEDGE: Run TWO tracks and report both — (a) from-scratch 600M + Engram + MLA + mHC, and (b) continued-pretrain / vocab-surgery on Qwen3-0.6B-Base. Evidence (SozKZ < Qwen-0.5B; Qolda-4B adaptation ~60; Sherkala adaptation SOTA) says adaptation is the safer route to top KazMMLU; the from-scratch track is the novel-architecture contribution. If from-scratch underperforms Qwen3-0.6B (~32.8 KazMMLU), the adapted track guarantees a shippable SOTA <=1B claim.

SCRIPT: Train and evaluate in CYRILLIC only (Latin Kazakh web data ~= 0). Serve the coming Latin transition via deterministic Cyrillic<->Latin transliteration augmentation at train and inference time, not native Latin corpora.

EVAL: Report KazMMLU 5-shot with the Kazakh-only subset (10,969 Q) broken out from the Russian subset; add TUMLU-mini Kazakh (700 Q, Cyrillic), Belebele-kaz, KazQAD F1, and FLORES-200 kaz<->eng/rus. Add a language-ID guard to detect Kyrgyz/Russian leakage in Kazakh generations. Competitive bar to beat for a SOTA <=1B claim: Qwen3-0.6B-Base ~32.8 KazMMLU; stretch target: approach Sherkala-Chat-8B's 41.4.
open_questions: Exact FineWeb-2 kaz_Cyrl TOKEN count is unconfirmed — only ~1.8B Cyrillic WORDS is documented (implies ~2.5-3B tokens); verify against the HF dataset viewer before finalizing the data budget.

Do Engram (validated at 27B) and mHC (validated at scale) retain their gains at <=600M? Neither has published small-scale results — this must be ablated and is a genuine risk to the from-scratch track.

No published <=1B model reports a strong KazMMLU score; the ~32.8 Qwen3-0.6B figure is the user's own measurement, not an independent leaderboard. An independent sub-1B KazMMLU leaderboard does not appear to exist as of mid-2026.
KazByte's byte-latent approach has zero empirical results (proposal only) — whether byte/morpheme-level beats morphology-aware SentencePiece for Kazakh is unresolved.
SozKZ did not report tokenizer fertility as an absolute number (only '2-3x better than multilingual'), so the exact from-scratch 50K-BPE Kazakh fertility is unverified.

Quantitative evidence that Turkish/Kyrgyz co-training specifically HELPS Kazakh (beyond tokenizer sharing) is weak (+2.2pp bilingual, +0.4pp CLT); the benefit may be mostly tokenizer/morphology sharing rather than knowledge transfer.

findings.claim: SmolLM2's smaller models were NOT multi-stage: 360M (4T tokens, ~11 tok/param) and 135M (2T, ~15 tok/param) used a single-stage high-quality-data recipe, while only the 1.7B used 4-stage mixing over 11T. WSD schedule, peak LR 3.0e-3 for 360M (5.0e-4 for 1.7B), 10-20% linear decay tail, global batch ~2M tokens, AdamW beta=(0.9,0.95), vocab 49,152. The decay/anneal stage up-weights the best data (FineMath4+, Stack-Edu, Cosmopedia v2, InfiWebMath).
findings.numbers: 360M=4T tok (~11/param); 135M=2T (~15/param); 1.7B=11T (~6.5/param); LR 3e-3(360M)/5e-4(1.7B); batch ~2M tok; vocab 49,152; decay=last 10-20%
findings.relevance: A 500M model is in the 'single-stage high-quality' regime, not multi-stage. Directly sets LR (~3e-3), batch (~2M tok), vocab (~50K matches user's Unigram-50K), and the anneal-on-best-data pattern for the Kazakh from-scratch run.
findings.source: arXiv 2502.02737 SmolLM2: When Smol Goes Big (arxiv.org/html/2502.02737v1)

findings.claim: MiniCPM's WSD scheduler yields a compute-optimal data-to-parameter ratio of ~192 tokens/param (vs Chinchilla ~20), and crucially: introducing high-quality + SFT-style data at the START of the decay/annealing phase gives far larger gains than adding the same data in a post-anneal SFT stage. muP-style hyperparameters were transferred from sub-100M 'wind tunnel' proxies to full scale.
findings.numbers: compute-optimal ~192 tok/param; anneal-injection >> post-anneal SFT injection; muP proxy <100M
findings.relevance: Compute-optimal for 500M is ~96B tokens — far more than ~10B unique Kazakh, confirming the corpus must be padded with transfer/synthetic data. The anneal-injection finding says: front-load curated Kazakh (textbooks/QA/CoT) into decay, don't reserve it for SFT.
findings.source: arXiv 2404.06395 MiniCPM (arxiv.org/html/2404.06395v1)

findings.claim: Data-constrained scaling: training up to ~4 epochs of repeated data incurs negligible loss penalty vs equivalent fresh tokens; returns decay sharply after, with ~16 epochs marking strong diminishing returns. Validated up to 900B tokens and 9B params.
findings.numbers: <=4 epochs ~= fresh data; ~16 epochs = diminishing; experiments <=900B tok, <=9B params
findings.relevance: With ~10B unique Kazakh tokens, repeating up to 4 epochs (~40B Kazakh 'visits') is provably near-free. Cap Kazakh at <=4 epochs and fill the remaining budget with Russian (code-switch), Turkic, English and synthetic data rather than over-repeating Kazakh.
findings.source: arXiv 2305.16264 Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models (Muennighoff et al., NeurIPS 2023)

findings.claim: Step Law gives directly usable fitted formulas for optimal hyperparameters: learning rate eta(N,D)=1.79*N^-0.713*D^0.307 and batch size B(D)=0.58*D^0.571 (N=non-embedding params, D=tokens). Claimed within ~0.09-0.5% of the exhaustive optimum, and shown topology-invariant across model shapes, robust across bilingual/code-heavy data mixes and MoE sparsity levels.
findings.numbers: eta=1.79*N^-0.713*D^0.307; B=0.58*D^0.571; error ~0.09% dense, <=0.5% MoE; for N~3.5e8, D~20B my plug-in gives eta~2e-3 and batch ~0.4-0.5M tokens
findings.relevance: Removes the need for an expensive muP sweep on the $264 budget: plug in N,D to get LR~2e-3 and batch ~0.4-0.5M tokens for a 500M/~20-40B run. Explicitly validated on bilingual corpora, matching the kk/ru code-switching setting.
findings.source: arXiv 2503.04715 Predictable Scale Part I: Step Law (arxiv.org/html/2503.04715)

findings.claim: Qwen3 (the user's strongest measured ~500M baseline at 32.8% KazMMLU) was pretrained on 36T tokens over 119 languages in 3 stages: ~30T general (4K ctx) -> ~5T STEM/coding/reasoning/synthetic (4K) -> long-context (32K). Qwen3-0.6B thus sees ~60,000 tokens/param (extreme deployment overtraining) and its thinking mode comes from a strong-to-weak distillation pipeline (off-policy then on-policy).
findings.numbers: 36T tokens, 119 langs; 30T+5T+long-ctx; Qwen3-0.6B ~60,000 tok/param; KazMMLU 32.8% (user-measured)
findings.relevance: Explains why beating Qwen3-0.6B on a ~$264 budget can't be won on raw token count — it must be won on Kazakh data density, tokenizer fertility (<2.0), and targeted architecture. The distillation-thinking pipeline is the template if adding a Kazakh reasoning mode.
findings.source: arXiv 2505.09388 Qwen3 Technical Report

findings.claim: All Gemma 3 sizes are trained with knowledge distillation: 256 logits per token are sampled and weighted by teacher probabilities, student learns via cross-entropy over that sample plus standard next-token loss. Gemma 3-270M was overtrained on 6T tokens (~22,000 tok/param) vs Gemma 3-1B on 2T; 256K vocab, 140+ pretraining languages. 270M reaches IFEval 51.2% vs Qwen2.5-0.5B 42%.
findings.numbers: 256 logits/token sampled; 270M=6T (~22k/param); 1B=2T; vocab 256K; 140+ langs; IFEval 270M 51.2% > Qwen2.5-0.5B 42%
findings.relevance: Concrete, cheap-to-implement logit-KD recipe (sample 256 teacher logits, not full 50K vocab) that fits limited memory. Shows overtraining a tiny model on 6T tokens materially helps — but requires a teacher that is fluent in Kazakh.
findings.source: arXiv 2503.19786 Gemma 3 Technical Report

findings.claim: 'Strong Teacher Not Needed' finds a stronger teacher is NOT always better in pretraining distillation: pushing the teacher to more params or more training tokens can saturate or even reverse the distillation gain, while even small/undertrained teachers improve larger students when the LM loss and KD loss are properly mixed. Distillation improves OOD/downstream generalization more readily than in-domain fitting.
findings.numbers: non-monotonic teacher-quality effect; small/undertrained teachers still help; KD helps OOD>in-domain (exact optimal size-ratio not verifiable from available text)
findings.relevance: De-risks teacher choice for Kazakh: a modestly-sized Kazakh-fluent teacher (e.g. Sherkala-8B) can beat a giant non-Kazakh one. Don't over-invest in the largest teacher; prioritize the teacher's Kazakh competence and mix KD with the LM loss.
findings.source: arXiv 2605.23857 Strong Teacher Not Needed? On Distillation in LLM Pretraining (Lu & Liu)

findings.claim: MobileLLM-R1-950M (22 layers, 1536 dim, 24 heads / 6 KV = GQA 4:1, 128K vocab, embedding tying) was pretrained on only 4.2T tokens (~4,400 tok/param, resampled from ~2T curated) in 2 WSD phases (peak LR 4.0e-3, 2K warmup, linear decay to 10% over 500K steps), with phase-1 logit KD from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. It matches/beats Qwen3-0.6B on math/code (MATH500 74.0 vs 73.0, AIME24 15.5 vs 11.3, LiveCodeBench 19.9 vs 14.9) using 11.7% of Qwen3's tokens; reasoning SFT gave large gains and SFT beat RL for the tiny model.
findings.numbers: 950M, GQA 4:1, 128K vocab; 4.2T tok (~4.4k/param); LR 4e-3; MATH500 74.0 vs Qwen3-0.6B 73.0; AIME24 15.5 vs 11.3; SFT>RL
findings.relevance: Proof that a sub-1B from-scratch model with careful data + light KD + reasoning SFT can beat Qwen3-0.6B — the user's exact goal. Validates GQA 4:1 (user has 2:1), LR ~4e-3, logit-KD from an 8B teacher, and a reasoning-SFT stage. 360M/140M variants exist too.
findings.source: arXiv 2509.24945 MobileLLM-R1 (arxiv.org/html/2509.24945)

findings.claim: Sherkala-8B (the Kazakh SOTA at 41.4% KazMMLU) is a continual pretrain of Llama-3.1-8B on 45.3B tokens: 19.45B Kazakh + 19.45B English + 6.4B Russian+Turkish, i.e. a 3:1:3 Kazakh:(Ru+Tr):English mix explicitly chosen to avoid English catastrophic forgetting. Tokenizer extended +25% with new Kazakh subwords, new embeddings initialized as weighted averages of nearest base embeddings; LSH dedup + language-specific cleaning.
findings.numbers: 45.3B tokens total; 19.45B kk + 19.45B en + 6.4B (ru+tr); 3:1:3 mix; tokenizer +25%; KazMMLU 41.4%
findings.relevance: A proven-for-Kazakh data mix and the strongest realistic Kazakh distillation teacher. The 3:1:3 ratio is a concrete starting point; the embedding-init-by-nearest-neighbor trick applies if extending a base tokenizer instead of training Unigram-50K from scratch.
findings.source: arXiv 2503.01493 Sherkala-Chat 8B (arxiv.org/html/2503.01493v2)

findings.claim: Aya Expanse (8B/32B) does NOT support Kazakh (its 23 languages exclude it); empirically it collapses to 15.7% on Kazakh direct eval and frequently outputs Kyrgyz instead of Kazakh. Gemma 3 (140+ langs) and Qwen3 (119 langs) nominally include far more languages.
findings.numbers: Aya Expanse: 23 langs, Kazakh excluded; 82.3% English vs 15.7% Kazakh; outputs Kyrgyz
findings.relevance: Disqualifies Aya as a Kazakh teacher despite its multilingual reputation. Teacher selection for KD/synthetic data must be verified on actual Kazakh output — favor Sherkala-8B, or verify Qwen3/Gemma3 Kazakh fluency before committing.
findings.source: arXiv 2412.04261 Aya Expanse; Kazakh failure numbers from arXiv 2603.21036 (Left Behind: Cross-Lingual Transfer)

findings.claim: Continual language addition without original-data replay: LayRA (LoRA applied only to the first ~10 and last ~2 transformer layers, rank 8, alpha 16, LR 3e-4 linear) gives the best forgetting-vs-learning tradeoff among full-CPT, LoRA-CPT, and layer-selective CPT on Llama-3.1-8B / Qwen-2.5-7B adding Galician/Swahili/Urdu (~1.2B tokens each). Standard replay (re-mixing original-language data) remains the most common forgetting mitigation when original data IS available.
findings.numbers: LoRA rank 8 alpha 16, LR 3e-4; first-10 + last-2 layers; ~1.2B tokens/new-language; 8B/7B bases
findings.relevance: If the path becomes continual-pretraining a strong small base (Qwen3-0.6B is already 32.8%) rather than from-scratch, LayRA gives a cheap, forgetting-safe recipe. Since the user HAS Kazakh+Russian+English data, explicit replay mixing (Sherkala-style) is preferable to replay-free.
findings.source: arXiv 2509.11414 Continually Adding New Languages to Multilingual LMs (arxiv.org/html/2509.11414v1)

findings.claim: FP8 pretraining yields ~34-37% throughput gain and ~42% memory reduction and can match bf16 accuracy, BUT native FP8 tensor cores exist only on Hopper (H100) and Blackwell (B200); naive FP8 is unstable and needs per-tensor scaling / selective bf16 layers. The user's A100 40GB (Ampere) has NO FP8 support.
findings.numbers: FP8: +34-37% throughput, -42% memory (H100); A100=Ampere, no FP8 tensor cores
findings.relevance: Hard constraint: on the specified 1xA100 budget, bf16 is the correct and only sensible precision. FP8 is irrelevant unless the run moves to H100/B200. Don't spec FP8.
findings.source: arXiv 2310.18313 FP8-LM; arXiv 2405.18710 To FP8 and Back Again; NVIDIA FP8 blog

findings.claim: YuLan-Mini (2.42B from scratch, 1.08T tokens, ~447 tok/param) reaches MMLU 49.1 / MATH-500 37.8 / HumanEval 64 — competitive with far-more-data models — using a documented small-scale stability kit: muP-style init sigma=sqrt(2/5d), WeSaR learnable-scalar reparam, embedding-output scaled x10, residual scaling 1.4/sqrt(n_layers), z-loss (1e-4), 10B-token warmup, embedding tying; WSD split 10B warm / 990B stable / 80B anneal (8%).
findings.numbers: 2.42B, 1.08T tok (~447/param); init sigma=sqrt(2/5d); residual 1.4/sqrt(L); z-loss 1e-4; anneal=8% of stable; MMLU 49.1
findings.relevance: Turnkey recipe to prevent loss spikes when training 500M from scratch on a tiny compute budget (spikes waste money). Adopt z-loss, residual/embedding scaling, muP-style init, long warmup, and an ~8-10% anneal tail wholesale.
findings.source: arXiv 2412.17743 YuLan-Mini (arxiv.org/html/2412.17743)

findings.claim: Textbook-quality synthetic data (Phi lineage) works, but for low-resource languages MT-translated data injects 'translationese' (non-native structures, NMT errors) that limits naturalness; prompt-space transforms recover up to +4.7pp on G-MMLU, and Phi-style 10-gram-overlap decontamination is needed to keep benchmarks clean.
findings.numbers: Phi: 6B filtered + 1B synthetic textbook tokens; translationese mitigation +4.7pp G-MMLU; 10-gram decontam
findings.relevance: Synthetic Kazakh is essential to pad the token budget, but must be generated by a Kazakh-fluent model (not raw MT) and prompt-space-diversified, then 10-gram decontaminated against KazMMLU/TUMLU/KazQAD to avoid inflating the very benchmarks the paper reports.
findings.source: arXiv 2306.11644 Textbooks Are All You Need (Phi-1); HF Cosmopedia; arXiv 2510.01631 Demystifying Synthetic Data in Pretraining

findings.claim: muP alone does not guarantee learning-rate transfer in practice — recent work argues weight decay may matter more than muP for LR transfer. Combined with Step Law's directly-fitted LR/batch formulas, an explicit muP sweep is largely avoidable for a single 500M target.
findings.numbers: muP width/depth transfer theoretically justified but WD-dependent empirically; u-muP adds unit-scaling for low precision
findings.relevance: On a one-shot 500M/$264 budget, skip a costly muP proxy sweep: use Step Law's formula for LR/batch and tune weight decay (~0.1) instead. Keep muP-style init (from YuLan-Mini) only for stability, not for HP transfer.
findings.source: arXiv 2510.19093 Weight Decay may matter more than muP; arXiv (ICLR 2025) u-muP

findings.claim: Reasoning/CoT capability can emerge in sub-billion models via careful data curation + reasoning SFT, and SFT outperforms RL at that scale (MobileLLM-R1); Qwen3-0.6B likewise obtains its thinking mode through distillation, not scale. But this requires reasoning-SFT data in the target language, which barely exists for Kazakh.
findings.numbers: reasoning emerges <1B; SFT>RL for tiny models; MobileLLM-R1 uses Tulu-3-SFT + OpenMath/Code/Science-Reasoning-2
findings.relevance: A light Kazakh CoT-SFT stage is worth including and can differentiate the paper, but the CoT data must be synthesized/translated (via a Kazakh-fluent teacher) since native Kazakh reasoning corpora are absent — a real risk and a novel contribution angle.
findings.source: arXiv 2509.24945 MobileLLM-R1; arXiv 2505.09388 Qwen3

findings.claim: Curriculum/order: starting from high-resource competence then adapting to the low-resource language exploits cross-lingual transfer and is effective, whereas naively mixing many languages from scratch triggers the 'curse of multilinguality' (per-language degradation as language count grows). For a focused set (Kazakh + Russian + Turkic + English) the curse is manageable.
findings.numbers: curse-of-multilinguality worsens with #languages; high-resource-first curriculum aids transfer
findings.relevance: Argues for a two-phase from-scratch curriculum: an English/Russian/Turkic-heavy early phase to build transferable structure, then a Kazakh-heavy stable+anneal phase — rather than a flat uniform-Kazakh mix or a many-language soup.
findings.source: General cross-lingual-transfer literature; consistent with Sherkala 2503.01493 mix design

recommendations: Token budget over Kazakh-only: build a ~30-60B-token training corpus. Cap unique Kazakh (~10B) at <=4 epochs (Muennighoff: near-free up to 4x), and fill the rest with Russian (models kk/ru code-switching), Turkic (Turkish + other Turkic for cross-lingual transfer), an English/code anchor, and Kazakh-fluent synthetic data. Do NOT over-repeat Kazakh past ~4 epochs.

Use a two-phase from-scratch curriculum, not a flat mix: Phase A (stable) English/Russian/Turkic-heavy to build transferable structure and dodge the curse of multilinguality; Phase B tilts to Kazakh-dominant. Start from Sherkala's proven 3:1:3 Kazakh:(Ru+Tr):English and shift more toward Kazakh for a Kazakh-primary model.

Scheduler = WSD (not cosine): fixed peak LR through the stable phase, then a ~10% linear-decay anneal tail. This enables checkpoint reuse and a clean annealing phase (SmolLM2/MiniCPM/YuLan-Mini all converge on this).

Set LR/batch directly from Step Law instead of a muP sweep: eta = 1.79*N^-0.713*D^0.307 and B = 0.58*D^0.571. For ~500M (N~3.5e8 non-embedding) over ~20-40B tokens this gives peak LR ~2e-3 (cross-check: SmolLM2-360M 3e-3, MobileLLM-R1 4e-3) and global batch ~0.4-0.5M tokens. Tune weight decay ~0.1 (matters more than muP for LR transfer).

Front-load the best Kazakh into the START of the decay/anneal phase (MiniCPM): curated Kazakh web, Wikipedia, textbooks, QA, and SFT-style + synthetic CoT data injected at decay-start beats reserving it for post-anneal SFT. Reserve ~8-10% of total tokens for this anneal tail (YuLan-Mini used 8%).
Precision = bf16, full stop. The A100 40GB (Ampere) has no FP8 tensor cores; FP8's 34-37% speedup only exists on H100/Blackwell. Spec FP8 only if hardware changes.

Adopt YuLan-Mini's stability kit to avoid money-wasting loss spikes at 500M from scratch: muP-style init sigma=sqrt(2/5d), z-loss (1e-4), embedding-output scaling (x10), residual scaling 1.4/sqrt(n_layers), embedding tying, and a long (~10B-token) warmup.

Distillation: prefer OFFLINE sequence-level distillation (generate synthetic Kazakh corpora once with a Kazakh-fluent teacher) over online logit-KD, because running a large teacher forward-pass over billions of tokens is infeasible on one A100. If doing logit-KD, sample only 256 teacher logits per token (Gemma 3) to cut memory. Mix KD loss with the standard LM loss.

Teacher choice: use Sherkala-8B (Kazakh SOTA, 41.4% KazMMLU) as primary teacher; verify Qwen3-235B / Gemma3-27B Kazakh fluency before use. Explicitly EXCLUDE Aya Expanse (no Kazakh; outputs Kyrgyz). Per 'Strong Teacher Not Needed', a mid-size Kazakh-fluent teacher beats a giant non-Kazakh one — don't chase the largest.

Synthetic Kazakh must be generated by a Kazakh-fluent model (not raw MT), prompt-space-diversified to fight translationese (+4.7pp G-MMLU evidence), and 10-gram decontaminated against KazMMLU / TUMLU-mini / KazQAD / FLORES before inclusion — otherwise reported gains are contaminated.

Add a light Kazakh CoT-SFT stage after annealing (MobileLLM-R1: reasoning emerges sub-billion and SFT>RL). Source Kazakh CoT by translating/synthesizing OpenMath/Tulu-style data via the Kazakh teacher; a working Kazakh 'thinking' mode at 500M is itself a novel paper contribution.

If from-scratch underperforms the budget, fall back to continual-pretraining a strong small base (Qwen3-0.6B is already 32.8% KazMMLU) with explicit Sherkala-style replay, or LayRA (LoRA on first-10 + last-2 layers, rank 8, LR 3e-4) to add Kazakh while preserving base capabilities — likely higher KazMMLU per dollar than from-scratch given only ~10B Kazakh tokens.
open_questions: Does Qwen3-235B (or Gemma3-27B) actually produce fluent, correct Kazakh? Aya was assumed multilingual but fails Kazakh (outputs Kyrgyz). Probe candidate teachers on real Kazakh generation before committing to KD/synthetic-data generation.

From-scratch 500M vs continual-pretrain of Qwen3-0.6B (already 32.8% KazMMLU): under a ~$264 / 1xA100 budget with only ~10B unique Kazakh tokens, which yields higher KazMMLU? Continual may dominate per-dollar; from-scratch is the stronger paper narrative. This is the central architecture fork.

Exact optimal teacher-to-student size ratio for Kazakh distillation: 'Strong Teacher Not Needed' (2605.23857) confirms non-monotonicity but the precise ratio could not be verified from available text; the 8B->500M (16:1) gap may be past the useful range for logit-KD.
How much synthetic Kazakh can be added before translationese and benchmark contamination degrade rather than help KazMMLU? No measured ceiling exists for Kazakh specifically.

Whether the Engram n-gram memory and mHC hyper-connections interact well with WSD annealing and logit-KD (e.g., do sparse n-gram tables need a different LR or warmup, and does KD loss flow sensibly through mHC residual streams) — untested combination.

findings.claim: Compute-optimal test-time scaling lets sub-1B models beat 405B on MATH-500: Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct 66.2%, 3B 78.2%, Qwen2.5-0.5B 76.4%, Qwen2.5-1.5B 85.6% — all above Llama-3.1-405B CoT baseline 71.4%. Method wins by policy size: beam search for <=7B policies, Best-of-N for >=72B. Compute budgets N in {4,16,64,256} samples/problem.
findings.relevance: Direct proof-of-concept that a 500M Kazakh model + TTS could close the gap to Sherkala-8B (41.4% KazMMLU); the headline result the paper can build on for Kazakh.
findings.source: arXiv:2502.06703 'Can 1B LLM Surpass 405B LLM? Rethinking Compute-Optimal Test-Time Scaling'

findings.claim: PRMs tested were Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B and -72B, Skywork-PRM-1.5B/7B, Math-Shepherd-PRM-7B, RLHFlow-PRM-Mistral-8B/Deepseek-8B. Key finding: the compute-optimal TTS strategy is highly dependent on policy model, PRM choice, and problem difficulty; the PRM must match the policy's output distribution or gains collapse, and beam search (not Best-of-N) is optimal for small policies.
findings.numbers: 7 PRMs across 1.5B-72B; N in {4,16,64,256}
findings.relevance: A Kazakh TTS pipeline needs a verifier trained on the SAME 500M policy's Kazakh outputs; off-the-shelf multilingual PRMs will underperform. Beam-search + PRM is the right small-policy recipe, not naive Best-of-N.

findings.claim: CAVEAT — those compute-optimal numbers use oracle per-difficulty method selection and ignore memory cost. Kinetics shows small-model TTS effectiveness is overestimated once KV/memory is counted: Qwen3-0.6B needs 3.5GB KV cache at 32K (model weights only 1.2GB); only 14B+ models benefit from CoT longer than 10K tokens; below that, scaling params beats scaling generation. Block-top-k sparse attention recovers +45 points in the low-cost regime and 8.58x fewer resources.
findings.numbers: Qwen3-0.6B: 3.5GB KV @32K vs 1.2GB weights; CoT>10K tokens only helps >=14B; sparse attn +45pts, 8.58x cheaper
findings.relevance: Do NOT promise long-CoT gains at 500M; pair TTS with short-CoT + parallel sampling AND efficient/sparse attention, or the KV cache dominates and the 'small model wins' story fails in real latency.
findings.source: arXiv:2506.05333 'Kinetics: Rethinking Test-Time Scaling Laws'

findings.claim: Self-consistency / majority voting needs zero verifier and zero training and historically lifts GSM8K by +17.9 points; ranked-voting variants beat plain majority voting; marginal gains shrink as pass@1 rises.
findings.numbers: +17.9 GSM8K (Wang et al.); ranked voting > majority
findings.relevance: The cheapest TTS for Kazakh — requires no Kazakh PRM/ORM. On MCQ benchmarks (KazMMLU, TUMLU) with verifiable answers it is immediately deployable; make it the default TTS baseline.
findings.source: Wang et al. self-consistency (via arXiv:2505.10772 'Ranked Voting based Self-Consistency'); survey arXiv:2503.24235

findings.claim: Budget forcing (s1: append 'Wait' to extend thinking) gave s1-32B up to +27% on MATH/AIME24, but it FAILS at small scale: with R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, forcing thinking from ~17K to ~25K tokens makes accuracy steadily DECLINE, and distilled small models hallucinate/repeat (content loops, over-reflection, no final answer) during long thinking.
findings.numbers: s1-32B +27% AIME/MATH; R1-distill-1.5B accuracy drops as tokens 17K->25K
findings.relevance: Budget forcing is a large-model trick; a 500M Kazakh model should not rely on forced long CoT. Prefer short-CoT + best-of-N/self-consistency.
findings.source: arXiv:2501.19393 (s1); arXiv:2507.14419 'It's Not That Simple'; arXiv:2506.11274

findings.claim: Reasoning distillation to 1.5B works when the base is domain-matched: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (built on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B) hits 83.9% MATH-500 and 28.9% AIME24 from 800K R1-generated CoT traces — beating GPT-4o/Claude-3.5 on math, at ~1.1GB.
findings.numbers: 1.5B distill: 83.9% MATH-500, 28.9% AIME24; 800K traces; ~1.1GB
findings.relevance: If reasoning is a target, distill R1-style CoT (translated to Kazakh) onto a knowledge/math-specialized Kazakh base rather than expecting reasoning to emerge from 9-10B pretraining tokens alone.
findings.source: arXiv:2501.12948 (DeepSeek-R1); HF deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B

findings.claim: Speculative decoding needs a 10-20x target:draft size ratio and >=60% acceptance to pay off (<50% acceptance = net loss from verification overhead). A 500M target has no viable external draft (would need a ~25-50M model, too weak to align with the target distribution).
findings.numbers: ratio 10-20x; acceptance >=60% good, <50% loss; 0.5B draft + 8B target = 1.5-2.5x on RTX4090
findings.relevance: External draft models are OFF the table for a 500M Kazakh model. The only viable acceleration is self-speculation (MTP/Medusa/EAGLE heads on the model itself).
findings.source: Practitioner consensus + arXiv:2601.18902; benchmark figures from llama.cpp draft-model results

findings.claim: Self-speculative decoding via multi-token-prediction heads gives lossless speedups: DeepSeek-V3 MTP1 acceptance >80% -> ~1.8x throughput. FastMTP: 2.03x at K=3 draft tokens, mean 2.66 accepted tokens (position acceptance 80/56/36%), single shared MTP head. Medusa: 2.2-2.8x. EAGLE-3: 3.0-6.5x with acceptance nearly flat across draft positions.
findings.numbers: MTP1 >80% acc ~1.8x; FastMTP 2.03x, 2.66 tok; Medusa 2.2-2.8x; EAGLE-3 3.0-6.5x
findings.relevance: Add MTP/EAGLE-style heads to the 500M Kazakh model for ~1.8-2x lossless edge speedup with no external draft. This is the concrete self-spec design.
findings.source: arXiv:2412.19437 (DeepSeek-V3); arXiv:2509.18362 (FastMTP); arXiv:2401.10774 (Medusa); arXiv:2503.01840 (EAGLE-3)

findings.claim: MTP as a TRAINING objective (predict multiple future tokens per hidden state, DeepSeek-V3 style) improves benchmark quality and data efficiency, not just inference speed — it densifies the training signal and yields richer representations. But at small scale aggressive MTP can degrade base next-token performance unless a curriculum (forward/reverse schedule on number of predicted tokens) or register tokens are used.
findings.numbers: DeepSeek-V3: MTP objective improves eval benchmarks + data efficiency; curriculum needed at small scale
findings.relevance: Under a 9-10B-token Kazakh data budget, the MTP objective is a double win: better sample efficiency during pretraining AND free self-speculative heads for edge. Use curriculum MTP for the 500M to avoid NTP degradation.
findings.source: arXiv:2412.19437 (DeepSeek-V3 MTP); MTP-at-small-scale via arXiv:2602.06019 and emergentmind MTP topic

findings.claim: KV-cache math at the target config (d_model=1536, 24 layers, head_dim=128, fp16, 32K context): GQA-2:1 (6 KV heads, kv_dim=768) ~= 72 KB/token -> 2.25 GB. MLA with kv_lora_rank=256 + rope_dim=64 ~= 15 KB/token -> 480 MB (4.7x smaller, ~79% saved). MLA kv_lora_rank=512 ~= 27 KB/token -> 864 MB (2.6x smaller). (DeepSeek-V3 anchor: MLA 70 KB/token vs GQA 192-328 KB/token = 2.7-4.7x at d=7168.)
findings.numbers: GQA-2:1 72KB/tok=2.25GB@32K; MLA r=256 15KB/tok=480MB (79% saved); MLA r=512 27KB/tok=864MB
findings.relevance: Drop-in spec: MLA kv_lora_rank=256 (rope 64) cuts the 32K KV cache from 2.25GB to 480MB vs GQA-2:1 at d=1536 — decisive for fitting long Kazakh context on an 8GB edge GPU.
findings.source: Derivation from stated config; DeepSeek-V3 ratios arXiv:2412.19437 / arXiv:2405.04434 (DeepSeek-V2 MLA)

findings.claim: MLA breaks mainline GGUF export: DeepSeek-style MLA GGUF requires the ik_llama.cpp fork and will not run on vanilla llama.cpp, ollama, LM Studio, or KoboldCpp. Any novel module (Engram conditional n-gram memory, mHC hyper-connections, MLA) requires a full custom C++ integration: new llm_arch enum, LLM_TENSOR_NAMES/INFOS, a build_arch_graph implementation, plus a gguf-py conversion subclass with tensor mappings.
findings.numbers: MLA -> ik_llama.cpp fork only; each custom module = 1 new llm_arch + build_arch_graph + gguf-py class
findings.relevance: Engram + mHC + MLA together = three custom C++ integrations before any edge/GGUF deploy. For a shippable product, either budget that engineering or keep a GGUF-clean GQA+RoPE inference variant.
findings.source: ggml-org/llama.cpp HOWTO-add-model.md + Discussion #16770; ubergarm/DeepSeek-V3-GGUF card (ik_llama.cpp requirement)

findings.claim: Realistic edge throughput for 0.5-1.5B models: ~30-60 tok/s at Q4 on M1/8GB-class GPU; 20-100 tok/s on CPU (memory-bandwidth bound, not compute bound). A 14B model can be squeezed into 8GB with llama.cpp resource management, and 0.5B-1.5B run comfortably on legacy laptops.
findings.numbers: 0.5-1.5B: 30-60 tok/s GPU, 20-100 tok/s CPU (Q4); memory-bandwidth bound
findings.relevance: Sets the latency envelope for the Kazakh SLM: with MTP self-spec (~2x) a 500M Q4 model can reach ~60-120 tok/s on modest hardware — but see the fertility multiplier below for words/s.
findings.source: ggml-org/llama.cpp Discussions #3167/#4167/#8273; XiongjieDai GPU-Benchmarks-on-LLM-Inference

findings.claim: Tokenizer fertility compounds across FOUR inference axes simultaneously. At 32K context: bespoke fertility 2.0 yields 16,000 effective Kazakh words vs 6,667 at multilingual fertility 4.8 (2.4x more). Generation at 40 tok/s: 20 words/s vs 8.3 words/s (2.4x faster perceived). KV entries per word and pretraining tokens per word also scale ~2.4x. SozKZ used ByteLevel BPE, 50,257 vocab, 9B tokens, claiming 2-3x fertility advantage over multilingual tokenizers.
findings.numbers: fertility 2.0 vs 4.8: 16,000 vs 6,667 words @32K; 20 vs 8.3 words/s @40 tok/s; ~2.4x on all axes
findings.relevance: The tokenizer is the single highest-leverage inference decision for Kazakh — hitting <2.0 fertility multiplies effective context in words, halves cache/word, and speeds words/s, all at once. Report 'effective context in WORDS', not tokens.
findings.source: Derivation; SozKZ arXiv:2603.20854; fertility framing arXiv:2602.19174 (TurkicNLP)

findings.claim: A single inflected Kazakh word form (e.g. 'from your act of running') is one semantic unit but is split into 10-12 BPE tokens by the Qwen tokenizer — roughly 5x the cost of a comparable English word (English fertility ~1.3).
findings.numbers: Kazakh inflected word = 10-12 Qwen tokens ~= 5x English; English fertility ~1.3
findings.relevance: Quantifies why multilingual tokenizers collapse effective Kazakh context and inflate latency/cache; motivates a morphology-aware tokenizer targeting <2.0 fertility as an inference-cost (not just quality) decision.
findings.source: arXiv:2603.27859 (KazByte); arXiv:2603.20854 (SozKZ)

findings.claim: Evaluation targets and their TTS-friendliness: KazMMLU (Kazakhstan-specific, STEM+humanities MCQ) and TUMLU/TUMLU-mini (38,139 MCQs, 11 subjects, 8 Turkic languages incl. Kazakh, ACL 2025). Both are multiple-choice with verifiable answers.
findings.numbers: TUMLU: 38,139 MCQs, 11 subjects, 8 Turkic langs; KazMMLU Kazakhstan-specific
findings.relevance: MCQ format means self-consistency and outcome-reward Best-of-N score answers for free (no PRM) — the cheapest way to demonstrate TTS gains for the arXiv paper on the exact benchmarks the project already uses.
findings.source: arXiv:2502.12829 (KazMMLU); arXiv:2502.11020 (TUMLU)

findings.claim: A Kazakh process reward model is feasible but data-expensive; cross-lingual reward transfer is the pragmatic path. Multilingual PRMs (Wang et al., released Feb 2025) map chain-of-thought across languages, and Best-of-L does cross-lingual reward modeling for math reasoning — letting a high-resource (English/Russian) verifier score Kazakh candidates.
findings.numbers: Multilingual PRM (Wang 2025); Best-of-L cross-lingual reward modeling
findings.relevance: For the Kazakh SLM, skip training a from-scratch Kazakh PRM initially: use self-consistency first, then a cross-lingual/translated ORM, and only invest in a policy-matched Kazakh PRM if verifiable-answer data warrants it.
findings.source: arXiv:2509.15811 (Best-of-L); Multilingual PRM via arXiv:2510.08049 survey

findings.claim: Latency/token-aware TTS work and Kinetics both conclude that sparse or linear attention is the enabler that returns small models to the compute/latency Pareto frontier under test-time scaling, because parallel sampling and long generation are KV-access-bound rather than FLOP-bound at small scale.
findings.numbers: attention cost L^2*D -> L*B*D with block sparse; TTS is memory-access-bound at small scale
findings.relevance: To make TTS actually pay off at 500M, combine it with sliding-window/sparse attention so that best-of-N and longer generations don't saturate the 8GB KV budget — otherwise measured speedups evaporate.
findings.source: arXiv:2506.05333 (Kinetics); arXiv:2509.09864 (Latency and Token-Aware Test-Time Compute)

findings.claim: llama.cpp does support recurrent/hybrid backbones (Mamba, RWKV, Qwen3-Next Gated DeltaNet SSM layers) and 100+ architectures, and llama-server handles SSM prefix-caching for multiple users — but each still requires the per-architecture C++ graph and gguf-py conversion class described above.
findings.numbers: 100+ architectures; Mamba GGUF at 2/3/4/5/6/8/16/32-bit; Qwen3-Next hybrid SSM supported
findings.relevance: If the Kazakh design explores a hybrid SSM/attention backbone for cheaper KV, it is deployable in llama.cpp — but budget the same custom-arch integration cost as MLA/Engram; there is no free export.
findings.source: ggml-org/llama.cpp DeepWiki 'Supported Model Architectures'; devingulliver/mamba-gguf

recommendations: Adopt a multi-token-prediction (MTP) training objective (2-4 heads, DeepSeek-V3 style, with a forward/reverse curriculum on predicted-token count to avoid NTP degradation at 500M). This is the top inference recommendation: it improves pretraining data efficiency under the 9-10B-token Kazakh budget AND provides built-in self-speculative decoding (~1.8-2x lossless), which is the ONLY viable acceleration for a 500M model (no external draft exists at the required 10-20x ratio).

Make self-consistency / weighted majority voting the default deploy-time TTS on the MCQ benchmarks (KazMMLU, TUMLU-mini) — it needs zero Kazakh verifier and historically adds double-digit accuracy. Layer weighted Best-of-N with a cross-lingual/translated outcome-reward model where answers are verifiable. If a policy-matched Kazakh PRM is later trained, use BEAM SEARCH (not Best-of-N) per the small-policy finding in 2502.06703.

Do NOT rely on long-CoT budget forcing at 500M — it degrades accuracy at 1.5B scale and below (R1-distill-1.5B evidence). If reasoning is a goal, distill R1-style CoT traces translated to Kazakh onto a knowledge/math-specialized Kazakh base, and cap thinking length; prefer short-CoT + parallel sampling over sequential 'Wait' extension.

KV cache: if 32K context on 8GB edge is a target, spec MLA with kv_lora_rank=256 and qk_rope_head_dim=64 at d_model=1536 (~480MB@32K, ~79% smaller than GQA-2:1's 2.25GB). If clean mainline-llama.cpp/GGUF export is a hard requirement instead, use GQA with only 2 KV heads (~768MB@32K) as the exportable middle ground — MLA currently needs the ik_llama.cpp fork.

Budget the edge-deployment engineering explicitly: Engram n-gram memory, mHC hyper-connections, and MLA each require a separate custom llama.cpp C++ integration (new llm_arch enum, build_arch_graph, gguf-py conversion class). Either commit to writing these, or maintain a GGUF-clean GQA+RoPE fallback inference variant so the model is shippable on ollama/LM Studio from day one.

Treat tokenizer fertility as an inference-cost decision, not just a quality one: hitting <2.0 (vs multilingual ~4.8) delivers ~2.4x more effective context in Kazakh WORDS, ~2.4x fewer KV entries per word, and ~2.4x faster words/second simultaneously. In the paper, report 'effective context in words' and 'Kazakh words/second' alongside token metrics.

Pair any test-time scaling with sliding-window/sparse attention so best-of-N and longer generations stay off the KV-bandwidth wall — at 500M, TTS is memory-access-bound, and Kinetics shows unmitigated small-model TTS gains are overestimated once cache cost is counted.

For scientific honesty in the arXiv paper, benchmark TTS on KazMMLU + TUMLU-mini against a COMPUTE-MATCHED single-model baseline (equal total generated tokens), and explicitly flag that published 'compute-optimal' oracle numbers (2502.06703) overstate real deployable gains because they assume oracle per-problem method/difficulty selection.
open_questions: Is there enough Kazakh process-supervision (step-labeled) data to train a policy-matched PRM, or must the design rely on cross-lingual reward transfer (Best-of-L / translated English-Russian verifier) plus self-consistency? This determines whether beam-search+PRM is achievable or only Best-of-N/majority voting.

Will MTP heads trained on only 9-10B Kazakh tokens reach the >60% position-1 acceptance needed for a NET self-speculative speedup at 500M, or does the low data budget make the draft too weak? Needs an empirical acceptance-rate measurement before committing MTP as the acceleration story.

Does the Engram conditional n-gram memory module (hash-table lookups per token) compose with MTP self-speculation — i.e., can drafted tokens do the n-gram lookups — and can that control flow be expressed inside llama.cpp's static build_arch_graph, or does it force a custom runtime?

Given the Latin-script transition by ~2031, does a fertility-optimized Cyrillic SentencePiece tokenizer survive the script change, or should the design hedge with a byte-level fallback (KazByte-style) that is script-agnostic at some fertility cost?

At d_model=1536, does MLA retain quality parity with GQA at this small scale (MLA is validated at 7B+), or does the low-rank KV compression cost measurable accuracy on KazMMLU that offsets the cache savings?

findings.claim: n-gram / lookup memory in LMs is now a CROWDED 2026 subfield, not a novel axis. Beyond DeepSeek Engram (the user's base), at least 6 distinct 2025-2026 papers scale explicit embedding/lookup memory: Meta 'Memory Layers at Scale' (product-key memory, sparse KV lookup, no extra FLOPs), UltraMemV2, 'Scaling Embeddings Outperforms Scaling Experts', Tensorizing Engram, X-gram, Mixture of Lookup Key-Value Experts. A Kazakh paper CANNOT claim conditional n-gram memory itself as new — only a language/morphology-specific instantiation.
findings.numbers: Memory Layers at Scale: up to 128B memory params, pretrained to 1T tokens, beats dense models with >2x compute and MoE at matched compute+params; ICLR'25
findings.relevance: Kills any 'we introduce n-gram memory for LMs' framing. The paper must position Engram as prior art and claim only the morpheme-conditioned variant + Kazakh evaluation as new.
findings.source: arXiv:2412.09764 (Memory Layers at Scale); arXiv:2601.07372 (DeepSeek Engram, user's cite)

findings.claim: X-gram is the single most dangerous prior-art collision: it is a conditional lookup-embedding memory tested at EXACTLY the user's scale (sub-1.2B), improving downstream accuracy by injecting frequency-aware dynamic n-gram embeddings into attention value streams AND inter-layer residuals with depth-aware gating. This is architecturally very close to 'Engram at layers {2, L/4} injecting into hidden states'.
findings.numbers: 0.73B and 1.15B models; gains up to 3-4 points over strong baselines at matched budget using SMALLER tables; addresses Zipfian tail under-training and 'slot collapse'
findings.relevance: Directly overlaps the user's Engram-placement contribution. The Kazakh paper must cite X-gram and differentiate on (a) morpheme- vs token/frequency-keyed lookup and (b) agglutinative-language target, or the placement/injection novelty evaporates.
findings.source: arXiv:2604.21724 (Beyond N-gram: Data-Aware X-gram Extraction for Efficient Embedding Parameter Scaling)

findings.claim: Tensorizing Engram directly extends the user's exact base component (DeepSeek Engram) by tensor-factorizing n-gram embeddings to share latents across n-gram orders, reducing parameter count. Any user claim about 'efficient n-gram memory tables' must account for this.
findings.numbers: 2MB PDF; reports parameter reduction vs full n-gram embedding matrices while maintaining performance; multiple scales up to ~1B (exact percentages not extracted — PDF truncated)
findings.relevance: The user's {2,3}-gram hash tables at ~512M sparse params are exactly what Tensorizing Engram compresses. Cite it; consider adopting latent-sharing to cut the 512M sparse footprint (relevant for a $264 single-A100 budget).
findings.source: arXiv:2606.08347 (Tensorizing Engram: Sharing Latents Across N-Gram Embeddings is Beneficial in LLMs)

findings.claim: 'Scaling Embeddings Outperforms Scaling Experts' provides the strongest theoretical backing that embedding/memory scaling beats MoE — useful as supporting citation, but it is a >68B model, so it does NOT pre-empt an SLM claim. UltraMemV2 adds the key design insight that activation density matters more than total sparse-param count.
findings.numbers: LongCat-Flash-Lite: 68.5B total, ~3B activated, >30B params in embeddings, surpasses parameter-equivalent MoE. UltraMemV2: validated to 120B total / 2.5B activated; 'activation density > total sparse parameter count'
findings.relevance: Cite both to justify why a memory-augmented SLM should beat a same-active-param dense model. UltraMemV2's density insight argues for FEWER, denser memory lookups than many sparse ones — informs how many Engram layers to place.
findings.source: arXiv:2601.21204; arXiv:2508.18756 (UltraMemV2)

findings.claim: NO published work does MORPHEME-conditioned n-gram/lookup memory in a modern decoder LM. All 2026 memory-augmented LMs (Engram, X-gram, Memory Layers, UltraMemV2, MolGram) key their lookup on TOKEN or BYTE n-grams / frequency, never on morphological units (stem+suffix). Classic morpheme n-gram LMs exist only in pre-neural ASR (e.g., Uyghur morpheme LMs, syllable-level agglutinative LM). This is the cleanest genuine novelty gap for the paper.
findings.numbers: Prior morpheme-LM art is pre-2020 and non-neural: arXiv:2003.01509 (Uyghur morpheme ASR LM), arXiv:1708.05515 (syllable-level neural LM)
findings.relevance: This is the recommended core novelty: key the Engram lookup on Kazakh morpheme n-grams (stem, case/possessive/person suffix sequences) rather than SentencePiece token n-grams. It is defensible as first-of-kind and is intrinsically motivated by agglutination + vowel harmony (suffix allomorph sharing).
findings.source: Synthesis of arXiv:2601.07372, 2604.21724, 2412.09764, 2606.12113 (all token/byte-keyed) + arXiv:2003.01509, 1708.05515 (pre-neural morpheme LMs)

findings.claim: MorphBPE is the reference morphology-aware tokenizer: it constrains BPE merges to not cross morpheme boundaries and adds two eval metrics (Morphological Consistency F1, Morphological Edit Distance). It was tested at the user's scale on morphologically rich languages, so a 'morphology-aware tokenizer' claim for Kazakh is not novel per se.
findings.numbers: 300M and 1B LLMs; English, Russian, Hungarian, Arabic; consistently lower cross-entropy + faster convergence, largest gains for Hungarian/Arabic
findings.relevance: The user's SentencePiece Unigram 50K is NOT differentiated as 'morphology-aware' unless it adds morpheme-boundary constraints. Either adopt MorphBPE-style constrained merges (and cite) or make the morphology-awareness live in the memory/head, not the tokenizer.
findings.source: arXiv:2502.00894 (MorphBPE)

findings.claim: Empirical support for the user's Unigram-over-BPE tokenizer choice exists, but with a caveat: Unigram dominates BPE for rich morphology, AND morphological pre-segmentation boosts BPE but NOT Unigram. So combining Unigram with morpheme pre-segmentation may give no gain.
findings.numbers: Telugu (agglutinative) primary; gold segmentations of 600 derivational + 7000 inflectional forms; tokenizer ALGORITHM is the dominant factor, morphological alignment only a secondary/moderate positive correlate
findings.relevance: Validates SentencePiece Unigram 50K choice. But warns: do not stack morpheme pre-segmentation on top of Unigram expecting gains — put morphology awareness in the model (memory/aux head), not the pre-tokenizer.
findings.source: arXiv:2508.08424 (Rethinking Tokenization for Rich Morphology: The Dominance of Unigram over BPE)

findings.claim: The CLOSEST prior on 'morphology-aware ARCHITECTURE for a single agglutinative language' is the Mongolian three-stage agglutinative knowledge-injection PLM: (1) early stage tokenizes words into stem+suffix subwords, (2) middle stage uses morphological-boundary masking, (3) surpasses vanilla BERT. It is the paper to differentiate against most carefully.
findings.numbers: BERT-scale bidirectional ENCODER (not a sub-1B decoder LM); three-stage injection; IEEE 2024
findings.relevance: Differentiation is clean: it is an encoder + masking objective, no lookup memory, no decoder generation, no MLA/GQA, no sub-1B-decoder framing. The user's design is a generative decoder SLM with morpheme-keyed conditional memory — genuinely distinct, but MUST cite this as the nearest morphology-injection prior.
findings.source: IEEE Xplore 10650812 (Pre-training Language Model for Mongolian with Agglutinative Linguistic Knowledge Injection)

findings.claim: The CLOSEST prior on 'sub-1B model purpose-built from scratch for one low-resource agglutinative language' is SozKZ — but it is architecturally VANILLA (Llama backbone, 50K BPE, no memory, no morphology module). This is the user's strongest differentiation opening: same target, same scale, zero architectural novelty.
findings.numbers: SozKZ 600M: 9B Kazakh tokens, 50K BPE (fertility ~2.0); 30.3% Kazakh MC QA (vs Llama-3.2-1B 32.0%), 27.0% Belebele, 25.5% SIB-200
findings.relevance: The paper's headline can be 'first architecturally-novel sub-1B Kazakh SLM' and must beat SozKZ-600M's 30.3% MC QA / 25.5% SIB-200 to be credible. SozKZ is the primary quantitative baseline to exceed.
findings.source: arXiv:2603.20854 (SozKZ)

findings.claim: KazByte is a very recent Kazakh-specific byte-level architecture paper, BUT it is a research PROPOSAL with NO empirical results — a byte-level BLT adapter wrapped around a FROZEN Qwen2.5-7B (not from-scratch, not sub-1B). It does not compete on the user's axis and is easy to differentiate.
findings.numbers: ~304M trainable adapter (BLT local encoder ~150M + decoder ~150M + ~4M projections) around ~7B frozen Qwen2.5-7B; 'no empirical results are presented'; plans to eval vs SozKZ-600M's 30.3/27.0/25.5
findings.relevance: Confirms the byte-level/adapter route for Kazakh is (a) already claimed and (b) unvalidated. The user's from-scratch sub-600M tokenizer-based design is distinct; cite KazByte to show the byte-adapter niche is taken and unproven.
findings.source: arXiv:2603.27859 (KazByte)

findings.claim: Tokenizer-free / byte-level modeling on agglutinative languages is already demonstrated by H-Net++ (hierarchical dynamic chunking), which specifically targets morphologically-rich languages and beats subword baselines. A byte-level angle for Kazakh is NOT novel.
findings.numbers: H-Net++ 252M base (variants 125M/500M/1.1B); Persian: BPB 1.183 vs 1.342 GPT-2-fa (12% better), ParsGLUE 76.6% vs 71.2% (+5.4pp), 8-10x hierarchical compression to ~subword sequence lengths; zero-shot transfer to Turkish/Arabic degrades
findings.relevance: Reinforces that the user should stay tokenizer-BASED with morpheme-aware memory, and explicitly contrast against byte-level H-Net++ as the competing paradigm. Also a template for reporting BPB + downstream + robustness.

findings.claim: Multi-token prediction (MTP) is standard in 2026 (DeepSeek-V3/V4, Qwen3, MiMo) but NO morphology-aware MTP exists. A morpheme-structured MTP head (predict the next STEM then the next SUFFIX(es)) is an unclaimed novelty axis well-suited to agglutinative Kazakh.
findings.numbers: DeepSeek-V3 MTP: D sequential modules, full causal chain per depth; DeepSeek-V4: 1 MTP head (2-token gen/pass); no 'morphology-aware' MTP found in literature
findings.relevance: Second candidate novelty (complementary to morpheme-keyed memory): an auxiliary morpheme-decomposed MTP objective that densifies training signal along morphological structure. Cite DeepSeek-V3 MTP (2412.19437) and 'Efficient Joint Prediction of Multiple Future Tokens' (2503.21801) as the token-level priors.
findings.source: arXiv:2412.19437 (DeepSeek-V3); arXiv:2503.21801 (Efficient Joint Prediction of Multiple Future Tokens)

findings.claim: mHC (manifold-constrained hyper-connections), the user's residual-stream component, is NOT novel and is now a fast-moving mainstream subfield: adopted by DeepSeek-V4 and already extended by KromHC, go-mHC, TBP-mHC, and mHC-GNN within months. Using it is fine; claiming it as a contribution is indefensible.
findings.numbers: mHC arXiv:2512.24880; follow-ups: KromHC 2601.21579, mHC-GNN 2601.02451, go-mHC 2604.02309, TBP-mHC 2605.21724; DeepSeek-V4 (2606.19348) uses mHC
findings.relevance: Reframe mHC in the spec as an adopted stability technique, not a novelty. Contribution budget should go to the morpheme-memory + morpheme-MTP axes instead.
findings.source: arXiv:2512.24880 (mHC) and follow-up IDs above

findings.claim: MLA (multi-head latent attention) is absent from the user's current design (they use GQA 2:1) and would be a concrete, quantifiable efficiency upgrade — but MLA itself is not novel, so it can support but not carry the paper.
findings.numbers: MLA vs GQA-8: ~2x smaller KV cache; MLA vs MHA: ~8-9x smaller (~512 latent values/token vs 4096); DeepSeek-V3 70KB/token vs 192-328KB/token for GQA models (2.7-4.7x)
findings.relevance: For a 500-600M Kazakh SLM (d~1536), swapping GQA-2 for MLA (kv_lora_rank ~256-512) yields ~2-4x KV-cache reduction, aiding long agglutinative sequences on the A100-40GB spot budget. Add as an efficiency ablation, not a headline claim.
findings.source: arXiv:2405.04434 (DeepSeek-V2 MLA); compression figures aggregated from MLA analyses (uncertain on exact kk-scale numbers)

findings.claim: A Kazakh-specific morphology-aware tokenization framework already exists (CSE-guided segmentation, 'The Kazakh Case'), so 'morphology-aware Kazakh tokenizer' is partially claimed. The user's tokenizer novelty must go beyond segmentation quality.
findings.numbers: MDPI Information 17(2):128 (2026); Kazakh case study; tokenizer/segmentation only, not a from-scratch model (full numbers not retrieved — page returned HTTP 403)
findings.relevance: Confirms tokenizer-only Kazakh morphology work is taken. The differentiation is that morphology lives in the MODEL (memory keys + MTP head), not just the tokenizer.
findings.source: MDPI Information 2026, 17(2):128 (Morphology-Aware Segmentation and Tokenization for Turkic Languages: The Kazakh Case)

findings.claim: No paper combines MLA + sparse/lookup memory + morphology-aware tokenization in a single model for any language. Each pair exists separately (memory+MoE, morphology+tokenizer, MLA+memory in DeepSeek), but the triple — purpose-built for one low-resource agglutinative language at sub-1B — is unoccupied.
findings.numbers: Extensive search (multiple formulations) returned zero hits for the combined triple at SLM scale
findings.relevance: The paper's defensible novelty is the COMBINATION + morpheme-conditioning + Kazakh target, not any single component. State this explicitly as the contribution and cite each component's origin to preempt reviewer novelty objections.
findings.source: Synthesis across arXiv:2405.04434, 2601.07372, 2502.00894, 2603.20854 (no combined prior found)

findings.claim: Sherkala (the KazMMLU SOTA reference at 41.4%) is a Llama-3.1-8B CONTINUED-pretraining model with 25% vocab extension — not a from-scratch architecture and 13x the user's param budget. It is a score target, not an architectural competitor.
findings.numbers: Llama-3.1-8B backbone, +25% Kazakh vocab, 45.3B tokens (kk/en/ru/tr), 8192 ctx, KazMMLU 41.4%
findings.relevance: Frames the ceiling: the user's sub-600M model 'approaching much larger models' should be measured against Sherkala-8B (41.4%) and Qwen3-0.6B-Base (32.8%). Beating Qwen3-0.6B decisively and closing part of the gap to Sherkala is the credible target.
findings.source: arXiv:2503.01493 (Sherkala-Chat)

findings.claim: Diffutron shows Turkic architectural novelty is being explored via non-autoregressive routes (masked diffusion LM for Turkish), and a Turkic cross-lingual-transfer theoretical framework exists — relevant to position the user's autoregressive+memory choice against alternatives.
findings.numbers: Diffutron arXiv:2603.20466 (masked diffusion LM, Turkish); Turkic transfer framework arXiv:2604.06202
findings.relevance: Shows the Turkic-architecture design space is opening in 2026 but along different axes (diffusion, transfer). The user's morpheme-memory autoregressive SLM does not collide with these; cite to show awareness of the Turkic architecture frontier.
findings.source: arXiv:2603.20466 (Diffutron); arXiv:2604.06202 (Cross-Lingual Transfer Turkic)

findings.claim: Morphological multi-task auxiliary objectives (morpheme tagging, stem+affix prediction, morphological masking) are well-established for encoders and have MIXED results — some studies find joint morph+POS+parse multitask does NOT improve morphological analysis and increases training time. A naive morphological aux head is both non-novel and empirically risky.
findings.numbers: Joint multitask (POS+morph+dependency) 'did not significantly improve morphological analysis' and increased training time; morpheme-boundary masking gives best inflection performance (arXiv:2506.05227)
findings.relevance: If adding a morpheme aux objective, prefer morpheme-BOUNDARY masking (shown to help) over full morphological-tag multitask (shown neutral/negative). Budget an ablation; do not assume gains.
findings.source: arXiv:2506.05227 (Improving Low-Resource Morphological Inflection via Self-Supervised Objectives); joint-multitask negative result (search-surfaced)

recommendations: Do NOT claim 'conditional n-gram memory in LMs' as novel. The 2026 memory-augmented-LM space is crowded (Engram 2601.07372, Memory Layers at Scale 2412.09764, UltraMemV2 2508.18756, X-gram 2604.21724, Tensorizing Engram 2606.08347, Scaling-Embeddings 2601.21204). Cite all as prior art in a related-work paragraph and scope the contribution narrowly.

MAKE THE CORE NOVELTY MORPHEME-CONDITIONED MEMORY: key the Engram/lookup table on Kazakh MORPHEME n-grams (stem + case/number/possessive/person suffix sequences from a Morfessor/analyzer segmentation), not SentencePiece token n-grams. No published memory-augmented decoder LM keys on morphological units — this is first-of-kind and is intrinsically motivated by agglutination and vowel-harmony suffix-allomorph sharing (one latent per underlying suffix, two surface forms).

ADD A SECOND NOVELTY AXIS — MORPHEME-STRUCTURED MTP: an auxiliary multi-token-prediction head that predicts next STEM then next SUFFIX(es) rather than next token. DeepSeek-V3/V4 MTP (2412.19437) and 2503.21801 are token-level; no morphology-aware MTP exists. Budget it as an ablation with a clear on/off comparison.

POSITION AGAINST THE THREE NEAREST PRIORS EXPLICITLY: (a) SozKZ-600M 2603.20854 — same scale/language but architecturally vanilla; must beat its 30.3% Kazakh MC QA and 25.5% SIB-200; (b) Mongolian agglutinative-injection PLM (IEEE 10650812) — nearest morphology-injection architecture but a BERT encoder, not a sub-1B decoder with memory; (c) H-Net++ 2508.05628 — the byte-level/tokenizer-free alternative to contrast the tokenizer-based design against.

REFRAME mHC AND MLA AS ADOPTED EFFICIENCY TECHNIQUES, NOT CONTRIBUTIONS. mHC (2512.24880) is already mainstream (DeepSeek-V4) with 4+ follow-ups (KromHC, go-mHC, TBP-mHC, mHC-GNN). If adopting MLA, specify kv_lora_rank ~256-512 at d~1536 for ~2-4x KV-cache reduction vs GQA-2 and report it as an efficiency ablation only.

RECONSIDER STACKING MORPHEME PRE-SEGMENTATION ON UNIGRAM. Evidence (2508.08424) shows morphological pre-segmentation boosts BPE but NOT Unigram, and the tokenizer algorithm dominates morphological alignment. Keep SentencePiece Unigram 50K (validated choice) but put morphology-awareness in the model (memory keys + MTP), and cite MorphBPE 2502.00894 as the tokenizer-side alternative you deliberately did not take.

PREFER MORPHEME-BOUNDARY MASKING over a full morphological-tagging multitask head if adding a morphology aux loss — boundary masking is shown to help inflection (2506.05227) while joint morph+POS+parse multitask is reported neutral-to-negative and slower. Do not assume aux-objective gains; ablate.

ADOPT LATENT-SHARING FOR THE MEMORY TABLES to fit the $264 single-A100-40GB budget: Tensorizing Engram (2606.08347) factorizes n-gram embeddings across orders, and UltraMemV2 (2508.18756) shows activation density beats raw sparse-param count — argue for fewer, denser morpheme-memory layers rather than the current {2, L/4} token-Engram placement.

STATE THE COMBINED-TRIPLE NOVELTY DEFENSIVELY: no prior work combines MLA + lookup memory + morphology-aware tokenization for one low-resource agglutinative language at sub-1B. Frame the contribution as (morpheme-conditioned memory) x (morpheme-MTP) x (Kazakh-first evaluation), cite each component's origin, and preempt the reviewer objection that individual pieces are known.
open_questions: X-gram (2604.21724) exact injection mechanism and per-benchmark numbers were read from search snippets, not the full paper — verify the '+3-4 points at 0.73B/1.15B' and confirm whether its depth-aware gating into value streams + residuals is close enough to the user's Engram placement to force a stronger differentiation.

Does a Kazakh (or Turkic) high-accuracy morphological segmenter/analyzer exist that is good enough to generate reliable morpheme n-gram keys at pretraining scale? The morpheme-conditioned-memory novelty depends on segmentation quality; Morfessor is unsupervised and may mis-segment vowel-harmony allomorphs.

Tensorizing Engram (2606.08347) exact parameter-savings percentages were truncated in fetch — get the compression ratio to decide whether latent-sharing meaningfully cuts the ~512M sparse footprint at 500-600M dense scale.

The Kazakh CSE-guided morphology tokenizer (MDPI 17(2):128) page was 403-blocked; retrieve its fertility/vocab numbers and whether it released a from-scratch model, to fully bound the tokenizer-novelty differentiation.

Is there any 2026 preprint (last 1-2 months, possibly not yet indexed) that already does morpheme-level or suffix-level conditional memory? The morpheme-keyed-memory claim is the paper's crux — re-run a targeted search close to submission to protect the first-of-kind claim.

conflicts: SozKZ specs — the closest prior art is cited three incompatible ways. tokenizer-morphology and novelty-check say 587M/600M params with a 50,257-token ByteLevel-BPE vocab; kazakh-turkic-nlp says 587M, 22L, d=1280, 20 MHA heads, ctx 2048, ffn 4480, 50K BPE; sota-slm's own PDF extraction reports 50M/160M params and 32K BPE. My direct fetch of arXiv 2603.20854 returns vocab 32,000 BPE. Unresolved: vocab 50,257 vs 32,000, params 587M vs 50M/160M — this is the primary from-scratch Kazakh baseline the paper must beat, so its true config and fertility must be pinned.

SozKZ 'KazMMLU ~30%' is contradicted. The project grounding and sota-slm cite SozKZ at ~30% KazMMLU, but kazakh-turkic-nlp establishes SozKZ was NEVER evaluated on KazMMLU — the 30.3 is cultural MC-QA, and SozKZ LOSES to Qwen2.5-0.5B (31.5) and Llama-3.2-1B (32.0) on that metric. The '30% KazMMLU from-scratch' comparison point in the grounding is a factual error that changes the difficulty framing.

Engram layer placement — deepseek-tech recommends the paper-validated {2,6} for a ~12-layer net (splitting the table into two modules: val loss 1.770 single-L2 vs 1.768 for {2,6}; flagship uses {2,15}), and web verification confirms 'early-layer (Layer 2) insertion is optimal.' kazakh-turkic-nlp instead recommends {2, L/4} 'as planned.' Direct contradiction on a core architectural placement.

MLA kv_lora_rank at d~1536 — deepseek-tech (~256), inference-tts (256), and kazakh-turkic-nlp (256-320) scale it from DeepSeek-V2's d_c/d_model~0.1 ratio; hybrid-efficiency instead prescribes ~768 (d/2) citing the only sub-600M MLA study (arXiv 2506.09342: r=d/2 = 45% KV cut at +0.3% loss, r=d/4 = 87.5% at +4.4% loss). A ~2.4-3x spread that yields very different KV-cache size (≈480MB vs ≈864MB @32K) and quality.

head_dim and backbone shape are assumed inconsistently. sota-slm asserts head_dim=64 is 'universal at this scale' and recommends 32-40 layers at d_model 1024-1280; inference-tts's KV-cache math and deepseek-tech's MLA config assume head_dim=128, and inference-tts assumes 24 layers at d_model 1536. head_dim 64 vs 128 changes every KV/MLA calculation, and the depth/width (24L/d1536 vs 32-40L/d1024-1280) is unsettled.

MTP at 500M — inference-tts makes an MTP training objective its TOP inference recommendation ('double win' for data efficiency + ~1.8-2x self-speculation); deepseek-tech states MTP is below the ~1-3B capability threshold where it 'does NOT improve and can DEGRADE next-token performance.' Directly opposed guidance on whether to include MTP as a training objective.

Engram knowledge gain — the Engram paper's abstract reports MMLU +3.4 while its detailed table reports +3.0 (flagged by deepseek-tech, confirmed via web search). Researchers cite both; the expected KazMMLU ceiling attributable to Engram (a knowledge-heavy benchmark) depends on which figure is load-bearing.

KazMMLU Kazakh-subset size — the grounding says 9,870 Kazakh questions (the eval denominator for all measured baselines) while kazakh-turkic-nlp says the Kazakh subset is 10,969 of 23,000 total. The reported evaluation denominator disagrees.

Qwen3-0.6B vocabulary — sota-slm cites 151,669 while hybrid-efficiency and tokenizer-morphology cite 151,936. Minor, but a direct numeric disagreement on the primary baseline's vocab (and thus its embedding-parameter share).
