findings.claim: There is a DIRECT sub-1B datapoint and it is NEGATIVE: vanilla Engram UNDERPERFORMS its MoE baseline at ~1B scale. Memory Grafting §4.2 states verbatim 'we also observe that vanilla Engram underperforms the MoE baseline in this 1B-scale setting, with 45.03 versus 45.62' (average over 9 benchmarks: ARC-C/E, BoolQ, SIQA, RACE, LAMBADA, WinoGrande, PIQA, HellaSwag). Config: 0.92B total / 0.29B active MoE, 64 routed experts top-4 + 1 shared, 50B tokens. Attributed cause: 'the limited Engram embedding table in 0.9B model, which lead to more hash collisions.'
findings.numbers: vanilla Engram 45.03 vs MoE baseline 45.62 (avg, 9 tasks); 0.92B total / 0.29B active MoE; 50B tokens
findings.relevance: This is the single most load-bearing fact for the paper: the 0-FLOP hash-lookup gain does NOT survive at ~1B even on an MoE backbone (and 0.29B active is smaller than the planned 600M dense). The central 'Engram lifts a 600M Kazakh model above Qwen3-0.6B 32.8%' claim is directly contradicted by the only near-scale evidence that exists.
findings.source: arXiv 2605.20948 — Memory Grafting: Scaling Language Model Pre-training via Offline Conditional Memory, §4.2

findings.claim: The original Engram paper contains ZERO dense+Engram configuration. Dense-4B (4.1B total / 3.8B active) appears ONLY as a no-Engram baseline (MMLU 48.6, TriviaQA 33.0). Every Engram-ATTACHED model is MoE: Engram-27B and Engram-40B (both 3.8B active, MoE+Engram), plus the compute-matched allocation regimes with 568M active (P_tot≈5.7B, 2e20 FLOPs) and 993M active (P_tot≈9.9B, 6e20 FLOPs) — all MoE. The ρ-allocation framework (ρ = fraction of inactive-parameter budget to MoE experts) structurally requires routed experts; ρ=0 (pure dense+Engram) is never tested.
findings.numbers: Dense-4B baseline (no Engram): MMLU 48.6, CMMLU 47.9, BBH 42.8, ARC-C 59.3, HumanEval 26.8, MATH 15.2, TriviaQA 33.0. Min active in any Engram config: 568M (MoE)
findings.relevance: Confirms the premise: no dense sub-1B (or any dense) Engram datapoint exists. The user's 600M dense design extrapolates entirely off the validated axis; the module is architecturally framed as a complement to MoE routing, not a dense-model booster.
findings.source: arXiv 2601.07372 — Conditional Memory via Scalable Lookup, Table 1 + §3.1 (sparsity allocation)

findings.claim: The optimal sparsity allocation keeps the MAJORITY of inactive budget in MoE experts, not in Engram: the U-shaped law's optimum sits at ρ≈75-80% (fraction to MoE experts), i.e. Engram is deliberately the minority axis complementing MoE. Engram is introduced as 'Conditional Memory, a complement to Conditional Computation in MoE.'
findings.numbers: optimal ρ≈75-80% of inactive budget to MoE experts; Engram gets the remaining ~20-25%
findings.relevance: The design's own scaling law is defined relative to a routed-expert budget. In a pure dense 600M model there is no MoE expert axis to trade against, so the U-shaped optimum and its benefit are undefined — the gain is entangled with MoE by construction, not merely by which scales were tested.
findings.source: arXiv 2601.07372 — Conditional Memory via Scalable Lookup, §3 (Sparsity Allocation / U-shaped law)

findings.claim: The 'Engram is the primary carrier of factual knowledge' evidence (suppressing Engram collapses TriviaQA to ~29%, 29-44% across factual benchmarks) is a post-hoc inference-time suppression on the full Engram-27B MoE model — NOT a small/dense result. It shows Engram is load-bearing when it already works at 27B MoE; it says nothing about whether it forms useful knowledge memory at 600M dense. Combined with the 1B underperformance datapoint, the load-bearing role at scale does not transfer down.
findings.numbers: TriviaQA retains 29% of original; factual benchmarks retain 29-44%; measured on Engram-27B (26.7B total / 3.8B active MoE, 5.7B Engram embedding, 2,262,400 slots)
findings.relevance: Prevents mis-citing the suppression ablation as evidence Engram will carry Kazakh facts at 600M. The knowledge-carrying property is demonstrated only where the module already has a multi-million-slot table and MoE support at 27B.
findings.source: arXiv 2601.07372 — Conditional Memory via Scalable Lookup, §6.3 (Engram suppression ablation)

findings.claim: The small-scale collision problem is FIXABLE, but only by abandoning the live token-ID hash-table Engram the user's design uses. Memory Grafting recovers at the same 1B scale (MG 46.98 vs MoE 45.62 vs vanilla Engram 45.03) via OFFLINE frozen conditional memory with exact longest-match retrieval (no live hashing). Lngram (2605.24869) similarly replaces tokenizer-ID hash keys with learned latent-space discrete keys to remove collisions; smallest config 0.42B active MoE, evaluated at 22B (MoE+Lngram 0.5288 vs MoE+Engram 0.5225 vs MoE 0.5146). Neither offers a dense datapoint.
findings.numbers: Memory Grafting @1B: 46.98 (MG) vs 45.62 (MoE) vs 45.03 (vanilla Engram). Lngram @22B: 0.5288 vs Engram 0.5225 vs MoE 0.5146; Lngram smallest = 0.42B active MoE
findings.relevance: If conditional memory is to help at 600M, the design must switch to a collision-robust variant (frozen exact-match memory or learned latent keys), which is a materially different, more complex module — changing both the engineering and the novelty framing of the paper.
findings.source: arXiv 2605.20948 (Memory Grafting §4.2) and arXiv 2605.24869 (Lngram, Table 1)

findings.claim: The smallest Engram-ATTACHED reference config in the original paper is a 12-layer 3B MoE with 0.56B active + a 1.6B Engram table, N={2,3}, Engram inserted at layers 2 and 6 — this is the config the user's design mirrors (Engram at layers {2, L/4}), and it is MoE, not dense. The full-scale instantiation uses N up to 3, 8 hash heads, d_mem=1280, and 2.26M-7.24M slots — far larger tables than a 600M dense model could afford at the user's ~512M sparse-param budget.
findings.numbers: Reference ablation: 3B MoE, 0.56B active, +1.6B Engram, N={2,3}, layers 2 & 6, 8 heads, d_mem=1280. 27B table: 2,262,400 slots; 40B table: 7,239,680 slots
findings.relevance: The layer-placement recipe the user copied comes from an MoE config. Table size is a first-order driver of the collision problem; a 600M dense budget forces a much smaller table, pushing collisions higher — exactly the failure mode blamed for the 1B underperformance, and worse for agglutinative Kazakh's huge surface-form inventory.
findings.source: arXiv 2601.07372 — Conditional Memory via Scalable Lookup, §4.1 / Appendix A

findings.claim: mHC (manifold-constrained hyper-connections) has NO sub-3B and NO dense validation. Smallest tested scale is 3B; all scales (3B, 9B, 27B) are MoE (Table 5: 64-72 routed experts, 6 active, 2 shared; mHC/HC expansion rate n=4 throughout). Reported gains are MoE-only: at 27B, +4.4 MMLU (59.0→63.4), +7.2 BBH (43.8→51.0), +7.1 GSM8K (46.7→53.8), and +2.1 BBH over plain HC. Overhead is 6.7% additional training time at n=4.
findings.numbers: Scales 3B/9B/27B, all MoE, n=4; 27B gains +4.4 MMLU, +7.2 BBH, +7.1 GSM8K; +2.1 BBH over HC; 6.7% time overhead
findings.relevance: The user's n=4 mHC on a 600M dense model is a 5x extrapolation below the smallest validated scale AND off the MoE axis — a second unvalidated bet stacked on the first. HC's known instability at small scale is the exact thing mHC fixes only at >=3B; the 6.7% overhead is non-trivial on a ~$264 single-A100 budget.
findings.source: arXiv 2512.24880 — mHC: Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections, Table 5 + results

findings.claim: The closest agglutinative-language DENSE Engram analog is TOBA-LM (Indonesian/Batak/Minang): 1.2B DENSE GPT-2 with Engram (500,000 x 768 embedding table). But it reports NO controlled with/without-Engram ablation on identical architecture — only an uncontrolled convergence-speed comparison vs a vanilla transformer (loss 6.4→1.7996 in 12,973 steps vs >70,000 steps). Not clean evidence that Engram raises benchmark accuracy on a dense agglutinative model.
findings.numbers: 1.2B dense GPT-2; 500,000×768 Engram table; convergence in 12,973 vs >70,000 steps (uncontrolled)
findings.relevance: The only public dense+Engram-on-agglutinative-language artifact provides no rigorous ablation, so it cannot be cited as validating the Kazakh design. If anything its tiny 500K-row table underscores the collision risk for agglutinative morphology.
findings.source: arXiv 2603.10006 — Adaptive Engram Memory System for Indonesian Language Model (TOBA LM)

recommendations: Do NOT rest the paper's central SOTA claim on live-hash Engram at 600M dense. The only near-scale evidence (Memory Grafting §4.2) shows vanilla Engram LOSES to its MoE baseline at ~1B (45.03 vs 45.62) due to hash collisions in the small table. Treat 'Engram helps a 600M dense Kazakh model' as an unproven hypothesis to be tested, not an assumption.

Make the missing dense ablation the paper's first experiment and its actual contribution: at 600M, run iso-param + iso-FLOP dense-vs-dense comparisons — dense baseline vs dense+vanilla-Engram vs dense+collision-robust-memory. This produces the sub-1B dense datapoint no one has published and de-risks (or kills) the design before the full run.

If keeping conditional memory, switch from live token-ID hashing to a collision-robust variant: Memory Grafting's offline frozen exact longest-match memory (recovers to 46.98 at 1B) or Lngram's learned latent-space keys. Note this changes the module and the novelty framing away from 'DeepSeek Engram as-is.'

Assume Kazakh AMPLIFIES the collision problem: agglutination (stem+plural+case+possessive+person) explodes surface-form n-gram vocabulary, so a small dense table collides worse than for English/Chinese. Mitigate with morpheme/lemma-level or subword-boundary-aware n-gram keys, a larger table within the sparse budget, or exact-match retrieval — and measure collision rate directly.

Budget an mHC ablation at 600M (n=2 vs n=4 vs plain residual): mHC is unvalidated below 3B and only on MoE. Be ready to fall back to standard residual or n=2 if the 6.7% time overhead (real on a ~$264 single-A100 run) doesn't pay off in stability/accuracy at small dense scale.

Reframe the paper's thesis to convert risk into contribution: position it as 'the first controlled dense sub-1B ablation of conditional n-gram memory + collision-robust keys for an agglutinative language,' rather than assuming the 27B-MoE Engram result transfers. This is a defensible, novel claim even if vanilla Engram's dense gain turns out small.

Keep MoE on the table as a hedge: since every positive Engram result requires a routed-expert budget to trade against (optimal ρ≈75-80% to MoE), a small MoE 600M-active backbone may be the only configuration where the published gains actually hold — evaluate a compute-matched MoE variant before committing to pure dense.
open_questions: Is there any newer (post-July-2026) revision of arXiv 2601.07372 or a follow-up that adds a true dense+Engram ablation at any scale? Could not find one; the dense datapoints remain baseline-only.

What exact Engram table size is feasible within the user's ~512M sparse-param budget at 600M dense, and what collision rate does that imply for a 50K Unigram Kazakh vocabulary with agglutinative surface forms? Needs direct measurement.

Does Memory Grafting's offline exact-match memory or Lngram's latent keys hold up specifically for Kazakh morphology (vowel-harmony allomorphs, kk/ru code-switching)? No Turkic/Kazakh evaluation exists for either.
TOBA-LM's dense 1.2B Engram result is uncontrolled — is there any reproducible with/without-Engram accuracy ablation for a dense agglutinative model anywhere? Not found.

gapFills.area: Kazakh morphological segmentation quality on noisy web text — feasibility of morpheme-conditioned memory keys and morphology-constrained tokenization at 10-30B-token pretraining scale

findings.claim: apertium-kaz FST reports ~94.5% NAIVE coverage (fraction of tokens that receive at least one analysis, NOT correct analysis) with 36,595 stems, but this is measured only on clean edited corpora: Bible 95.29%, Azattyq news 95.07%, and Wikipedia (wp2013, 18.2M words) just 90.10%. There is NO published coverage measurement on true noisy web crawl (CulturaX/HPLT/mC4), which is dominated by borrowings, kk/ru code-switching, typos and OOV names.
findings.numbers: 36,595 stems (27,433 vanilla); overall ~94.5%; Wikipedia 90.10%; Bible 95.29%; news 95.07%; Quran 96.71%. 150 CG disambiguation rules. Naive coverage != correct.
findings.relevance: Naive coverage is an upper bound: on cleaner-than-crawl Wikipedia it is already only 90.1%, and it counts any analysis, not the correct one. Morpheme n-gram keys built naively over CulturaX/HPLT would be corrupted on exactly the OOV/borrowing/code-switch tokens that dominate web text.
findings.source: wiki.apertium.org/wiki/Apertium-kaz (apertium-kaz transducer stats page)

findings.claim: The 2025 hybrid Kazakh analyzer (KazMorphCorpus-2025) shows the affordable FST-only stage is only 81.5% accurate on OPEN vocabulary (96% closed-vocab); reaching 92.3% requires stacking FST+CRF+KazRoBERTa. The analyzer's dominant errors are precisely web-text failure modes: words absent from the 15K-stem lexicon (names, borrowings, technical terms), with error mix affix-chain 34.0%, segmentation 31.5%, borrowing 14.9%.
findings.numbers: FST alone open-vocab 81.5%; closed-vocab 96%; FST+CRF 89.0%; FST+CRF+KazRoBERTa 92.3%; KazRoBERTa 90.8% F1 90.7 vs mBERT 82.6%. Lexicon ~15,000 roots + 200 suffixes. Error breakdown: affix-chain 34.0%, segmentation 31.5%, borrowing 14.9%.
findings.relevance: The segmenter you can actually run at scale (FST) mis-analyzes ~18.5% of open-vocab tokens, concentrated in borrowings/OOV/long-affix-chains — the exact content of web crawl. This directly caps the reliability of morpheme-conditioned n-gram keys.
findings.source: Frontiers/PMC12741073 (Hybrid AI architectures for automatic text correction in Kazakh, 2025); doi 10.3389/frai.2025.1708566

findings.claim: KazMorphCorpus-2025 and every high-accuracy Kazakh segmentation result are measured on curated/gold/synthetic data, NOT noisy monolingual crawl. KazMorphCorpus-2025 is 150,000 sentences / 2.04M tokens from literature (EPUB), news, curated social media, Wikipedia and transcribed speech — hand-verified (~50K forms), Cohen's kappa 0.881. No published number exists for segmenter accuracy on CulturaX/HPLT/mC4-style text.
findings.numbers: 150,000 sentences, 2,040,000 tokens; literature 45K / news 37.5K / social 30K / Wikipedia 22.5K / spoken 15K sentences; ~50,000 manually verified forms; POS kappa 0.881, lemma agreement 92.3%.
findings.relevance: The whole novelty (morpheme-conditioned memory) and tokenizer edge are gated on segmentation quality at crawl scale — a number that literally does not exist in the literature. Producing it on your own CulturaX/HPLT shards would itself be a first-of-kind contribution and de-risk the claim.
findings.source: Frontiers/PMC12741073 (KazMorphCorpus-2025 spec, Table 1)

findings.claim: On a clean lab-annotated Kazakh gold set (16,000 train words / 2,000 test words), UNSUPERVISED segmenters collapse: Morfessor 27.26% F1, BPE 27.83% F1, MMSeg 35.22% F1; only SUPERVISED models reach FEMSeg 92.34% / FEMSeg-CRF 92.84% F1. Critically, MMSeg's OOV recall on Kazakh is just 8.52% (vs 46.69% on Uyghur), attributed to long stems and morphological ambiguity.
findings.numbers: Kazakh gold: Morfessor F1 27.26%, BPE 27.83%, MMSeg 35.22%, FEMSeg 92.34%, FEMSeg-CRF 92.84%. MMSeg Kazakh OOV recall 8.52% vs Uyghur 46.69%. Data 16K train / 2K test words, 5,686 morpheme types, lab-annotated (not web).
findings.relevance: This is the single strongest quantitative signal against the plan: unsupervised Kazakh segmentation is near-useless (~27% F1) and even the best model generalizes to unseen stems at only 8.52% recall. Web crawl is overwhelmingly OOV, so naive corpus-wide morpheme keys would be systematically wrong on novel words.
findings.source: MDPI Applied Sciences 14(13):5369, 'A Benchmark for Morphological Segmentation in Uyghur and Kazakh' (Tables incl. OOV Table 8)

findings.claim: No paper reports an isolated vowel-harmony suffix-allomorph mis-segmentation rate for Kazakh. The signal is indirect: the FEMSeg_kaz tokenizer architecture explicitly adds three phonological embedding channels (vowel/consonant class, front/back harmony class, stem-final boundary) specifically to cope with allomorphy, and the benchmark notes harmony causes junction phenomena (deletion, addition, weakening) — but gives no per-allomorph error number.
findings.numbers: FEMSeg_kaz phonological channels = 3 (vowel/consonant class, front/back harmony, stem-final boundary). No published allomorph-specific mis-segmentation %.
findings.relevance: The requested 'allomorph mis-segmentation rate' is an unquantified gap in the literature. That researchers hard-code harmony channels to fix it implies it is a real, non-trivial failure mode — so it cannot be assumed solved for noisy input.
findings.source: MDPI Information 17(2):128 (CSE-guided Kazakh tokenizer, FEMSeg_kaz architecture); MDPI Applied Sciences 14(13):5369 (junction phenomena note)

findings.claim: The CSE-guided Kazakh morphology tokenizer's headline segmentation F1 (FEMSeg_kaz_v2 morph_F1 99.62%; v3 95.55% on an external manual test, 3.48% edit distance) is achieved on 2.33M SYNTHETIC harmony-generated wordforms plus a 284,707-sentence web-collected PARALLEL corpus — clean/curated, not noisy monolingual crawl. No OOV rate and no noise-robustness benchmark are reported. Token-count gain is modest: 113,142 (BPE_Kaz) vs 130,605 (mT5) on 4,999 sentences (~13% fewer).
findings.numbers: FEMSeg_kaz_v2 morph_F1 99.62% (P 99.58/R 99.67, 2,329,377 wordforms); v3 95.55% F1, edit distance 3.48%; train corpus 284,707 sentences; vocab 32k (16k/50k options); BPE_Kaz 113,142 vs mT5 130,605 tokens.
findings.relevance: The 95-99% segmentation F1 that would justify morphology-constrained tokenization is unverified at web-crawl noise; it is on synthetic + parallel data. Do not assume it transfers to raw CulturaX/HPLT.
findings.source: MDPI Information 17(2):128 / doi 10.3390/info17020128, 'Morphology-Aware Segmentation and Tokenization for Turkic Languages: A CSE-Guided Framework'

findings.claim: Cross-lingual evidence (Southern Quechua, another agglutinative LRL) shows fertility<2.0 is achieved by plain BPE WITHOUT any morphology (BPE 1.636 at 16k) but that BPE scores only 6.67% morphological boundary accuracy — pure surface-form memorization. The morphology-aware PRPE tokenizer gets 83.33% MorphAcc at fertility 1.797. Caveat: MorphAcc is computed on only a 15-word evaluation set, so absolute numbers are statistically fragile.
findings.numbers: BPE: fert 2.233/1.918/1.636 at 4k/8k/16k, MorphAcc constant 6.67%; Unigram MorphAcc 66.67%@4k -> 26.67%@8k -> 33.33%@16k; PRPE fert 1.797, MorphAcc 83.33%; OOV ~0% (byte_fallback). Eval set = 15 words.
findings.relevance: Kills 'fertility<2.0' as the tokenizer's defensible edge: plain BPE already hits it. The only morphology-based differentiator is boundary accuracy (MorphAcc / Morphological Consistency F1) — which for Kazakh remains unproven on noisy text. Frame the tokenizer contribution around boundary quality, not fertility.
findings.source: arXiv 2606.23943 'QuechuaTok: Morphological Boundary Accuracy as a Necessary Metric for Tokenizer Evaluation in Agglutinative Low-Resource Languages' (Jun 2026), Tables 1 & 3

findings.claim: The direct baseline SozKZ (600M) already reaches KazMMLU ~30.3% with a plain ByteLevel BPE (50,257 vocab) and NO morphological segmentation, trained on 9B tokens from the identical noisy sources you target (CulturaX, HPLT 2.0, mC4, MADLAD-400, mOSCAR, Wikipedia; cleaned to 13.7M docs, 48.2% pass), claiming a 2-3x fertility advantage over multilingual tokenizers.
findings.numbers: SozKZ-600M 587M params, 9.0B tokens, BPE vocab 50,257, 2-3x fertility advantage, KazMMLU ~30.3%. Data cleaned to 13.7M docs (48.2% pass rate). No morphology used.
findings.relevance: Confirms that on the SAME noisy corpora, plain BPE already gets low fertility and ~30% KazMMLU without morphology. So the morphology angle must beat this on a morphology-specific metric under noise, not on fertility — and morpheme-conditioned memory must add value on top of, not instead of, a robust BPE fallback.
findings.source: arXiv 2603.20854 'SozKZ: Training Efficient Small Language Models for Kazakh from Scratch' (Mar 2026)

recommendations: Do NOT gate the core novelty on full-corpus morpheme segmentation. The only affordable at-scale segmenter (apertium-kaz FST / rule-based) is ~81.5% accurate on open vocabulary and its errors concentrate on borrowings/OOV/long-affix-chains — exactly what dominates CulturaX/HPLT/mC4. Unsupervised alternatives (Morfessor 27%, MMSeg 35% F1, 8.52% Kazakh OOV recall) are unusable on crawl. Build morpheme-conditioned memory keys ONLY over high-confidence FST analyses, with a character/hash fallback for the (large) unanalyzable remainder, so noise degrades gracefully instead of poisoning keys.

Measure it yourself: run apertium-kaz naive coverage + a manual FST error audit on a real sample of your CulturaX/HPLT/mC4 Kazakh shards. No such crawl-scale number exists in the literature, so publishing the 'confident morpheme-coverage fraction on noisy Kazakh web text' is itself a first-of-kind, defensible contribution and directly de-risks both the memory and tokenizer claims.

Reframe the tokenizer edge from 'fertility<2.0' to morphological BOUNDARY accuracy. Plain BPE already achieves sub-2.0 fertility on Kazakh (SozKZ 2-3x advantage; QuechuaTok BPE 1.636) with near-zero morphological correctness (6.67% MorphAcc). Report Morphological Consistency F1 / MorphAcc (a la QuechuaTok/MorphBPE) as the differentiator, and — critically — show it survives noisy input, since all existing 95-99% Kazakh F1 numbers are on clean/synthetic/gold data.

Use a SOFT morphology constraint, not a hard FST-boundary constraint: morphology-aware initialization or boundary-biased BPE merges (MorphBPE/PRPE style) that fall back to byte/BPE segmentation on OOV, rather than forcing FST boundaries that will be wrong on ~18%+ of open-vocab web tokens.

Borrow the FEMSeg_kaz harmony trick as cheap robustness: add front/back vowel-harmony and stem-final-boundary features/embeddings to whatever segmenter or boundary predictor you use, since allomorph junctions (deletion/addition/weakening) are the documented hard case and no one has quantified the residual error.

Position the paper's defensible axis as 'morpheme-conditioned memory that is robust to segmentation noise' (i.e., confidence-gated, fallback-backed) rather than 'requires accurate whole-corpus segmentation' — the latter is empirically unsupported for Kazakh at 10-30B-token scale and would be the paper's weakest, most attackable claim.
open_questions: What is apertium-kaz's naive coverage AND correct-analysis rate specifically on CulturaX/HPLT/mC4 Kazakh (not Wikipedia)? Unmeasured in the literature — must be produced in-house.
What fraction of morpheme n-gram keys derived from FST analyses of noisy crawl are consistent/correct vs the confident subset? No published number.

What is the actual isolated mis-segmentation rate on vowel-harmony suffix allomorphs (e.g., -лар/-лер/-дар/-дер/-тар/-тер) under noisy input? Only indirect evidence exists (hard-coded harmony channels), no rate.

Does morpheme-conditioned memory add measurable KazMMLU/TUMLU gain OVER a plain-BPE SozKZ-style baseline once keys are confidence-gated, or does the fallback fraction get so large that the memory rarely fires on real web text?

Can the FST-only (81.5% open-vocab, ~10K tok/s on 8 cores => ~35 CPU-days for 30B tokens) pipeline be run at scale without the KazRoBERTa disambiguation stage (670-1,060 tok/s GPU => ~330-520 GPU-days for 30B tokens, infeasible on the ~1xA100 budget)? The compute math strongly favors FST-only, which caps achievable segmentation accuracy.

gapFills.area: Architecture fork: from-scratch 600M (Engram+mHC+MLA) vs continual-pretraining / tokenizer-transplant onto Qwen3-0.6B-Base for Kazakh KazMMLU, at equal ~9-10B-token / single-A100 budget

findings.claim: The single most on-point datapoint says from-scratch loses on knowledge: SozKZ-600M (from-scratch, ~9B Kazakh tokens, dedicated 50,257 ByteLevel BPE with a stated 2-3x fertility advantage) scores 30.3% on Kazakh multiple-choice cultural QA and 27.0 Belebele, BELOW Qwen2.5-0.5B (31.5 MC QA, 30.0 Belebele) which had NO Kazakh training; from-scratch only wins SIB-200 topic classification (25.5 vs 19.1). So a smaller, un-adapted Qwen base already out-knows the best from-scratch 600M.
findings.numbers: SozKZ-600M: 30.3 MC QA / 27.0 Belebele / 25.5 SIB-200. Qwen2.5-0.5B: 31.5 / 30.0 / 19.1. Llama-3.2-1B: 32.0 / 26.7 / 20.1. Trained on 8xH100 for the 600M run.
findings.relevance: Directly implies Qwen3-0.6B-Base at 32.8% KazMMLU is a stronger knowledge starting point than a from-scratch 600M can reach within 9-10B tokens. SozKZ used the same recipe class the paper proposes minus the novel modules.
findings.source: arXiv 2603.20854 (SozKZ), Table 2

findings.claim: SozKZ's reported knowledge benchmark is a cultural multiple-choice QA set (labelled 'MC QA'), NOT KazMMLU itself; the paper does not report KazMMLU. The grounding's 'SozKZ ~30% KazMMLU' should be read as ~30% on a cultural MC-QA proxy, so the head-to-head vs Qwen3-0.6B-Base on KazMMLU specifically remains unpublished.
findings.numbers: SozKZ evaluates on: MC cultural QA, Belebele, SIB-200 only. Vocab 50,257 ByteLevel BPE, ~9B Kazakh tokens.
findings.relevance: Confirms the user's premise that no published Kazakh KazMMLU head-to-head (from-scratch vs adapted-Qwen) exists; the paper can BE that experiment. Prevents mis-citing SozKZ as a KazMMLU result.
findings.source: arXiv 2603.20854 (SozKZ), Table 2 + benchmark section

findings.claim: The only published low-resource head-to-head that pits tokenizer-swap continual pretraining against from-scratch on the SAME data (NorMistral, Norwegian) favors continual on EVERY metric, including the knowledge-QA task most analogous to KazMMLU. Their 3-stage recipe = build new tokenizer, realign embeddings (only 1000 frozen-body steps), then full CPT.
findings.numbers: Continual vs from-scratch: NorQuAD 64.8 vs 43.7 (+21.1 F1); NRK-Quiz-QA 57.9 vs 48.2 (+9.7); NoReC 84.9 vs 80.3 (+4.6); Tatoeba 57.2 vs 53.4 BLEU (+3.8). Full training 250B tokens / 60k steps; embedding realign = 1000 steps.
findings.relevance: Closest experimental analog to the fork; adaptation-with-swapped-tokenizer beats from-scratch even on knowledge QA. Direction is strong; magnitude not transferable (11B model, 250B tokens >> Kazakh 600M / 9-10B budget).
findings.source: arXiv 2412.06484 (Small Languages, Big Models / NorMistral-11B), Table 4

findings.claim: The from-scratch camp's core justification (a Kazakh-native tokenizer) is largely capturable by adaptation: a good training-free transplant grafts an efficient tokenizer onto a strong base near-losslessly. OMP retains 99.1% of MMLU on Qwen->Llama-1B zero-shot and recovers to 101.4% after only 2B CPT tokens; FOCUS retains just 73.4% and WECHSEL 63.0% for the same swap.
findings.numbers: Qwen->Llama 1B MMLU: OMP-K64 36.4 vs 36.73 base (99.1%); after 2B-token CPT 101.4%. FOCUS 73.4%, WECHSEL 63.0%, ZeroEmbed 99.1%. (Llama->Mistral-12B: OMP 96.4%, FOCUS 35.6%.)
findings.relevance: You can transplant a low-fertility Kazakh tokenizer onto Qwen3-0.6B-Base and keep ~all of its 32.8% starting knowledge, then CPT on 9-10B Kazakh tokens — getting BOTH the fertility win and a knowledge head-start from-scratch cannot match. Prefer OMP-style init over FOCUS/ZeTT for retention.
findings.source: arXiv 2506.06607 (Training-Free Tokenizer Transplantation via Orthogonal Matching Pursuit), results tables

findings.claim: Critical caveat that specifically threatens KazMMLU (STEM-heavy): cross-scheme tokenizer transplants catastrophically break numeric reasoning unless digit tokenization is preserved. GSM8K collapses -78.7% (Qwen->Llama) and -73.8% (Llama->Mistral) after transplant; a same-numeric-scheme transfer (NeMo->Qwen) drops only -5.6%.
findings.relevance: KazMMLU includes STEM subjects with numbers; a naive Kazakh-tokenizer swap that re-tokenizes digits could wipe out STEM accuracy. Strong argument to (a) preserve Qwen's digit/number tokenization in any transplant, or (b) run a no-swap CPT arm as the safe control.
findings.source: arXiv 2506.06607 (OMP transplant), math/GSM8K analysis

findings.claim: Under equal-budget framing, continual pretraining is Pareto-cheaper than from-scratch by extended scaling laws — it reaches the same loss with meaningfully fewer FLOPs — but the transfer benefit shrinks logarithmically the more the base was already pretrained (Qwen3-0.6B is heavily overtrained, so the edge is real but bounded).
findings.numbers: Reported CP/reuse FLOP savings ~26% (progressive training to equal loss) up to ~40% (context CP with ~no loss); benefit decays log with base-model pretraining tokens.
findings.relevance: At a fixed single-A100 budget, adaptation converts more of the 9-10B tokens into Kazakh gains rather than re-learning general competence. The heavy pretraining of Qwen3-0.6B caps but does not erase this advantage.
findings.source: arXiv 2510.06548 (Reusing Overtrained LMs Saturates Scaling); arXiv 2407.07263 (Reuse, Don't Retrain); arXiv 2405.18392

findings.claim: Field-wide prior: every published Kazakh SOTA at any size is an adaptation of a strong base, none from-scratch. Sherkala-8B = continual pretraining of Llama-3.1-8B (45.3B tokens, 19.45B Kazakh) -> 41.4% KazMMLU; Qolda(-AVL) = Qwen3-4B / Qwen3-VL-4B adaptation -> 69.47% KazMMLU and beats its own backbone. KazByte proposes adapting Qwen2.5-7B but is a position paper ('empirical validation is ongoing', no results yet).
findings.numbers: Sherkala-8B 41.4% KazMMLU (continual, Llama-3.1-8B). Qolda-AVL 69.47% KazMMLU (Qwen3-VL-4B base), outperforms backbone. KazByte: no numbers reported.
findings.relevance: A from-scratch novel-architecture headline must beat this adaptation prior, not assume it. It also means a defensible SOTA-<=1B KazMMLU claim very likely does NOT require the novel Engram/mHC/MLA modules — adapting Qwen3-0.6B-Base is the higher-probability route to the headline number.
findings.source: arXiv 2503.01493 (Sherkala); MDPI 10.3390/bdcc10060192 + HF issai/Qolda; arXiv 2603.27859 (KazByte, position-only)

findings.claim: A naive full tokenizer swap may need far more than the Kazakh budget to fully recover base parity (literature suggests re-optimizing a swapped tokenizer toward base parity can want >=50B continuation tokens), though strong init (OMP) recovers most within ~2B. With only 9-10B Kazakh tokens, a poorly-initialized swap risks spending the budget on recovery rather than Kazakh learning.
findings.numbers: >=50B tokens cited for tractable full tokenizer re-optimization; OMP/FOCUS init recovers 'much' with ~2B-token CPT.
findings.relevance: Concrete budget constraint: at 9-10B tokens either (a) keep Qwen's tokenizer and accept the ~4.7-4.9 fertility hit (knowledge fully intact, cheapest control), or (b) swap with OMP-style init + digit preservation to minimize recovery cost. A ZeTT/FOCUS swap with weak retention is the worst option under this budget.
findings.source: Tokenizer-optimization survey (emergentmind) + arXiv 2506.06607 recovery experiments

recommendations: Reframe the paper's likely headline: the defensible SOTA-<=1B KazMMLU claim almost certainly does NOT require the novel from-scratch modules. The highest-probability route to beat Qwen3-0.6B-Base (32.8%) and prior from-scratch (~30%) is ADAPTATION: OMP-style tokenizer transplant + CPT onto Qwen3-0.6B-Base, which keeps ~99% of its 32.8% head-start (arXiv 2506.06607) while fixing fertility.

Make the actual head-to-head the paper's core contribution: at ~600M / equal 9-10B-token / single-A100 budget, run (A) from-scratch Engram+mHC+MLA, (B) no-swap CPT on Qwen3-0.6B-Base, (C) OMP-transplant + CPT on Qwen3-0.6B-Base, all on KazMMLU/TUMLU/KazQAD. No published Kazakh datapoint exists, so this experiment is novel and citable regardless of which wins — and resolves the fork the three researchers flagged.

If the from-scratch novel architecture is kept as headline, do NOT stake it on KazMMLU knowledge (the evidence points the other way). Stake it where from-scratch already wins or is uncontested: tokenizer fertility/throughput, SIB-200-style classification (SozKZ already beats Qwen there: 25.5 vs 19.1), and Turkic transfer (TUMLU) — and report the KazMMLU head-to-head honestly rather than omitting it.

For any tokenizer transplant, PRESERVE Qwen's digit/number tokenization to avoid the -74% to -79% STEM/math collapse seen in cross-scheme swaps (arXiv 2506.06607); KazMMLU is STEM-heavy so this is decisive for the knowledge score.

Use OMP-style embedding init, not FOCUS/ZeTT, for the transplant (99.1% vs 73.4% retention on the analogous Qwen->Llama-1B swap), and precede full CPT with a short frozen-body embedding-realignment warmup (as in NorMistral stage 2, ~1000 steps) to stabilize the new vocabulary before spending Kazakh tokens.

Include a no-swap CPT arm (Qwen3-0.6B-Base + 9-10B Kazakh tokens, original tokenizer) as the honest cheap control: it keeps all 32.8% knowledge intact and only pays the fertility penalty; it may already beat from-scratch on KazMMLU and sets the bar the novel modules must clear.

Position the novel modules (Engram conditional n-gram memory, mHC, MLA) as architecture-ablation science, not the SOTA vehicle: report them as a controlled from-scratch baseline and, if feasible, test whether any (e.g., Engram memory as a bolt-on) can be grafted onto the adapted base to combine novelty with the adaptation head-start.
open_questions: Does OMP-init tokenizer transplant + 9-10B-token CPT on Qwen3-0.6B-Base actually clear a from-scratch 600M on KazMMLU at equal single-A100 budget? No published Kazakh datapoint exists at this scale (all supporting evidence is from adjacent languages/larger models) — it must be run to be claimed.

Can Engram (conditional n-gram memory), mHC, or MLA be grafted onto or combined with an adapted Qwen3-0.6B-Base, or are they strictly from-scratch? If any can bolt on, the paper could keep BOTH the architectural novelty and the adaptation knowledge head-start — the strongest possible framing.

What fraction of KazMMLU (Kazakh subset) is numeric/STEM, and how much would a digit-changing Kazakh tokenizer transplant actually hurt it? This determines whether digit preservation fully neutralizes the STEM-collapse risk or whether a no-swap CPT arm is safer for the headline number.

How much of the 9-10B Kazakh budget does OMP-init transplant recovery consume before net-positive Kazakh learning begins at 600M scale specifically (the ~2B-token recovery figure is from a 1B model on English DCLM, not 600M on Kazakh)?

gapFills.area: Parameter-counting convention and iso-size accounting: does a 500M-dense + ~512M-Engram (~1B total) Kazakh SLM legitimately sit in the "<=600M" class, and does "beats every ~500M SLM" survive an iso-total comparison?

findings.claim: The Engram paper defines THREE parameter metrics and explicitly counts the memory table as part of TOTAL params. Section 3.1: P_tot = total trainable params (excluding only vocab embedding & LM head); P_act = activated params per token (this alone determines FLOPs); P_sparse = P_tot - P_act = the 'inactive/free budget'. The Engram table lives in P_sparse: 'For Engram, only a constant number of slots are retrieved per token, so scaling the number of embedding slots increases P_tot without increasing per-token FLOPs.' So a ~512M Engram table adds ~0 FLOPs but is fully counted in P_tot. There is NO convention in the source paper under which the table is not a parameter — even its generous P_tot (which drops vocab) still includes the whole table.
findings.numbers: 3 metrics: P_tot, P_act, P_sparse=P_tot-P_act. User model under P_tot (excl vocab) ~= 450M backbone + 512M table = ~960M; on-disk total incl. embedding ~= 1.0B; P_act ~= 500M.
findings.relevance: The only convention that yields '<=600M' is P_act (active/FLOP). Under total params — the metric reviewers use to size-class SLMs, and the metric the Engram paper itself headlines — the model is ~1B, not 500M.
findings.source: arXiv 2601.07372 (Cheng et al., DeepSeek-AI, Jan 2026), Sec 3.1 'Compute-matched formulation'

findings.claim: Engram's OWN headline comparison is iso-TOTAL-parameter AND iso-FLOP simultaneously — it never claims a memory-augmented model beats a model with fewer TOTAL params. Abstract: 'we scale Engram to 27B parameters, achieving superior performance over a strictly iso-parameter and iso-FLOPs MoE baseline.' Sec 3.1 protocol keeps BOTH P_tot and P_act fixed: at C=2e20 FLOPs P_tot~=5.7B & P_act=568M (baseline 106 experts); at C=6e20 FLOPs P_tot~=9.9B & P_act=993M (baseline 99 experts), constant P_tot/P_act~=10. Therefore invoking Engram to justify 'beats 500M with a 1B-total model' contradicts the source: Engram's framing would require comparing the user's ~1B-total model against a ~1B-total baseline.
findings.numbers: iso-P_tot: 5.7B (568M active) and 9.9B (993M active); MoE baselines with same total AND same FLOPs; sparsity ratio P_tot/P_act ~= 10.
findings.relevance: The paper cannot lean on Engram precedent to escape iso-total comparison — DeepSeek explicitly does iso-total. deepseek-tech's objection is correct and is baked into the very paper being cited.
findings.source: arXiv 2601.07372, Abstract + Sec 3.1 'Experimental protocol'

findings.claim: All three named Kazakh/peer comparators are DENSE, so for them total == active; there is no sparse/inactive budget to hide the memory. Qwen3-0.6B: 0.6B total / 0.44B non-embedding (~0.16B tied embedding, vocab ~151,936), 28 layers, GQA 16Q:8KV — every param is active. SozKZ 600M: dense Llama, 50K BPE, 9B tokens, all 600M active. Gemma3-270M: 270M total = 170M embedding (256K vocab) + 100M transformer, dense. Comparing a ~500M-active/~1B-total model to these on 'params' is only apples-to-apples on the ACTIVE axis; on the TOTAL/footprint axis the user model is 1.7x-3.7x larger than these peers.
findings.numbers: Qwen3-0.6B 0.6B tot/0.44B non-emb; SozKZ 600M dense; Gemma3-270M 270M (170M emb + 100M blocks). All total==active. User ~1.0B total vs 0.27-0.6B.
findings.relevance: Because the peers are dense, a reviewer's default 'params' means total, and the user model is one size class up (~1B) — Qwen3-0.6B/SozKZ/Gemma3-270M stop being the right comparators under iso-total.
findings.source: HF Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B model card; arXiv 2603.20854 (SozKZ); Google Developers Blog 'Introducing Gemma 3 270M' + apxml.com/models/gemma-3-270m

findings.claim: The 'beats every best-tier ~500M SLM' claim does NOT survive an iso-TOTAL comparison: at ~1B total the honest peer set is the ~1B dense models, where the measured bar is much higher than the 500M models. From the user's own measured baselines: at ~1B total the true peers are Llama-3.2-1B (25.1% KazMMLU), Gemma3-1B-it (28.7%), and the still-larger Qwen2.5-1.5B (34.3%). Qwen3-0.6B (32.8%) and SozKZ-600M (~30%) sit BELOW the user's total-param class, so beating them does not establish superiority over iso-total peers. The claim is true on the active/FLOP axis but a reviewer will re-bracket the model into the 1B class, where 'beats every 500M SLM' is a category error.
findings.numbers: ~1B-total peers: Llama-3.2-1B 25.1%, Gemma3-1B-it 28.7%; next up Qwen2.5-1.5B 34.3%. 500M peers (below user's total class): Qwen3-0.6B 32.8%, SozKZ-600M ~30%, Gemma3-270M 24.4%.
findings.relevance: Central quantitative claim is at reviewer risk exactly as flagged: the target-beating comparison must be re-run vs ~1B models, or the model must be shrunk to actually be <=600M total.
findings.source: User grounding (measured KazMMLU 5-shot, Kazakh subset, 9,870 Q); peer sizes per HF cards / arXiv 2603.20854

findings.claim: Engram's 0-FLOP argument addresses COMPUTE only, not memory footprint — and SLM reviewers weight footprint heavily. The Engram table is real stored weights so large the paper OFFLOADS it off-GPU: Sec 2.5 / abstract, 'offloading a 100B-parameter table to host memory incurs negligible overhead (<3%)', with a multi-level cache hierarchy (GPU HBM -> host DRAM -> NVMe SSD). For an on-device Kazakh SLM this is decisive: a 512M table at fp16 is ~1GB, at INT8 ~0.5GB of extra storage the device must hold. By contrast Gemma3-270M's entire pitch is footprint — INT4 QAT ~125-240MB, 'runs on your phone', 0.75% battery for 25 conversations on a Pixel 9 Pro. So on the memory axis the user model is not remotely in the 270-600M class regardless of the FLOP story.
findings.numbers: Engram tables offloaded to host/NVMe (<3% overhead for a 100B table); 512M table ~1GB fp16 / ~0.5GB int8; Gemma3-270M INT4 ~125MB, full-precision ~0.5GB.
findings.relevance: If the paper's selling point is 'efficient on-device Kazakh SLM', the total/footprint axis is the one reviewers weigh most, and the 0-FLOP defense does not answer it. Must report the table's on-disk bytes at train + quantized precision.
findings.source: arXiv 2601.07372 Sec 2.5 + Abstract; Google Developers Blog + localaimaster.com/models/gemma-3-270m

findings.claim: The field size-classes sparse (MoE) models by TOTAL params, not active — active is a secondary efficiency stat. Mixtral 8x7B is universally called a 47B model (13B active); DeepSeek-V3 is 'the 671B model' (37B active, 5.5% activation ratio). Capacity/knowledge is credited to total params, compute to active. This precedent cuts AGAINST the user: even the MoE convention the paper would invoke to report '500M active' still groups the model by its ~1B total. No major model claims membership in a smaller size class than its total param count.
findings.numbers: Mixtral 8x7B: 47B total / 13B active. DeepSeek-V3: 671B total / 37B active (5.5%). Named/bracketed by total in both cases.
findings.relevance: Reporting only '500M active' to claim the 500M class runs against community naming norms and will read as size-class gaming; the safe move is to report both and bracket by total.
findings.source: arXiv 2401.04088 (Mixtral of Experts); arXiv 2412.19437 (DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report)

findings.claim: Engram's own U-shaped scaling law both (a) shows the user's ~512M table is NOT oversized on the efficiency axis, and (b) shows the user is OUTSIDE the regime the law validates. Optimum is rho ~= 75-80% (val loss 1.7248 at pure MoE -> 1.7109 at rho~=80%, delta 0.0139), i.e. reallocate ~20-25% of the SPARSE budget to Engram. In the 10B regime that optimum is Engram ~= (1-0.80) x P_sparse ~= 0.2 x (9.9B-993M) ~= 1.03B of memory on 993M active — a ~1:1-to-1.8:1 memory:active ratio. The user's ~512M table on ~500M active (~1:1) is thus in-range for capability. BUT the law is derived on an MoE backbone with a large P_sparse to reallocate; a DENSE 500M backbone has P_sparse ~= 0, so adding Engram is pure ADDITION to total, not a reallocation — the user is applying the ratio outside its validated setting.
findings.numbers: Optimum rho~=75-80%; delta val-loss 0.0139 (10B regime); Engram-optimal memory ~1.03B on 993M active (~1:1); user 512M on ~500M active (~1:1) is in-range for efficiency but adds to a dense (P_sparse~=0) backbone.
findings.relevance: Tells the sizing decision: the table is fine for capability-per-FLOP, so the ONLY reason to shrink it is the total-param/footprint claim. To be honestly <=600M TOTAL, a ~440M backbone leaves only ~100-160M for the table (a ~3-5x shrink), or shrink the backbone to ~350-400M and give ~150-200M to Engram.
findings.source: arXiv 2601.07372 Sec 3.1-3.2, Fig 3 (derived arithmetic on their reported P_tot/P_act)

recommendations: DECIDE BEFORE TRAINING (it sets the table size). Recommended = Option A (reviewer-proof): shrink the Engram table so the model is honestly <=600M TOTAL on disk. Budget e.g. ~440M dense backbone (Qwen3-0.6B-class non-embedding) + ~100-160M Engram {2,3}-gram hash tables + ~50M tied embedding ~= 590-640M total. Then 'beats every best-tier ~500M SLM' survives iso-total against Qwen3-0.6B (32.8%) / SozKZ-600M (~30%) / Gemma3-270M (24.4%). Always report BOTH total and active params in a table so the accounting is auditable.

Option B (honest but concedes size-class): keep the ~1B-total design, RE-BRACKET it as a ~1B model, and make the headline an efficiency claim, not a size claim: 'a 500M-ACTIVE / ~1B-total model with a 0-added-FLOP conditional-memory branch matches or beats 1B-total dense models on Kazakh at half the active FLOPs.' Then the mandatory iso-total comparators become Llama-3.2-1B (25.1%), Gemma3-1B-it (28.7%), and Qwen2.5-1.5B (34.3%) — beating Qwen2.5-1.5B is the real bar. Drop or heavily qualify 'beats every 500M SLM.'

NEVER report only active params and silently claim the 500M class — that is exactly the iso-size objection, and it is contradicted by the cited Engram paper itself (which compares iso-TOTAL and iso-FLOP). Any active-only headline must be paired with the total in the same sentence/table.

Report THREE numbers per model everywhere, mirroring Engram Sec 3.1: total params (incl. embedding), active params / per-token FLOPs, and on-disk footprint in bytes at training precision AND at INT4/INT8 (the axis Gemma3-270M competes on). SLM reviewers weight footprint; the 0-FLOP argument does not answer it, since the table is stored weights (Engram even offloads such tables to host DRAM/NVMe).

If keeping any sizeable table, run and report an ISO-TOTAL ablation: a dense ~1B Kazakh model trained on the same tokens vs the 500M+table model, both at ~1B total. The paper's real contribution is 'memory beats dense compute at iso-total, iso-data' — this is the claim Engram makes and the one a reviewer will demand; winning it is far stronger than beating a 500M model.

Precisely define what the '500M backbone' includes (embedding in or out) in the paper, because Engram's P_tot excludes vocab/LM-head while on-disk total includes them — pick one convention, state it, and keep it consistent so totals are reproducible from config.json.
open_questions: What exact hidden size / layer count / vocab does the '500M backbone' assume? Needed to compute the embedding contribution (50K x d) and thus the exact total; determines how much table budget remains under a 600M cap.

Is the target claim framed on capability-per-FLOP (active axis, favorable) or capability-per-footprint (total axis, unfavorable)? The paper must commit to one primary axis in the abstract; the two lead to opposite comparator sets.

Does a small Engram table (~100-160M, the <=600M-total budget) still deliver the n-gram/knowledge-retrieval gains on Kazakh, or do those gains require the ~512M scale? Engram's log-linear memory-scaling curve suggests smaller tables give proportionally smaller gains — needs a Kazakh-specific slot-count sweep before fixing the size.

On a DENSE (non-MoE) backbone, does Engram's rho-allocation law even transfer? The U-shape was measured against MoE experts (P_sparse from unselected experts); a dense model has no such budget, so the optimal Engram fraction for a dense Kazakh SLM is unvalidated and should be measured directly.

gapFills.area: Kazakh tokenizer fertility vs. byte premium vs. data quantity as the dominant lever for Kazakh SLM (<=600M) accuracy

findings.claim: The exact Kazakh (Cyrillic) byte premium relative to English is 1.76x measured on NLLB parallel text and 1.88x on FLORES-200 (byte_coef_nllb=1.7646, byte_coef_flores=1.8764; English=1.0 by definition). Crucially the premium is script-driven, NOT morphology-driven: each Kazakh Cyrillic character costs ~1.80 UTF-8 bytes (bytes_per_char_nllb=1.7977 vs English 1.0034), while Kazakh uses slightly FEWER characters than English for content-matched text (char_coef_nllb=0.9751 < 1.0) because agglutination compresses meaning. So byte premium ≈ 0.975 chars × 1.80 bytes/char ≈ 1.76.
findings.numbers: kaz_cyrl byte premium 1.7646 (NLLB) / 1.8764 (FLORES-200); bytes/char 1.7977; char coef 0.9751; English reference 1.0
findings.relevance: This is the exact Kazakh-specific number missing from the literature. It shows the corpus is ~1.76-1.88x byte-inflated relative to English purely due to Cyrillic 2-byte encoding, and that morphology does NOT inflate character count. It quantifies exactly how byte-inflated the ~9-10B-token budget is when compared to English on a byte-equity basis.
findings.source: catherinearnett/byte-premium-tool (all_merged_20240223.tsv, GitHub) + arXiv 2403.00686 'A Bit of a Problem: Measurement Disparities in Dataset Sizes across Languages', Arnett/Chang/Bergen, SIGUL 2024

findings.claim: Because the Kazakh byte premium is entirely script-driven, the planned Latin-script transition (~2031) would nearly HALVE it: Latin Turkic languages sit near English — Turkish (tur_latn) byte premium = 1.044 and Azerbaijani (azj_latn) = 1.076, versus Cyrillic Kazakh 1.76. Other Cyrillic Turkic languages confirm the script effect: Kyrgyz 1.964, Tatar 1.855, Bashkir 2.272, Russian 1.823.
findings.numbers: tur_latn 1.044; azj_latn 1.076; kaz_cyrl 1.765; kir_cyrl 1.964; tat_cyrl 1.855; bak_cyrl 2.272; rus_cyrl 1.823
findings.relevance: Directly relevant to the arXiv paper: a Latin-script Kazakh tokenizer would cut byte premium from ~1.76 to ~1.05, roughly halving effective data inflation and compute per unit content — a concrete, quantified tokenizer/script contribution independent of fertility.
findings.source: catherinearnett/byte-premium-tool (all_merged_20240223.tsv, byte_coef_nllb column)

findings.claim: arXiv 2411.14198 finds tokenizer fertility and morphology explain almost none of the cross-lingual performance gap. A regression using tokens-per-word (fertility) and word length as predictors had adjusted R²=0.021 (2.1% of variance). MorphScore (morphological alignment) had NO significant correlation with perplexity: F(1,13)=0.323, p=0.580. Rényi entropy (tokenization quality) explained R²=0.030 vs 0.100 for morphological type, full model R²=0.144. Agglutinative languages had only 3.5% longer sequences on average.
findings.numbers: fertility+word-length adjusted R²=0.021; MorphScore F(1,13)=0.323, p=0.580; Rényi entropy R²=0.030; morph-type R²=0.100; full model R²=0.144; +3.5% sequence length
findings.relevance: This is the paper's central counter-evidence to a 'fertility<2.0 as top accuracy lever' claim. If fertility explains only ~2% of variance, driving it from 2.0 to <2.0 is not a first-order accuracy move; it is an efficiency/context move.
findings.source: arXiv 2411.14198 'Why do language models perform worse for morphologically complex languages?', Arnett & Bergen (html full text)

findings.claim: arXiv 2411.14198 shows the gap is data-quantity driven once byte-premium-adjusted: 'accounting for byte premiums by scaling training data reduces most of the variance previously accounted for by morphological type,' and after byte-premium scaling the performance gap becomes statistically insignificant. Conclusion quote: 'no language is harder or easier for a language model to learn on the basis of its morphological typology. Differences in performance can be attributed to disparities in dataset size.' Byte premiums reach up to 5x for extreme scripts (Khmer at 3 bytes/char).
findings.numbers: gap becomes non-significant after byte-premium scaling (reported t(137.36)=1.180); byte premiums up to 5x vs English
findings.relevance: This is the load-bearing source behind the question's thesis: the binding constraint is byte-premium-adjusted DATA QUANTITY, not tokenizer fertility. Supports reframing the paper's tokenizer claim to necessary-but-not-sufficient.
findings.source: arXiv 2411.14198 (html full text)

findings.claim: Kazakh's data-quantity constraint is severe and quantified: in the XLM-R / Common Crawl corpus the Kazakh subcorpus is 117x smaller than English and 5.8x smaller than Turkish. Combined with the 1.76x byte premium, the effective (content-equity) Kazakh data deficit is even larger than the raw ratio implies.
findings.numbers: Kazakh CC subcorpus 117x smaller than English; 5.8x smaller than Turkish
findings.relevance: Names the actual binding constraint for a Kazakh SLM. The ~9-10B token budget looks reasonable in tokens but represents a small amount of unique content that is further byte-inflated; maximizing unique/clean content and cross-lingual (Turkic/Russian) transfer matters more than shaving fertility below 2.0.
findings.source: arXiv 2411.14198 / arXiv 2403.00686 (Arnett/Chang/Bergen)

findings.claim: SozKZ (the referenced from-scratch Kazakh SLM) empirically corroborates that a great tokenizer does not buy accuracy: SozKZ-600M uses a dedicated ByteLevel-BPE 50K tokenizer with a 2-3x fertility advantage over multilingual tokenizers, trained on ~9B Kazakh tokens (15.3:1 data:param), yet scores only MC QA 30.3% / Belebele 27.0% / SIB-200 25.5% — LOSING to Qwen2.5-0.5B (MC QA 31.5% / Belebele 30.0%) which tokenizes Kazakh ~5x worse. Best tokenizer, no accuracy win.
findings.numbers: SozKZ-600M: MC QA 30.3%, Belebele 27.0%, SIB-200 25.5%; Qwen2.5-0.5B: MC QA 31.5%, Belebele 30.0%, SIB-200 19.1%; SozKZ fertility advantage 2-3x; data:param 15.3:1
findings.relevance: Direct Kazakh-domain evidence that fertility is not the dominant accuracy lever — a from-scratch model with an excellent Kazakh tokenizer still loses to an off-the-shelf model with terrible Kazakh fertility. Strongest single corroboration that the qymyzlm/KazLLM-v2 headline tokenizer claim needs hedging.
findings.source: arXiv 2603.20854 'SozKZ: Training Efficient Small Language Models for Kazakh from Scratch' (html) + Table 6 in arXiv 2603.27859

findings.claim: KazByte quantifies the fertility problem the tokenizer solves but frames it as an EFFICIENCY/context lever, not an accuracy lever: the Qwen2.5 tokenizer splits one inflected Kazakh word ('from your act of running') into 10-12 BPE tokens ≈ 5x a comparable English word; expected English fertility E[f(w)] ≈ 1.3 tokens/word while Kazakh is 'much higher.' KazByte presents its byte-level adapter as a research proposal with NO empirical accuracy results yet.
findings.numbers: one Kazakh word -> 10-12 Qwen tokens ≈ 5x English; English fertility ≈1.3 tok/word; no empirical benchmark deltas reported
findings.relevance: Confirms the 5x tokenizer tax is real and worth fixing for tokens-per-FLOP and context length, but that even a dedicated fertility-focused proposal has no accuracy evidence — reinforcing 'necessary but not sufficient.'
findings.source: arXiv 2603.27859 'KazByte: Adapting Qwen models to Kazakh via Byte-level Adapter' (html)

findings.claim: Counter-evidence that tokenizer quality is NOT irrelevant (the other side): Parallel Tokenizers (arXiv 2510.06128) shows improving fertility 1.89 -> 1.57 and parity 1.14 -> 1.07 yielded downstream gains of +0.92/1.28/0.72/1.22 F1 at 100/50/10/1% training-data levels. Effect is real but small (~1 F1), consistent with fertility being a second-order lever, largest in low-data regimes.
findings.numbers: fertility 1.57 vs 1.89; parity 1.07 vs 1.14; downstream +0.72 to +1.28 F1
findings.relevance: Keeps the finding balanced: pushing fertility below 2.0 gives modest, real downstream gains (especially valuable in Kazakh's low-data regime) but not the multi-point KazMMLU jump a headline 'top accuracy lever' claim would need.
findings.source: arXiv 2510.06128 'Parallel Tokenizers: Rethinking Vocabulary Design for Cross-Lingual Transfer' (html)

recommendations: Reframe the paper's tokenizer contribution as necessary-but-not-sufficient. Its verified benefits are (a) tokens-per-FLOP — more content fits in the fixed ~1x A100 compute budget — and (b) 2-3x longer effective context, NOT a direct KazMMLU accuracy lever. Do NOT headline 'fertility<2.0 raises accuracy'; the evidence (2411.14198 adjusted R²=0.021 for fertility; SozKZ's excellent tokenizer losing to Qwen2.5-0.5B) does not support it.

Keep a fertility target below ~2.0, but justify it on efficiency/context grounds and cite the modest downstream gain (~1 F1 in low-data regimes, Parallel Tokenizers 2510.06128), not as the primary accuracy driver. This survives peer review; a strong causal accuracy claim would not.

Treat byte-premium-adjusted DATA QUANTITY/quality as the binding constraint and say so explicitly. Report the corpus in byte-premium-adjusted terms: with a 1.76x Kazakh byte premium and Kazakh CC being 117x smaller than English (5.8x smaller than Turkish), the ~9-10B tokens is efficiency-comfortable but content-limited. Prioritize maximizing unique, deduplicated Kazakh content and cross-lingual (Turkic/Russian) transfer over further tokenizer polish.

Add the missing causal ablation as a genuine paper contribution: hold data and architecture fixed and vary tokenizer fertility (e.g. ~3.5 multilingual vs ~2.0 vs <1.7 dedicated), then measure the KazMMLU/TUMLU delta. No published Kazakh-specific fertility->accuracy ablation exists; producing one would let the paper make a defensible, quantified claim instead of an assumed one.

Make the script-driven byte premium a distinct, quantified contribution: Kazakh Cyrillic byte premium 1.76x is almost entirely UTF-8 encoding (1.80 bytes/char), and a Latin orthography would cut it to ~1.05 (Turkish 1.044, Azerbaijani 1.076). Tie this to the ~2031 Latin transition to show how much effective data/compute a script change alone would recover — orthogonal to fertility.

Recompute the data-vs-compute allocation on a byte-premium-adjusted (Chinchilla-style) basis. If content quantity is the binding constraint, spend the marginal compute/effort on more and cleaner data plus transfer, not on driving fertility from 2.0 to 1.6, which the evidence says returns ~1 F1 at most.
open_questions: No published Kazakh-specific ablation isolates tokenizer fertility (2.0 vs <2.0) -> KazMMLU accuracy with data/architecture held fixed; the causal 'fertility is a top accuracy lever' claim is therefore unverified in the literature and is the single most important missing experiment.

How much of the 1.76x Kazakh byte premium a dedicated 50K tokenizer at fertility ~2.0 actually absorbs into tokens (byte->token conversion for Kazakh) is not measured in the literature — this determines how byte-inflated the 9-10B-token budget really is in token (vs byte) terms.

2411.14198's central results are on perplexity/LM loss across languages; whether the 'data-quantity, not morphology/fertility' conclusion transfers cleanly to few-shot KazMMLU accuracy specifically is plausible but not directly demonstrated for Kazakh.

The exact test statistic for the byte-premium-scaled gap in 2411.14198 (reported as t(137.36)=1.180 with p=0.077) appears internally inconsistent in the extracted text; the qualitative conclusion (gap becomes non-significant after byte-premium scaling) is solid but the precise p-value should be re-checked against the published table before citing.

gapFills.area: Novelty check — has any 2026 preprint implemented morpheme/suffix-level conditional memory, and do Lngram or X-gram subsume the proposed morpheme-keyed-Engram contribution?

findings.claim: As of submission (July 2026) NO preprint keys conditional memory by morphological units. A terminology trap exists: every Engram-lineage paper says 'suffix n-gram', but 'suffix' means the trailing TOKEN IDs of the context sequence (last-k tokens, exact longest-match), NOT linguistic morphological suffixes. This is confirmed verbatim in Engram, Memory Grafting ('suffix n-grams ending at x_{b,t}', token-ID tuples), X-gram, and Tensorizing Engram ('suffix n-grams ending at the current token via token indices'). The morpheme-keyed contribution therefore remains genuinely unoccupied, but the naming collision is a reviewer landmine.
findings.numbers: Engram arXiv 2601.07372; Memory Grafting 2605.20948; X-gram 2604.21724; Tensorizing Engram 2606.08347 — all use sequence-suffix token-ID keys, zero morphological segmentation
findings.relevance: The paper's crux ('morpheme-keyed') survives, but the abstract/intro MUST explicitly disambiguate 'morphological-suffix keys' from the field's existing 'sequence-suffix n-grams' or reviewers will read the contribution as already-done.
findings.source: arXiv 2601.07372 (Engram / Conditional Memory via Scalable Lookup); 2605.20948 (Memory Grafting); 2606.08347 (Tensorizing Engram)

findings.claim: Lngram does NOT subsume the morpheme-keyed contribution: it learns latent binary discrete symbols from hidden states via hard-threshold binarization (b=1[z>0], d channels split into R routes of M=4 bits => K=2^M symbols per route), then does temporal n-gram lookup over these LEARNED symbols. It is purely latent/self-learned, has no linguistic/morpheme keys, and is evaluated ONLY on English NLP + vision-language/VLA — never on agglutinative or multilingual text. Its edge over Engram is modest: +0.63pp average (0.5288 vs Engram 0.5225) on a 22B MoE trained on 35B tokens; injected at layers 2 and 12 of 24, ~0.5B params reallocated, <10% activated-param overhead, decode ~6.7% slower.
findings.numbers: arXiv 2605.24869, submitted 2026-05-24; M=4 bits/route; Lngram avg 0.5288 vs Engram 0.5225 (+0.63pp) vs MoE 0.5146 (+1.42pp) at 22B/35B tokens; domain-adapt Qwen3-1.7B +5.54pp BDD
findings.relevance: Lngram competes with the MOTIVATION ('remove tokenizer-ID dependence') but not the mechanism. Reframe morpheme keys as the linguistically-grounded, interpretable, zero-training-signal alternative to Lngram's learned binarization — and note Lngram's gains are English-only and untested on the vowel-harmony/allomorphy that motivates morpheme keys.
findings.source: arXiv 2605.24869 (Lngram: N-gram Conditional Memory in Latent Space)

findings.claim: X-gram does NOT subsume morpheme keys either — its keys are pure token IDs (Qwen3-0.6B vocab, 151,936); the novelty is refining retrieved 1-gram vectors into variable-length local features via multi-scale depthwise SwiGLU ShortConv (kernels {3,5,7} inter-layer, {3,5} attention-value), not any linguistic unit. BUT it is the strongest SMALL-scale n-gram-memory result and directly overlaps the ≤600M target: +4.4pt over vanilla backbone (48.5 vs 44.7 avg) and +3.2 over Engram (47.2) at 0.73B; up to 49.5 at 4x config; 50.8 at 1.15B (+2.3 over Engram); ~1.00-1.02x FLOP overhead. No morphology/multilingual/Turkic evaluation.
findings.numbers: arXiv 2604.21724; 0.73B: X-gram 48.5 vs baseline 44.7 (+4.4), Engram 47.2 (+3.2), MoRT 45.8, Retoken 45.0; 1.15B: 50.8 vs baseline 47.4; val PPL 17.702 vs 18.420 w/o ShortConv
findings.relevance: X-gram is a mandatory small-scale baseline to beat/cite; its +4.4/+3.2 margins at 0.73-1.15B are the number your Kazakh morpheme-keyed variant will be measured against. It threatens the 'better n-gram features' pitch, not the morpheme claim.
findings.source: arXiv 2604.21724 (Beyond N-gram: Data-Aware X-gram Extraction for Efficient Embedding Parameter Scaling); code github.com/Longyichen/X-gram

findings.claim: The closest existing work to 'morpheme + Engram' is TOBA LM (Adaptive Engram Memory System for Indonesian/Batak/Minangkabau), but it does NOT actually key by morphemes: it applies UNMODIFIED DeepSeek Engram on a syllable-tokenized vocabulary (2,843 units), computing E2gram=Lookup(x_{t-1},x_t) and E3gram=Lookup(x_{t-2},x_{t-1},x_t) over token indices, then INTERPRETS the 2-gram/3-gram pathways post-hoc as 'capturing morpheme structures' and 'morphophonological dependencies'. No morphological segmenter/analyzer is integrated and it does not claim morpheme-level memory as a novel contribution.
findings.numbers: arXiv 2603.10006 (Feb 17 2026); 1.2B params (36 blocks, d=1280, 20 heads); Engram table 500,000 x 768; syllable vocab 2,843; loss 6.4 -> 1.7996 in 12,973 steps
findings.relevance: This partly stakes the 'Engram for a morphologically rich, agglutinative language' narrative, so 'first Engram on morphology-rich language' is NOT a safe claim. The defensible, still-unoccupied novelty is EXPLICIT morphological-segmenter-keyed memory (running a segmenter to build keys) — which TOBA does not do — plus vowel-harmony/allomorph key normalization and Turkic eval.
findings.source: arXiv 2603.10006 (Adaptive Engram Memory System / TOBA LM)

findings.claim: Morpheme-aware TOKENIZERS/segmenters for Turkic already exist and are recent, so morpheme keys are technically feasible to source — but none feeds a conditional-memory table, leaving morpheme-keyed memory open. Morpheus (Turkish, reversible neural morpheme-boundary tokenizer) reports MorphScore macro-F1 0.61 (vs ~0.32 for subword family), BPC 1.425, ~19% less GPU memory than 64K subword tokenizers; MorphBPE and a Kazakh-specific CSE-guided morphology-aware segmentation framework also exist.
findings.numbers: Morpheus arXiv 2606.18717 (June 2026), MorphScore F1 0.61, BPC 1.425; MorphBPE arXiv 2502.00894; Kazakh CSE-guided framework MDPI Information 17(2):128; VerChol arXiv 2603.05883
findings.relevance: Reviewer risk: 'why not just morpheme-tokenize (Morpheus/MorphBPE) instead of morpheme-keying a memory?' Pre-empt by arguing the memory adds 0-FLOP sparse capacity ON TOP of tokenization and decouples rare-morpheme knowledge from the compute path — and consider using such a segmenter as the key source, citing it.
findings.source: arXiv 2606.18717 (Morpheus); arXiv 2502.00894 (MorphBPE); MDPI Information 17(2):128 (Turkic/Kazakh CSE-guided segmentation)

findings.claim: The memory-augmentation field is confirmed to move roughly monthly and NONE of the variants touches Turkic/Kazakh/agglutinative evaluation: Engram (Jan 2026, scaled to 27B) -> X-gram (Apr) -> Lngram + Memory Grafting (May) -> Tensorizing Engram (Jun 6, CP-decomposition latent sharing) -> Morpheus (Jun). Adjacent memory-layer lines (UltraMemV2 scaling to 120B, arXiv 2508.18756; Mixture of Chapters, arXiv 2603.21096; Mixture of Lookup Key-Value Experts, arXiv 2512.09723) are all token-ID / learned-slot keyed, no morphology.
findings.numbers: Tensorizing Engram 2606.08347 (Jun 6 2026): TN-gram 48M params val BPB 1.071 vs Engram 60M/1.070 at 18 layers; UltraMemV2 2508.18756 (120B); Mixture of Chapters 2603.21096
findings.relevance: Confirms the novelty-check's 'crowded, monthly-moving' concern and justifies re-running this exact search at camera-ready. As of now the morpheme axis is still unclaimed, but a morpheme/latent-unit variant could land any month — ship soon and keep the search query on file.
findings.source: arXiv 2606.08347 (Tensorizing Engram); 2508.18756 (UltraMemV2); 2603.21096 (Mixture of Chapters); 2512.09723 (Mixture of Lookup Key-Value Experts)

findings.claim: VERDICT: Neither Lngram nor X-gram subsumes the morpheme-keyed-Engram contribution, and no 2026 preprint has implemented morpheme/suffix-level (morphologically-segmented) conditional memory. However, three forces erode the raw 'first-of-kind' framing and must be answered in-paper: (a) the 'suffix n-gram' naming collision, (b) TOBA LM already applying Engram to an agglutinative language with morpheme-flavored framing, and (c) Lngram's 'learn your own lookup units, drop tokenizer IDs' motivation directly rivaling the argument for hand-specified keys. The surviving, defensible novelty = EXPLICIT morphological-segmentation-keyed memory + vowel-harmony/allomorph-normalized keys + first Turkic/Kazakh benchmarked memory augmentation.
findings.numbers: 3 competing preprints to distinguish (Lngram 2605.24869, X-gram 2604.21724, TOBA 2603.10006); morpheme-KEYED memory count in literature = 0
findings.relevance: Directly answers the question: the crux holds, but the contribution statement should shift from 'first conditional memory for morphology' to 'first explicit morpheme-segmentation-keyed, allomorphy-aware memory, validated on Turkic', with head-to-head vs X-gram (small-scale SOTA) and an ablation vs Lngram-style learned units.

recommendations: Reframe the contribution precisely: NOT 'first conditional memory for a morphologically rich language' (TOBA LM 2603.10006 already applied vanilla Engram to Batak/Minang and framed 2/3-gram pathways as morpheme-capturing), but 'first memory whose keys are produced by an explicit morphological segmenter, normalized for Kazakh vowel-harmony allomorphy, and benchmarked on Turkic'. That triad is unoccupied.

Kill the naming collision up front: add one sentence in the intro/related-work defining that prior 'suffix n-grams' (Engram, X-gram, Memory Grafting, Tensorizing Engram) are trailing TOKEN IDs of the sequence, whereas your keys are morphological suffixes/stems from a segmenter. Without this, reviewers will assume subsumption.

Make X-gram (2604.21724) the primary small-scale baseline, not just Engram: it posts the strongest sub-1.2B numbers (+4.4 over backbone, +3.2 over Engram at 0.73B; 50.8 at 1.15B). Report your Kazakh morpheme-keyed variant against a re-implemented X-gram at matched ≤600M scale, and ideally combine ShortConv refinement WITH morpheme keys (they are orthogonal — X-gram refines vectors, you change the keys).

Add an explicit ablation vs Lngram-style learned latent units: implement a hard-threshold-binarization (M=4 bits/route) latent-key head alongside morpheme keys and show that on agglutinative Kazakh the linguistically-grounded morpheme keys match or beat learned units at lower cost / higher interpretability — this neutralizes Lngram's 'drop tokenizer IDs' motivation on the one axis (morphology) where it was never tested.

Consider sourcing keys from an existing Turkic morpheme segmenter (Morpheus 2606.18717, MorphBPE 2502.00894, or the Kazakh CSE-guided framework MDPI Information 17(2):128) and cite it, both to strengthen rigor and to pre-empt the 'why not just morpheme-tokenize?' objection — argue the memory adds 0-FLOP sparse capacity for rare morphemes on top of tokenization.

Re-run this exact novelty search at camera-ready (the field moves monthly: Engram Jan -> X-gram Apr -> Lngram/Memory Grafting May -> Tensorizing Engram/Morpheus Jun). Keep a saved query for 'morpheme/morphological-segmentation-keyed conditional memory' + '2606/2607/2608'; a morpheme or latent-unit variant landing first would collapse the first-of-kind claim.
Ship soon. The morpheme axis is currently unclaimed but the surrounding space is saturated and accelerating; the defensible window is measured in months, not quarters.
open_questions: Does an even more recent (late-June/July 2026) preprint outside the top search results already introduce morpheme- or subword-morphology-keyed memory? Search was thorough but arXiv indexing lags days-to-weeks; must re-verify at submission.

Would combining morpheme keys with X-gram's SwiGLU ShortConv refinement compound gains, and is that combination itself novel enough to be the headline (morpheme-keyed + conv-refined) rather than morpheme-keying alone?

Can the paper empirically show morpheme keys beat both (a) TOBA-style syllable-token Engram and (b) Lngram-style learned latent units on Kazakh at ≤600M — the two-front comparison needed to defend the crux — within the ~$264 / 1x A100 compute budget?

Exact per-task Lngram-vs-Engram breakdown is not published (only the +0.63pp average and 'surpasses Engram on 4 of 5 tasks'); if a reviewer demands it, the number may need to be reproduced rather than cited.
